THE TWO WISHES. His Wish. "I wish for a wife," said a youth who had learned That a penny saved is a penny earned; "She must not be too vain or too proud, Too fond of show in a dazzling crowd; I would have her c )mely, and good, and neat, With graces and gifts you rarely meet; Her heart must be tender, her knowledge fair, Her presence must lighten my weight of care. I do not mind if her parse is small, Or whether she has a purse at all, And I crave not beauty, nor set it above The weightier matters of goodness and love." Her Wish. "When I take a husband," a maiden said, "I shall wish a man with a level head; Who does not dwell on dress, and knows That a girl is not made by furbelows ; Who can earn a penny, and save it, too; Who is good and honest, tender and true; Who doea not put mere beauty above The higher blessing of earnest love. I would have his lineage honest and fair, But for his money I do not care, When such a one I chance to see, shall wish him success, if he comes for me." Perhaps these wishes may somewhere meet, In hall or parlour or field or street; For they are worthy who place above Mere show and gewgaws the heart's true love.

SOME FUNNY FRUIT. 'Way down in the orchard there stands an old tree, As crooked an "apple " as ever you'd see; Such buds as it puts forth in bright early spring, And such fruit as its blossoming promises bring! Well, beneath this old apple tree, one sunny day, A grandpa, with paper and briar pipe lay; When, on looking above, lo! what did he see, 'Way up on a branch of this very old tree? Why, a scarlet striped stocking, one little bronze boot. And he knew very well trees ne'er bore such queer fruit Above them a petticoat's white ruffle gleamed: Not at all like an apple tree all this sight seemed! "What's this," exclaimed grandpa, "a strange sight indeed! I'd very much like to secure the rare seed; Why. I believe I behold a round pippin' up there; It's either a pipoin or golden bright hair! "And a rosy checked 'Spitzenberg there, too, I see, Or a very red flashing face, too, it may be, And 'Rusiets' besides! why what marvellous fruits This old apple tree bears; or, are those two bronze boots? "and a scarlet streaked Baldwin'—ah, its pardon I beg If I make a mistake, and its but—a striped leg! Well, well," went on grandpa, "I really don't know But this tree to the great pomological show "Should be sent, for all sights I ever did see"— "Pleae, dranpa, don't stold ; it t'aint apples, it's me!" And like Newton's discovery, down at h:s feet Dropped his answer—a little girl, rosy and sweet, As round as an apple, and blushing and red, Because she'd been "caught" up above " dranpa's head." "Ha, ha!'" then laughed grandpa, to see her affright, "Ha, ha! of this dumpling I'll now have a bite; "For a proof of the pudding's the tasting, you see, And I really must taste what has grown on this tree !" And he kissed her so hard, she was fain to refute His theory of thinking her some fanny fruit!

While admonishinga number of children who had been confirmed recently, Archbishop Gibbons told this story of a little boy in East Baltimore, who was lost a month or two ago, and was taken to the station hoase for the night : " After he was put to bed," said the Archbishop, "he called the officers back and sail be had forgotten to say his pray- ers, and in their presence the little fellow bravely knelt down and recited ' Our Father,' which waq, perhaps, the first ser- mon any of them had heard in along time; certainly it was elf. nest."

_ FCgNT AMERICAN VERDICTS.—A Kansas jury gave the following verdict in a case, where a man died in a state of intoxication: "Death by hanging—round a rum shop."— An Indiana jury recently returned a written verdict of " Blade to penes bi the biler bustin."—" Jury," said a Western judge, "you kin go out and find a verdict. If you can't find one of your own, get the one the last jury used." The jury returned with a verdict of "Suicide in the ninth degree."—A Rhode Island jury were five days debating on a hog case involving seven dollars, and then came in, found the hog not guilty, and recommended both plaintiff and defendant to the mercy of the court—A. Pekin, Illinois, coroner's jury rendcred a very singular verdict, that a man , whose body was foand in the river, came to his death by a blow on the head, "which was given either before or after the drowning." THE PLACE you SPINSTERS.—Women are, or were, so scarce in the mining regions of Utah, that the mere sight of one was sufficient to set the whole camp in commotion. Mark Twain relates how on one occasion, when a calico dress was seen hanging from an emigrant's waggon, the miners crowded around the husband and ordered him to "Fetch her out!" to which command he replied: "She is my wife, gentlemen, she is sick; we have been robbed of money, provisions, everything, by the Indians; we want to rest." "Fetch her out ' We've got to see her." "But gentlemen, the poor thing, she—" "Fetch her out!" Be fetched her out, and they swung their hats, and sent up three rousing cheers and a tiger; and they crowded around and gazed at her, and touched her dress, and listened to her voice with the look of men who listened to a memory rather than a present reality ; and then they collected $2,500 in gold, and gave it to the man, and swung their hats again and gave three more cheers, and went home satisfied. REASONABLE BEASTS —Beasts are undoubtedly possessed of reason, or the power of drawing conch sinus from pre- mises; and this faculty of reason is something altogether different from instinct, and is often exercised in direct oppo- sition to it. "Some years ago there was a dog at Margate which knew the use of money. He used to beg for pence, and take them to a baker to be exchanged for biscuits, at a saop in the narrow hilly lane which is pleased to assume the title of High-street. One day the baker, wishing to see how the dog would behave if he played the animal a prac- tical joke, took his penny, and gave him a burnt biscuit. Neat time that the dog had a penny, he took it to the baker an usual, showed it to him, then went off to another baker who lived nearly opposite. This he afterwards did invari- ably, showing the penny to the baker who had offended him, and then transferring his custom to the rival on the oppo- site side of the narrow street." The whole of these proceed- ings were dictated by pure reason, and instinct had nothing to do with them. It was, in fact, doing on a small scale precisely what the dog's master would have done on a large scale, if a tradesman had taken his money and given a bad article for it. He would have withdrawn his custom from the offender, and given it to another man who he thought would serve him more honestly. MIRACLES: AN ARGUMENT AND A CHALLENGE —Dr. Cox has published in a little work of about 150 pages three articles on miracles that appeared in the Expositor for 1882 and 1883. In a short preface he gives reasons for doing so, and mentions works from which much of his material was drawn. His position will be seen in the following pas- age : —" We of the modern school do not contend, whatever our forefathers may have done, that laws of nature must be , suspended, abrogated, or ravened when a miracle is wrought. I We say that they tilt:int be used by an intelligence infinitely higher than ours, and therefore an intelligence which may I well produce effects most strange and wonderful to us. We I point to the use which man has made of them in a thousae4 different ways—by his use of them changing the face of , the whole world; and we argue that God may use them, for ' worthy ends, still more potently and admirably." He adds "I have read, I think, nearly all that the leading sceptics and agnostics have said on the subject of miracles, but I have never fallen in with any reply to the argument con. 'tamed in the last chapter of this book; and it is high time that such a reply, if reply is to be had, were forthcoming. . .. So far from fearing any candid and sincere op- position, we respectfully invite the friends of reason and truth to drive us from the ground on which we stand if they can. Will any of them take up the challenge ?" The Waterford police have captured a gang of six men and a woman, who have carried on a system of sheep and cattle stealing in the counties of Carlow, Kilkenny, Wex- ford, and Wicklow. They lived a gipsy life, encamping in the fields, professing to follow the avocation of hawkers by day, and stealing at night. Considerable sums of money were found upon the prisoners, who are relations. OXFORD RAM FAIR.—The annual ram fair was held on , Wednesday, in the close adjoining the Swan Brewery, Ox. ford. There were over 1,600 animals penned, but the trade was generally dull, especially for Cotswolds and Hamp- shires. bee Oxfordshire Down ram, from the flock of Mrs. Prat, of [laseley, realised 41 guineas and was purchased by Mr. A. Brassey, of Ley throp; and another was pur- chased for 40 guineas, from the flock of Mr. Gillett, by Sir Charles Mordannt A few weeks ago, a mare, the property of Mr. G. W. Catton, Aberdour, Fife, dropped a fine foal, and shortly afterwards expired, when the idea of putting the foal to a mulch cow was suggested. On this being tried, the cow sternly refused to entertain such an unnatural•looking youngster, and commenced to box and kick. After a little perseverance, however, the plan proved successful. Both are now quite reconciled to each other, and we understand the foal is thriving very well under the care of the foster- mother. A Caren KILLED BY A shocking occurrence has taken place in the Commure of Rush. The servant of a pig-breeder in the Rue de Courbevoie, whilst taking some water to the animals' was accompanied by a little child of two years old, which had been momentarily left in her charge. As the thirsty pigs rushed to the bucket it became upset, and the child was also thr )wn down by one of the creatures, which instantly tore open the stomach of the hapless infant. Before medical assistance had arrived the child had expired, and the Commissiry of Police, after drawing up his report, ordered the ferocious brute to be at once slaughtered.

DECREASED VALUE OF LAND.—The following facts illus- trate the great fall in the value of really good land. At Crowland, in South Lincolnshire, there was lately offered by auction a farm of 70 acres, with farmhouse and build- ing, situate beside the Welland bank. Only one bid was made, amounting to about £32 per acre. The same land a dozen years ago would have readily made £9O per acre. Another farm near Dowslale, in the same alluvial district, was recently sold for a little over £3O per acre. On this farm is some of the finest bullock feeding land in the country. Land lying near to it, and not at alt better, was bought about 15 years ago at over £l.OO per acre. ENSILAGE AND MILK FEVER.—Dr. Pratt, the well-known , Holstein importer and breeder, of Elgin, 111., when in the office of The Farni,rs' R3tiew, Chicago, a few days since, said that since he commenced to feed ensilage, four years ago, he had not lost a single cow by milk fever, wh is be- fore that time he thought himself fortunate if be got a herd of 40 cows through the winter without the loss of one or more from this cause. His theory is that the feeding of ensilage keeps the bowels open and loose, and prevents the tendency to constipation which attends the feeding of dry food, especially if in large quantity, and of stimulating quality for milk production, and which causes a feverish condition of the system, which develops into milk fever at the period of parturition. During the coining season he will increase his silo capacity from SO to 160 tons.

_ BRAN As A MILK PaonucEn.—Bran as it is now made consists almost wholly of the husk of the grain, and is rich in oil and in phosphates. But it is not so good a fond as when the inner hu•lt of the grain is mixed with it, This is sometimes called shorts, and sometimes coarse middlings. This, nye a contemporary, mixed with the bran, makes an excellent food, as it contains Outen and starch. For dairy cows it is the best of all foods for producing milk ; but for butter it is bettor to mix a third part of corn meal or cotton- seed meal, or both, with the bran and middlings. A. moder- ate ration of this mixed food is three pounds daily ; a full ration if six pounds to eight pounds. It will pay to use this even for cows on pasture when rich milk is desired, as it largely increases the quantity of cream in the milk. It may be given to the cows dry, or with come short grass or clover, moistened a little, so hat the meal cannot be swal- lowed without adequate mastication. Tan HARVEST OF 1884.—Mr. Henry F. Moore's seventh annual report on the harvest of the United Kingdom, drawn up for M. B. Estienne's volume on the crops of the world, is as follows:—" The prospect for the English farmer is to day brighter than daring any one of the post seven years. At no time has the year been one of brilliant promise, but it has been a year which could at no time be described as un- favourable. The open winter allowed plenty of scope for all tillage operations, and I shall be surprised if our agricul- tural returns thia year do not show a slight increase in the area of winter wheat. The spring was not unfavourable, but the long drought which occurred late in spring and early in summer—good as it was for wheat—proved slightly adverse to the crow, and almost destroyed the entire plant of turnips and swedes. Since then we have had rain in abundance, accompanied by heavy storms, the latter beating down many of our fields of grain. The rains have given a vigorous growth to most crops, and have saved and brought forward those pieces of roots that survived the drought; but the storms have made it next to impossible to We the reaping mall) ine in many parts of England, and so much of our harvest will hove to he reaped by the sickle. During the past f ntnight the rains have given place to intense heat, and this I has ripened off the corn so qnickly th it in many Darts of the country we are unexpectedly in the midst of the harvest. As usual, I have sent out my inquiries over the whole of the , United Kingdom. I have asked, as for years past, for the lopidions of farmers actaallv engaged in growing the crops ' on the crops of the year, these to be given by numbers- -100 being taken as representing an average crop. An "average crop" also is not taken as representing an un- known quantity. In 1382 I a.ked each of my correspon- dents the question—For the whole time that you have been engaged in actual farming what have you found your aver- age crops to be ? The result was that I received, in a very large number of cases, actual yields for over 30 years on given areas, and from these and numerous other reports I found 29 bushels of wheat, 35 bushels of barley, 40 bushels of oats, five tons of potatoes, 27 bushels of beans, 28 bushels of peas, and LI, tons of hay might well be assumed as the average crops per acre, and so I have adopted these in the returns sent out. Thus, the figures 100 would in each case mean that quantity. In all, 294 replies have been received, against 230 last year and 418 in 1882. They give the fol- lowing as the figure picture of the promise of the crop this year, as compared with those of the previous three years:—

.; .; p. s kci 8 •1., 4 a atl b2A 1881 900 1000 800 980 SO 0 650 1882 92 2 984 105 1 964. 1031 101 6 107 1 1126 1194 1883 91 6 94 0 106 6 120 6 987 107 8 1094 984 108 4 1884 112 2 981 94 3 108 4 881 91•4 78 8 79 1 824 Tbe report speaks in detail of the various crops, and states that several bad reports come on wheat from large wheat- growing districts, while in the barley districts the reports on th t crop are good. The yield of wheat is estimated at about 11 million quarters, leaving us dependent on foreign supply for only 13 million quarters—a smaller quantity than for years past. So far as markets are concerned, the coming year bids fair to see them glutted with wheat, while even lower prices may be expected.

div.head: CROP REPORTS.
div.p: CROP REPORTS.

I WEST LANCASEIRE.—A correspondent who has been through West Lancashire writes :—From Ormskirk to Bun- cough the grain crops are later still, both oats and wheat wanting a few days more sun to bring them ready for cut- ting. There is some excellent wheat in the district, and oats are very fair, but not heavy. Potatoes are looking very well, and there are some very good cabbages. The second crops of grass very fair. After leaving Burscongh there is a run of two or three miles through some very ' heavy crops of grain, consisting of wheat, oats, and some barley; the land is excellent for croping. The barley is about ready for the sickle, but the wheat which is very well fed and of excellent colour wants a week's sun. Oats are only a few days short of maturity. Potatoes are not quite so early here, but they are as vigorous as possible, and are apparently growing fast. Other crops are equally good and forward. Along the Yarrow and the Lostock there will be no grass unhoased after this week. Some of the oats here are fully a fortnight later than those Seuth of the Alt, and have hardly reached to the point of changing colour. The crop is good as a rule, and there is some very good wheat. Potatoes are later still, but looking very well. Along Leyland and Farington mosses there are many good oats and some capital wheat, but both are later, being still , mostly green; oats are only just beginning to turn. There are some capital crops of second clover and a very fair quantity of them. Coming from Preston towards South- port by the West Lancashire line there was still a good deal of unharvested hay between Penwortham bank and the Douglas, and about Much Hoots village and sloping to- wards the Douglas there were several meadows to cat, the grass being heavy. The general features of the country seem to indicate more labour bestowed on laud since the railway was opened and there is ample room for improve- ment. From the Douglas to Southport are seven or eight miles of tillage ground, and this tract stretches as far east- ward. Farther from the shore oats have done well, but along the coast they have hardly done so well as they pro- mised before Whit-week. The wheat crop is an important one here and has done well. By the middle of next week cutting will become more general. Potatoes, of which many are grown here, are looking very well. Other roots look well, and beans promise very well. On the hard land there was a considerable quantity of old meadow hay to get, and good second crops of clover were being got rapidly in. It Is not until one gets a few miles on the south side of South- port that the suspicions of potato disease are aroused. There are several small plots on the sand ground which betray signs of going wrong in this respect. The grain crops are mostly satisfactory. As we reach the water- shed of the Alt there are many fine fields of wheat and oats cut, and cutting is more or less advanced as far as llirkdale, the wheat crops more especially being good, There are some good oats also and potatoes; mangels are generally satisfactory. Everywhere their is an abundance of sweet grass on the pastures, and the eddish crops are promising well. Taking the whole of this large area of moss, sand, clay, and mixed ground, with their various stages of growth and different methods of treating the land, it gives me pleasure to say that the country is as full and as rich as I have seen it for many years past. Cattle and sheep are looking very well and, all round, this cannot be reckoned among the bad years. In some places it is an extraordinary pod one, though some farmers, who have suffered heavily from the grubs spoiling their oats, may justly complain. GENERAL NO ri,..—The editor of the Mark Lane Expre3s writes :—"The combined influence of dry easterly winds

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 23, 1884,
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 23, 1884,

and tropical sunshine arrested at once the progress of fun- goid parasitism, and the grain has been matured and finished in exceptionally good form. All the earliest wheats, whether standing or otherwise, are now in perfect milling condition, and, the straw being unusually free from rubbish, that por- tion of the crop which remains standing—other than the late wheats in backward districts—is now in a position to be cut and carried immediately, whether for stacking or thrashing. With regard to the other cereals, barleys appear to be a variable crop, and oats still more so. In some dis- tricts the barleys are excellent, whilst in others they are poor ; the greatest drawback to the crop, as a whole, would appear to be the irregularity with which all but the earliest sown plants have come to maturity. Spring beans seem to he an absolute failure. Practically all the crops have come together to harvest. The potato crop is not likely to prove a very large one, but it is more free from disease than has been the case for many years past. Throughout the past week the new wheats have been making an appearance in the markets, and whilst the quality and yield is spoken of as variable, the condition is something phenomenal for new wheats." •
THE MANAGEMEN r OF POULTRY.
POULTRY FOR FARMER.

Whatever concerns the success of agriculture is interest- ing and the question of the most suitable breed of poultry for farm yard purposes is one that necessarily commands a large share of attention. We must and do hope great things from the developing of poultry-keeping by cottagers and suburban residents, the one to sell and the other for I their own use; but, whilst remembering these, we must not I forget the farmers, who have opportunities not possessed by I other., both in the way of abandonce of room and in that of ability to feed the fowls much cheaper than could be by any one who has to buy all the food consumed. Therefore, I the question of farm yard fowls is a very important one, I and cannot be neglected, if we wish to discuss the whole question or to improve the numbers and quality of fowls kept. Farm yard poultry is proverbially bad. True it is that a great improvement has taken place during the last few years, and we find on many farm yards really good birds. In those cases the owners have thought it not ; beneath them to give thought and attention to the fowls, I and as a natural result of this they have refused to be con- tent with miserable mongrels, and have got birds that would I really pay for their keep and leave a profit also. Bat in the majority of instances this is not dole, and hence it is we find such poor specimens of domestic poultry in farm yards, and hear the cry that "Poultry does not ply." ; It may be wondered why farmers require any but the ordinary breeds, but that is not difficult to define; as a rule they require good all round fowls, that is, good as layers, yet possible on the table, and also Jitters and mothers. Thus fecundity, size, quality of flesh, and maternal quali- ties hive all to he token into account. And 33 no breed has all these in excess, it is generally found that anyone that has them all, but in moderation, is the best in the long run. Of course, circumstances alter cases, and in some places ' eggs are the first consideration, when such breeds as Minorca, Leghorne, or Andalusians should be kept; or in others tibia fowls, as in Sussex, are desired most of all, I where Dorkings or French are the best varieties. But in the majority of instances the farmer prefers that the birds shall possess both these qualities, even though it be in a modified decree. The object is that not only shall the hens have a good number of eggs, but also both the hens and I the cockerels, when kilhd, shall come up to the market standard in point of quality. Unless the latter is the case, there will be loss when the birds have to be sold, which will perhaps be more than the additional gain from the eggs. Noce of the best laying breeds above named can be called good table fowls, and if they are kept another breed must also, as a rule, be kept. On many farms the fowls are simple, mongrels, bred anyhow, and without regard to needs or profit. There are fortunately a number of breeds which present to U 3 the qualities which are desirable, and of these a few words will not be out of place here. First and foremost we place the Houdans, but they are wanting in one respect, namely, they are non.sitters. This is a want that can be easily remedied in most places, for a few Brahmas or Cochins wilt do all the work, and the eminently good laying and table qualities will amply recompense the trouble which the nonositting involves. Hondens are heavy layers cf large eggs, and are large in body, with meat of a capital quality. Near to the [louden we should place the Leugehan, which is a remarkably good layer of good-sized, white-shelled eggs. The body is large, and the deep breast carries plenty of meat, which is of a beautifully white colour, fine tex- ture, and flavour. Lengehans make good sitters and mothers, and thus can be recommended as really first-rate all. round fowle. We hope shortly to give a fuller descrip- tion of this breed. The Plymouth Rocks are also very good all-round fowle, though not quite equal, we think, to the two already named. It is a breed of American manufacture, and can only be said to be pure in that the type is now fixed, and the birds breed fairly true. It Jr a pretty good layer, but the eggs are small in comparieoa with its size, though •of very rich quality. The frame is large and the bones thick and heavy, giving almost a Cochin appearance, but there is a surprising amount of meat on them, and thi3, in the young fowls, very well placed and fine in flovour. There is something of the turkey appearance about these birds when on the table, and they have sometimes been thought to be turkeys. Another new useful fowl is the Scotch Grey; a good. layer, capital on the table and as a sitter, and, having white legs, is preferred by many for selling as table fowls. In previous articles we have dealt very fully with the question of crossing, showing how first-rate crosses are to be made. Of these, for farm purposes, one of the best is the Hondan„ with the Plymouth Rock. As an interesting ac- count of a valuable cross for farmyard fowl, we give the fol- lowing extract from a letter written by Mr. Jas. Howard, M.P., to a contemporary some time ago. Mr. Howard Bays :—"Nearly twenty years ago I came to the conclusion that we had not got what we may cell an all-round fowl, and I determined to supply the want. From experiments in the breeding of various animals, I came to the conclusion that the two following cardinal points ia the art of breeding had been established From the female parent are de- rived the internal structure, the vital organs, and, in a much greater proportion thou from the male, the constitu- tion, temper, and habits—hence in fowls the laying quali- ties. 2. That from the mile parent is mainly derived the external structure, configuration, and outward characteris- tics—the locomotive peculiarities inclusive. I therefore selected Partridge Cochin pullets (kept separate from their chickenhood) and a black-breasted Game cock with white legs (very rare to be met nowadays). I have bred many thousands of birds from this cross. The result has been, without a single exception, an enlarged Game cock, and a hen with all the laying properties to match. By careful selection of the Cochins, I soon established a breed of clean, white-legged fowls, and having four farm homesteads,l had no trouble about change of blood. I determined to repeat the experiment in the cross, and about ten years ago I mated another white-legged Game cock (obtained for me by Messrs Baily, Mount-street), with other Cochin pullets, and with the same results. I named the breed Tankervilles, as the first Game cock I had came from the Earl of Tankerville. For laying qualities, for activity as foragers, for hardihood, for table purposes, and as mothers, I do not think they can be excelled."

NATIONAL EDUCATION. The report of the Committee of the Privy Council on the proceedings of the Education Department during the past year was issued recently in a Blue Book. In the year ending 31st August, 1883, the inspectors visited 18,510 day schools in England and Wales, to which annual grants were made, containing 27,330 departments under separate head teachers, and furnishing accommodation for 4,670,413 echol ars. There were on the registers of these schools the names of 4,273,304 children, Of whom 1,336,929 were under seven years of age; 2,743,383 between seven and 13; 150,245 between 13 and 14; and 42,747 above 14. Of these scholars 3,705,338 were present on the day of the inspector's visit to their respective schools, and 3,127,214 were, on an average, in daily attendance throughout the year. In the schools in- spected under the Code of 1881 (eight months, September to April), 2,191,955 scholars having made the requisitenum- ber of attendances were qualified to bring grants to their schools, 514,742 (being under seven years of age) without individual examination, and 1,577,213 (above seven) on passing a satisfactory examination in reading, writing, and arithmetic. In the schools inspected under the ;Code of 1883 the number of scholars whose names had been on the school registers for the last 22 weeks of the school year was, in infant schools and classes, 294,707 ; in schools and classes for older scholars, 712,678. No grant was directly payable on the examination of the scholars in the infant schools and classes, but 31,093 being upwards of seven year of age were individually examined in Standards I. and 11., while the number of older scholars presented for examination was 665,279. The returns, therefore, for the whole year show that 2,276,014 were actually presented for individual examination, and while of these 1,483,269 passed the pre. scribed test without failure in any one of the three sub. jecte, 89 14 (89.22) scholars out of every 100 examined passed in reading, 82 03 (8192) in writing, and 77 51 (7727) 'in arithmetic. The figures within brackets show the pro- portion who passed in the previous year. While the in- crease of the population during the year is estimated at 1 35 per cent., the accommodation has increased by 132,123 school places (or 2 91 per cent) ; the scholars on the regis- ters by 83,692 (2.0 per cent.); the average attendance by 112,063 (3.7 per cent ) •, and the number of children indi- vidually examined by 156,610 (or 739 per cent.). The local effort which has resulted in this improvement may be mica- *lured by the continued support derived from voluntary con- tributions (£717,089 from 267,821 subscribers), and by an 1 advance in the contributions from rates to the maintenance of board schools from £808.121 to £840,917. TilLo school- -1 pence have risen from £1,585,928 to £1,659,743. The an. nual Government grants to elementary day schools rose in the Year from £2,393,394 to £2,522,511, or from 15s. 10d. Ito 16s. I,ld. per scholar in average attendance. The night schools examined daring the year were 932 in number ; 28,293 scholars above 12 years of age were, on the average, in attendance each night; 32,937 scholars were qualified by attendance for examination. Of these, 22,546 were actually 1 examined, and out of every 100 scholars so examined, 90 77 , passed in reading, 69.41 in writing, and 46 72 in arithmetic. The inspectors found 37.280 certificated teachers at work in the aided schools which they visited, while the 41 training colleges, from which the supply of such teachers is mainly recruited, were attended in 1883 by 3,138 students. These students, with a few exceptions, and 2,213 acting teachers, were examined for certificates in December last. At mid- summer, 1883, 5,191 were examined for admission to the 1,633 vacancies declared in the training colleges, of whom 3,361 passed creditably, and 1,623 are now in their first year of residence, along with 1,586 students of the second year. The 18,540 elementary day schools in England and Wales, inspected in 1883, provided accommodation in 27,330 de. pertments for 4,670,443 scholars, and 37,280 certificated teaches Were employed in their instruction. The average daily attendance in these schools amounted, as we hive shown, to only 3,127,214. The accommodation in the great proportion of these schools is so much in excess of the number of children attending them that the existing staff of certificated teachers wanld probably be sufficient to meet ' a very large accession to the ranks of their scholars. But even if teaching power is provided for the increased attend- ance, to which we look forward by the employment of ad- ditional assistance, it is probable that the present supply of I certificated teachers will fall short of what will be required to meet the wants of the country at large. There were on the 31,t of December, 1869, 12,842 pupil teachers, 1,236 ' assistant teachers, and 12,027 certificated teachers at work In schools under inspection. These numbers have now risen to 26,428 pupil teachers, 12,390 assistant, and 37,280 certi- ficated teachers; while the pupil teachers in the first year of their service have increased from 3.392 in 1869 to 6,219 in 1883. An addition of 3,224 was made to the number of certificated teachers as the result of the last Christmas exa- mination, when 690 male and 831 female students of the second year, and 260 male and 1,443 female acting teachers obtained places on the class list of candidates for certifi- c ttes. Fourteen students also left after one year's residence. Since the let of May, 1871, moreover, certificates have been granted, without examination, to 1,289 male and 1 868 1 female teachers on whose schools the inspectors have re- ported favourably, while provisional certificates (which ' hold good till the teacher completes his or her 25th year) have been granted to tB5 male and 3,402 female ex-pupil teachers, qualifying them to take charge of small schools, with lees than 60 children in average attendance through- out the year. The large number of pupil teachers who yearly complete their engagement satisfactorily, and cannot be admitted to training colleges for want of room, furnish a valuable supply of teachers for these small schools. The training colleges under inspection in England and Wales, which have been established at a cost of £114,483 to the public purse, and of some £520.272 3s 21d. to the pro- moters, provide accommodation for 3,297 students, and 3,214 are in residence. These colleges can, therefore, at pre- sent furnish a yearly supply of 1,500 teachers who have been trained for two years. This supply would be of itself sufficient to fill up the waste (calculated at 6 per cent.) in a staff of 25,000 teachers. Looking at the number of duly qualified persons who yearly enter the profession through other recognised channels, and to the probable effect of recent changes in the code, in attracting a superior class of teachers from the universities, and in improving the educa- tion of the uncertificated assistant teachers employed by school boards, we see no reason to doubt that, even taking into account the extent to which certificated assistants are now being employed in large schools that have been estab- lished during the last few years, the supply of teachers trained in the existing colleges and in others that will shortly claim annual grants will be found sufficient to meet the requirements of the country. The extent to which the training colleges have contributed to the present supply of efficient teachers he England and Wales is shown by the fact that of 15,368 masters employed in schools reported on last year 9,353, or 60 86 per cent., had been trained for two years; 1,020, or 6 61 per cent., for one year; and 225, or 146 per cent., for less ,than one year, while 4,770, or 31-04 per cent,, were untrained. In like manner, of 21,912 schoolmistresses, 9,379, or 42 80 per cent., had been trained for two years; 992, or 453 per cent., for one year; 203, or 093 per cent., for less than one year, and 11,338, or 51 74 per cent., were untrained. Of the teachers, however, who, from whatever cause, have not attended a training college, a considerable proportion cannot, except in a technical sense of the word, be classed as untrained, having, under the superintendence of some of our best teachers, passed through the pupil teachers'e course, and served as assistants in large schools, before passing the examination for a certificate, and undertaking independent charges. A considerable number of teachers who have not passed through the training col- leges will always be required for service in the small schools throughout the country. The average salary of a certificated master, which in 1870 was £95 12s. 9d., is now £119; that of a schoolmistress was £57 16s. sd. in 1870, and is now £72 Is. 91. In addi- tion to their other emoluments, 6,138 out of 14,827 masters, and 5,317 out of 21,270 mistresses are provided with resi- dences free of rent. These averages are calculated upon the whole of the certificated teachers whether principal or as- sistant. It may be worth while to note here the great and Increasing proportion of female teachers now employed in elementary schools. In 1869, for every 100 teachers of each class, 48 certificated teachers, 60 assistant teachers, and 57 pupil teachers were females. These proportions have in- creased in 1882 to 59 certificated teachers, 68 assistant teachers, and 71 pupil teachers. The number of female pupil teachers in 1869 was 7,273; they now member 18,725, an increase of 157 per cent. The male pupil teachers, who numbered 5,569, have increased to 7,703, or by about 38 per cent. Grants for the maintenance of schools were paid to 1,721 boards in England and to 267 boards in Wales, being an increase of 52 in England and eight in Wales over the number to which grants were paid in 1881.2; the sum paid being £855,812, as against £790,796 in 1881-2. The sum expended by school boards in England during the year under review amounted to £4,272,346, as compared with £3,916,317 in the previous year; and in Wales to £257,895, as compared with £269,456. In England.B 6 per cent., and In Wales 88 per cent, of the current expenditure, including the cost of enforcing attendance at school, is incurred in carrying out the provisions of the Education Acts; 20 per cent. in England, 184 per cent. in Wales in providing school accommodation, and 71.2 per cent. in England, 72 per cent. in Wales in instructing the children. The results of the past year show that the average cost of the maintenance of board schools decreased slightly, and that the ratepayers in England and Wales were called upon to contribute Os. 10. per child less than the average sum contributed in 1875-8 During the same period the average cost of voluntary schools increased from it 13e. qd. to Ll 14e. 101 d., this increase being more than met by an increase in the grant and school fees.

OF AN ECONOMICAL Truax OF MIND.—" Of all the plans for economising space," said a patent lawyer, "the man who has just left this office evolved the funniest. He had a drawing of a sleeping car that he wished me to get patented for him. He thought it was a good thing, that would bit the railroad manager hard, because it nearly doubled the number of births in a car. I saw right away that the beds were ridiculously short. I asked their length. Four feet and a half,' he said, 'and that's plenty long enough. A careful investigation has proved to me that there is really no use in a bed being as long as the person in it. Not one man in fifty ever sleeps straightened out, and women inva- ably draw up their knees, so that they don't require much more than a four-foot bed. It is a discovery of this fact as to sleeping that I wish to protect by the patent. I should stick up in each compartment a printed notice explaining that the middle of the car is much safer than the sides, and, therefore, the closer their legs are hauled in toward the centre partition, where their heads are to be, the less they are liable to be hurt by collision." The lawyer did not take the case. He also declined that of a man who wanted to patent a spring bottom for coffins, the idea being that, if people were ready to buy easy couches for their bedrooms, they would be still more desirous of comfort in their graves.

div.head: SEASONABLE HINTS.
div.p: SEASONABLE HINTS.

Some time ago we mentioned that the sexes should be separated in the stock of chickens, and now it will be found advisable to separate the young pullets also, putting them into stocks of about twenty in each house, as they are found to thrive much better than when kept in larger numbers. If they can be scattered about in groups widely apart they will thrive all the more, and the alvantages of putting the young stock on the fields after harvest will be found in the extra size and stamina obtained by them. If kept in very large numbers they worry each other, and do not thrive so well, retarding both their growth and the time when they will begin to lay.

EARLY LIFE OF THE QUEEN OF ROUMANIA.—Rushing down the stairs one day with her habitat impetuosity, she slipped and would have fallen to the bottom had not a gentleman who was ascending at the same moment caught Der in his arms. It was a fall laden with unexpected con- sequences, for she had fallen into the arms of her future husband. But as yet she was not to rest in them for good. The young princess evinced an almost savage dislike to matrimony, and in response to all proposals of marriage made to her, replied "I do not want to marry unless I can be Queen of Roumania." The reply seemed a very safe one in those days,when Roumania had but just been founded, and only as a principality, under the boyard rule of the worthless Prince Couxa. She little realised that later she would be taken at her word. Meantime she went home again to Wied, and resumed her offices in the sick room and her studies; for until she was 25, indeed until she married, Princess Elizabeth never ceased to take lessons

Meanwhile E ,ropean public events were changing, a change destined to affect the "wild rosebud of Wied," as her friends loved to call her. In 1868, Prince Charles of Hohenzollern had been chosen ruler of Roumania, and in the autumn of the next year he came to the Rhine to remind the Princess Elizabeth of her desire to tale over that kingdom. Even so it was a little while before she could consent to resign her fiercely•cherished independence; but she yielded, and in November of the same year he took her to his home amid the Carpathians, after she had been married to him four times over, namely, according to the German civil code, ac- cording to the Lutheran (her own religion), according to the Roman Catholic (which is, his), and according to the rites of the Greek Church (which is the creed of their king- dom).—By Helen Zimmern, in the " Century,"

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

ONIONS.—Those sown this time last year should be suffi- ciently matured to be taken up. After being exposed to the scan for two or three days they may be stored in any dry airy position. They should not be exposed to the rain after being taken out of the soil, and it is as well to place them on boards or old hamper lids, so that they can be readily removed under cover. Autumn sown onions are not so liable to attacks from grubs as those sown in the spring, hence it becomes a matter of consideration whether we ought not to increase this sowing so as to be independent of the others till the new year. There is no reason why they should not maintain their qualities up to then. According to reports from various districts there are very few perfect heads of spring sown onions this season, and some growers have lost their entire crop. The onion is at all times a gross ieeder, consequently the land must be well supplied with well-decayed manure. For light soil we would prefer that of the cow, horse dung being more suitable for tenacious, heavy soils. After the ground is mannred and dug, it may I remain so for a few days if it has beerr turned up lumpy. When it becomes thoroughly dry it should be watered at night, and in the morning all will crumble sufficiently fine to form a seed bed. A dozen gallons of water will cover a few square yards, and if there is no rain it is much better to resort to it than wait many days, as it makes a difference In sowing at this time much more than at spring. The sowing may be made broad-east or in drills quarter of an inch deep and eight inches distant. A south aspect should be selected. The varieties of Tripoli are the most suitable for autumn sowing, and seedsmen, if requested, will mix the various sorts so that the cottager may have half-a-dozen kinds out of the one packet of seed. Shallots have com- pleted their growth, and should be treated similar to the onion as regards drying and storing. When thormghly dry and divested of any loose coatings, they may be tied in paper bags and occasionally examined to see if any are decaying and injuring the others. Many experienced growers of the shallot maintain that small offsets will yield as good a crop as the finest bulbs. We would therefore select them out at the time crop is stored, and place them by themselves.

FRONT GARDEN.—Attention should be paid to the tying of Dahlia shoots, as they are easily injured by the wind or heavy rain, which may snap some of the beat shoots off un- expectedly. Instead of running a string round the whole of them, we prefer to pat one to each of the main shoots, and tie it round the stake fixed in the centre. The common error of" bundling them up" must be avoided.—Geraniums: Any of these which may be growing out of proportion, or have some of their shoots extending beyond their allotted space, should be taken off with from four to six joints, ac- cording to the firmness of the wood, as soft, sappy pieces will shrivel up and die. The centre of the plants may be also searched for a few suitable pieces for cuttings, which now form roots freely, and make good plants to keep through the winter. In preparing the cuttings the leaves should be cat from the two lower joints, and the bag, of the cuttings should be cat clean just below the lowest joint. The cut- tings may be now left for a few hours till the wounds are healed, when they may be inserted in pots, which are best outside, or planted in a sunny position in the open ground. They require but little water before roots are formed, whether they are in pots or in the ground, as the sap they contain will maintain vitality for several days. TEE WINDOW.—The cineraria is usually raised from seeds and offsets or suckers, which spring from the base of the dead flower stem. If these are carefully removed they will have as many roots as will fill a small pot in which they should be placed. The potting material should be light soil, composed of loam, leaf, mould, and sands, and if they cannot be accommodated with a frame, they should be placed in some shady corner and supplied with a sprink- ling of water every evening in imitation of a slight shower. Chrysanthemums are made to adorn many windows in autumn. They are naturally tall, but by inserting cuttings late, or better still for the cottager, by layering, they are made eligible window plants it suitable kinds are only selected. Fur layering a few small pots should be filled with soil made moderately firm, and plunged into the earth half their depth. A suitable branch is selected, and re- ceives a twist at the point where It can be brought in con- tact with the soil in the pot. By the assistance of a peg it is held down. The peg should pass through the hole in the pot into the soil below to insure a firm hold; and the point at which the shoot is bent should be covered with soil, so as to induce it to root quicker. Each shoot should have a stake to support it, as the twisting will have weakened so much that the slightest wind might break it at that point.

Bonus DIPLOMAS.—A Philadelphia correspondent says the defunct Medical University of Philadelphia, which has caused great annoyance and trouble by sellng bogus dip- lomas, has reappeared. The English Consul at Philadel- phia, Mr. Clipperton, states that he is in receipt of letters from various parts of Great Britain asking far information about the standing of the college and to what extent its diplomas are accepted. The United States Government has done all in its power to stop the traffic in diplomas, by cancelling the charter of the college and closing it. If (the correspondent adds) imposters are still committing fraud upon the public, through agencies in England, they should be prosecated by the British authorities. THE BRITISH ASSOCI &TION'S VISIT TO CANADA.,—EIIbOTate preparations have been made at Montreal for the visit of the British Association to Canada this month, Montreal having been selected two years ago as the place of meeting for 1834. The success of the gathering is now more than assured, and the earliest fruits of this effort to bring British scientists together in her Majesty's Trace-Atlantic dominions are very satisfactory. Not only will there be a large attendance of members from these islands, but the association this year will have a very large accession to its strength in the shape of subscribers belonging to the Dominion, and the attend- ance of British and Canadian members promises to surpass the number which generally attends the meetings of the association in the mother country. In anticipation of the meeting at Montreal, a considerable number of members have already gone to Canada with the view of enjoying a holiday there before the business of the association com- mences, and to-day many more members will set sail from Liverpool. At Montreal a strong reception committee has been formed, whilst the Dominion Government has liberally voted £5,000 to cover the expense which will be incurred in Montreal in connection with the visit. Reception commit- tees have also been organised at Toronto and Winnipeg, both of which places will be visited in due course by mem• bets of the association ; and altogether a most cordial wel- come is being prepared by the Canadians for their coming guests. After the sittings of the association terminate, some seven hundred members of it will, on the invitation of the Canadian Pacific Hallway Company, pay a flying visit to Manitoba and the far North-West, going as far as the railway has been built—namely, to Stephen Station, at the summit of the Rocky Mountains. In making that visit the savants will traverse a tract of country from Regina to Calgary, which has hitherto been considered unsuited for agriculture. Recently, however, the Minister of the Interior, Sir David Macpherson, has received information from a number of experimental farms which have been laid out by the Canadian Pacific Railway, some fifty miles apart, through the district mentioned, that the crops grown on these farms are of an unusually good quality, and that the territory (which consists of about 200 millions of acres) is much more productive and fruitful than was anticipated. The members will also have an opportunity, *hen at Cal- gary, of visiting the enormous cattle ranches which only a few years ago were occupied by the buffalo, the elk, and the deer, and upon which there are now some 150,000 head of cattle. Lord Polworth, Mr. Staveley Hill, Q C., and a number of other prominent gentlemen in this country are largely interested in these ranches, which, owing to the slight fall of snow in that territory, are even better adapted for sheep-raising than the raising of cattle, though in all respects admirably suited for the latter, and it is now within the range of possibility that in a few years the English markets will be supplied with mutton from this very district.

SANITATION AND LONGER LIFE.—LI it not worth know- ing, even as a simple matter of fact, that the young genera- tion now growing up around us—to speak exactly, those born since 1870—are likely to enjoy better health, and like- wise to live fully two years and a half longer than their parents, or at least than the average lifetime of the genera- tion which is passing away? This is taking boys and girls together; but, as usual, the chances of life are in favour of "the weaker sex"—the recent increase in the average dura- tion of life for females being almost three and a half years, and two years for males. A very important portion of this change has undoubtedly been due simply to the remarkable general prosperity which began with the latter half of this century, and of which the fruits still so largely remain. People who are "better off" can and do take better care of their health, and have more time for their holidays and re- creation. And that such a change has occurred is plainly shown by the shorter hours of work and increased habits of pleasure-taking among all classes of our people. But the main and most manifest cause of increased longevity must be ascribed to legislation—to the Factory Acts, to the " in- spectorship" or official supervision of certain kinds of in- dustry, the additional precautions for personal safety in the working of coal pits, and the measures taken to prevent adulteration of the articles of diet ; also, very notably, the Public Health Acts of 1871 and 1875; and, not least, the great works of sanitation and urban improvements under- taken by many of the municipal bodies throughout the kingdom, of which the" main drainage" works of London (which cost about twelve millions sterling) are the most notable example. Concurrently, and, indeed, as the source of these things, there has been a strong public sentiment of philanthropy, which gave birth to the "Saturday half- holiday," and to a general encouragement and promotion of popular recreation. Altogether there has been a marked growth of humane and generous feeling; and any one of mature years has only to compare his own boyhood with the pleasanter conditions of life which now sur- round the young, to see how great and happy has been the wide social change effected during his own life- time. Nevertheless, for a long time there existed great doubts as to whether the new sanitary works and regulations were really efficient, and would accomplish their beneficient purpose. The cost was heavy as well as obvious, while the results were apparently nil. Our national life•statiatics began to be kept in 1838 ; and for seventeen years thereafter there was no improvement—the death-rate and duration of life remained, on the average, unchanged. It -seemed as if the conditions of human longevity were fixed too deeply in the nature of things to be appreciably altered by human effort. The rate of mortality was at its highest in the years 1847 and 1849, when in. fluenza and cholera were epidemic—bad years, in fact, in all ways, with famine in Ireland, revolutions on the Con-

tinent, and bad trade everywhere. In those two years the annual death-rate was respectively 247 and 251 per thousand. On the other hand, in the five years 1841-5, when on the whole the weather was fine and trade good, the death-rate averaged only 214; and in the year 1856, with its beautiful summer, the rate was only 205. But still, as already said, taking the whole period (1838.54), people in Great Britain died just at the same rate throughout; the average death-rate for the period being about 231 per thousand annually. This, was, no doubt, disappointing. But, besides the fact that the sanitary works and legisla- tion were still in their infancy, and also that new condi- tions require time to operate upon the physical frame, acting cumulatively, it needs further to be remembered that there was in progress a great increase of town life—a shift- ing of population from the country into the large towns, producing an aggregation and modes of life much less favourable to health than the open-air life of rural districts. It is also worthy of notice that although, owing to the com- bination of causes, there has been for a generation past a general tendency for the rural population to stagnate, and in many counties to diminish, the influx from the country into the towns is greatest in bad times. In the following statistics of the remarkable growth of population in London during the present century, it will be seen that the highest per-centages of increase occurred in the two decennial periods, 1821-30 and 1841-50, when the industrial condition of the kingdom was at its worst, and political discontent (as usual) was peculiarly rife:— Population of Increase per cent. Year. Landon. in decade,. 1801 1811 1821 1831 1841 1851 ....... ........ 2,363,236 1861 .....,.........2.803.989 1871 1881 Liman Ann 1801, 2,857,620. Accordingly, although the sanitary improvements were at that time inadequate to reduce the rate of mortality through- out the kingdom, they at least served to nullify the insalu- brious effects of the rapid increase of town life then in pro- gress. Thereafter, however, the desired and expected change came quickly, and in so manifest a manner as to leave no doubt that "sanitation" was capable of doing its work effectively. In the five years 1871-75 the death-rate fell perceptibly, averaging 22 per thousand; in the next five years (1876 80) it fell 20 8 ; in the year 1881 it fell to 18 9 ; in 1882 it stood at only 18 6 ; and in the autumnal quarter of last year to only 166 per thousand of the population of England. For the whole of last year the death-rate in Eng- land was 195, and, if the great towns be excluded, 177 per thousand. Thus, for a dozen years past, the rate of mor- tality has been steadily and greatly on the decrease, and when the cumulative influence of sanitary work is con- adored it may fairly be expected that the decline of the death-rate is far from having reached its limits.—Cornhill Magazine.

div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF _ _ GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. There *ere present— Messrs Greening (chairman), Derbyshire, Appleton. Brown, John Houghton, Coaper, Jolley, Forster, Bonnell, Harrison, Broadbent, Gibson, Hunt, Kilshall, ; Rev G F Roberts; J C Sutton (clerk), and S Sutton (assistant clerk). SCHOOL COMMITEE.—LETTERS FROM OLD SCHOLSRS. The minutes of the School Committee stated that the doctor had reported that the children in the school were well In health. It was also stated that Mr Mines read letters from old scholars trained by him at the schools who were now in good positions in India and Africa in connection with regimental bands, and the committee congratulated Mr Mines on the success of his old pupils.—Mr DARBYSHIRE, In moving the confirmation of these minutes, said that with regard to the question alluded to at the previous meeting of the appointment of bandmaster, the committee did not see its way at the present time to move in the matter. There was another question of appointing at the same time a drill- master, and they did not know whether it would not be better to have both the drillmaster and bandmaster as one person. It was therefore decided to postpone the matter. Alluding to the letters received 137 Mr Mines from the boys in India and Africa, he said the committee were very much delighted to hear the letters that had been sent occasionally to Mr Mines. The boys seemed to have got into very good positions, and to be doing very well. They spoke well of the Board of Guardians of Warrington and of the good they received from the schools and wished to be remembered to the Guardians and to all in connection with the Union. Altogether they seemed to be very much pleased with the learning they had acquired in connection with the Uaioni and it had been of very great benefit to them.—The CLERK said the boys were connected with regimental bands, which was rather a better position than being in the ranks.—Mr APPLETON thdßght the Board might congratulate themselves on the usefulness of the band in connection with the schools. It was the very means by which these lads bad attained the postions they now occupied. The band, he thought, deserved their full support as these were but instances of the good it had done (Hear, hear.)—The Cwarnisresr said he was very much pleased indeed to hear of those letters, and the more so be- cause he believed that the late Mr Wm Smith and himself were the two who started the band. It was first started as a drum and file band, and when the application for instru- ments was first made the request was rather laughed at by corns members of the Board, but when the instruments had been got the band had gene on very successfully ever since. —Mr JOLLEY remarked that he had listened with very great interest to the remarks that had been made and he hoped the school committee would not let the thing res', but would appoint a band master and drill master in one person, be- cause he considered drilling to be a very important part of the lads' edecation.—The CHAIRMAN said the Schools Com- mittee would no doubt take the matter into their considers- tion.—The minutes were then confirmed.

The CHAIRMAN referred to the vacancies on the Board caused by the deaths of Major Certwright (Warrington), and Mr Walmsley (Newton), and said it would be for the Board to decide whether these two vacancies should be fil- led up now or left till the time of election. They would re- member that they had something like another 18 months yet to go before their time of service expired. Illseemed to him that they ought to fill up the vacancies seeing that there was So long a time to elapse, and he moved that the Local Government Board be asked to grant the order for filling up the two vacancies—Mr COOPER a_conded this proposal.— Mr APPLETON asked if the places could be filled up without an election.—The CHAIRMAN: That is a matter for the pub- lic.—Mr APPLETON said that as far as Newton was concerned they could spare a guardian very well. If they were to have an election it would cost £2O at least, and therefore he should not go in for applying for the sanction of the Local Government Board.—The CHAIRMAN said that even if they had the order they would not be obliged to use it.—Mr AP• PLETON said that if they were to fill up the vacancy for Newton there was sure to be an election —The CHAIRMAN: Do you think so.—Mr APPLETON: I am certain.—Mr HAR- RISON said that an election which would involve such a cost would be rather a serious matter, and he considered that, seeing the number of guardians they had for Warrington, it would be a useless expenditure of money. .He thought they might very well go on to the end of their tether, so to speak in the condition they were at present. If there were three or four guardians absent it would be a different matter.— Mr APPLETON did not think the Board would be inconve- nienced at all by going on as at present. They had still three guardians for Newton —The CHAIRMAN said that if they could get the vacancies filled up without an election it would be desirable but he for his own part should not like to go to the cost of an election. He believed the clerk could tell them that his experience was that they never had had a contested election to fill a vacancy. The CLERK said be never remembered an instance within the last few years. He also mentioned that on former occasions a vacancy had al- ways been filled up although the members were only elected for 12 months, whereas now they were elected for three years, and in the preetAt instance a considerable part of that time was yet to run. The reason given by Mr Ap- pleton for not filling up the vacancies would be the very reason why the Loci]. Government Board would insist upon filling them up. Mr Appleton stated that he felt eatisfied that in the event of the vacancies being filled up there would be a contest in Newton township. He (the clerk) presumed that Mr Appleton meant that there was a divided public opinion upon some matter that that Board was capable of moving in. Well, they would be excluding from that Board a representative of that public feeling whom they had no right in law to exclude. It seemed to him that the anti- vaccinationists of Newton in their present feeling would bring forward a candidate, and it was perfectly lawful for them to do so, and the Board was not in a position to ex- clude them from the enjoyment of that right. He also men- tioned that the cos,s of an election were not paid by the whole Union, but by the particular parish in which they took place; and concluded by saying that the old practice in- variably was to fill up a vacancy even though they sat only for one year.—Mr HARRISON said that considering that they had nine Guardians actively engaged for Warriagten, arid only one short for Newton, their wisest course would be to go on and take no notice of the vacmcies. Although they were technically wrong, he was quite satisfied they would be morally right in taking no notice of the vacancies. —Mr JOLLEY : Supposing we go on in the way we are and sty nothing to the Local Government Board, is. there any power in law to compel us to fill up these vacancies ? The CLERK: You cannot fill them up without the order of the Local Government Board.—Mr JOLLEY : If we do not write to the Local Government Board but juat go on work- ing with a diminished number of Guardians, is there any power to compel the present Guardians to au up the vacan- cies ? that is the question.—Mr APPLETON: No ; the Clerk has said so already.—Mr DARBYSIIIRE said the vacancies had always hitherto been filled up when they occurred, and he did not see any reason for not doing so in this instance. They knew it was the custom with members of Parliament and with members ci Town Councils, and it had always been the custom of that Board to fill up vacan- cies when they had occurred, and he did not know of any reason for departing from the usual course. His opinion was that they were not a properly constituted Board of Ceuardians unless they had full numbers.—Mr BROWN thought they were really going on. exceedingly well, and

the attendance Was very respectable. Thera was alstalk quorum present, and the business appetred to be going on very satisfactorily. The point taken by the clerk was cer- tainly an important one, and he for one should not be pre- pared to recommend that, if there was an expression of opinion at Newton, this opinion should not be represented. But he was not so sure that there was any excitement. At Warrington there was no anti-vaccination feeling, the chief I feeling there being political, and that appeared to he very quiescent at present. For his own part he should be inclined to let things remain as they were.—Mr HARRISON then moved as an amendment that no communication be made to the Local Government Board with respect to the two vacan-• cies. He did not see any reason why the Board should cot go on as satisfactorily as when the two members were pre- sent, and although they had not their full compliment of members everything the Board did at present was practicallY and legally binding. If the ratepayers of Newton or the ratepayers of Warrington were to request them to have two. fresh members nominated he would be the last to say any- thing about it, but inasmuch as no action had been taken. The CLERK said that action had been taken. Mr Appleton brought a requisition there signed by a considerable number of Earlestown ratepayers, so that the very thing that Mr Harrison said would influence him had taken place. At the time he had told Mr Appleton that it was a matter for the Beard, and not for the people of Newton to interfere.--Mr HARRISON asked if it was very numerously signed.—Mr APPLETON: No.—Mr HARRISON said he would then put it in this way, that if there had been a strong expression of opinion on the part of a considerable number of ratepayers they should proceed' to take steps to fill these vacan- cies up, but he should be very sorry to say anything against.it, but inasmuch as there was nothing of the kind, and inasmuch as their transactions were legally binding, it would appear a waste to authorise that additional expense. —Mr APpLETON seconded this proposal, and explained that a requisition had been brought to him signed by a certain number of ratepayers of Earlestown, stating that if there was an election to fill up the vacancy they wanted to notni- nate a certain individual. But those who signed the requi•- sition seemed only to desire to nominate a person if there was anyone else nominated, and when he explained to them the cost of an election they appeared to take his view of the case, and said that rather liban spend any money upon an election they would not press the matter—The CLERK suggested that they write to ask the Local Government Board whether or not they were compelled to fill up the vacancy.—Mr JOLLET said he should support the amend- ment, because he felt there was no necessity for filling uP the vacancy. He did not think there was the slightest feel- ing in the matter, either political or othe,wise.—Mr Bstosn• BENT suggested that they ask the Local Government Board what was the proper course to take.—The Rev G F ROBERTS thought it was certainly their duty to see that places were represented.—Mr HARRISON said the places were represented—there were already nine for Warrington and three for Newton.—Mr ROBERTS said that was not fully represented.—The CLERK mentioned that iri Town Councils and the House of Commons vacancies/ were always filled up, and he was very much inclined to think himself that the Local Government Board, inasmuch as their number was 30, would consider they were not a properly constituted Board.—Mr Hammon said there wasa statutory enactment which rendered it .obligatory on the House of Commons as well as Town Councils to fill up vacancies, but there tvas no such enactment with regard to Boards of Guardians.—The CLERK said he was net quite sure about that.—The amendment that no action te taken tn fill up the vacancies was then put, and carried by ten votes to six. -

A RESIGNATION. A letter was read from Miss Pugh, a nurse in the hospi- tal, resigning her position and thinking the Bard for their kindness to laer.—The CHAIRMAN said be was very sorry to receive that resignation, as Miss Pim% was an excellent nurse. They bad Geyer had one who suited the place better. —Mr BROADBENT : What is the cause of her leaving. Mr Chairman P—The CHAIRMAN The cause is well known to the committee.—Mr Bow : Matrimony.—Mr BROADBENT Oh.—On the motion of the Chairman the resignation was accepted.

THE CHAIRMAN'S HOLIDAYS. Mr JOLLEY said he understood that the chairman was go- ing to take a holiday and was going across the Atlantic, and he therefore as a Guardian wished him God speed —Several other Guardians also expressed similar wishes, and the chair .- man in a few words expressed his thanks for their kind expressions,

A REQUEST FOB THE BAND. Mr HARRISON asked for the use of the School Band on the 28th hist, at a Miyor "At Home" he intended to hold in the Town Hail.—The request was unanimously granted. —This concluded the business.

WHAT PARLIAMENT HAS DONE. We take the following from last week'a Pall Hall Gazette :—Whatever estimate may be placed upon the legis- halve result of the Parliamentary session which closes to- day, the members of the people's House can at least say that they have passed through a most arduous period. Since the assembling of Parliament on February 5 until the pro- , rogation to-day the House of Commons has sat on 128 days, the aggregate duration in hours amounting to 1,086, or an average of si a day. What with an unusual number of morning sittings, and the protracted discussions in Com- mittee of Supply, the members of the Government espe- cially have been sorely tried. Frequently in these latter days of the session the House has not adjourned until three and four, and even five o'clock, in the morning, so that the 'Bitting has been prolonged to ten or twelve, and on one occasion to over thirteen hours. Thus, while there has been an absence of sensational long sitting, there has been a suc- cession of even more trying ones, averaging about ten hours. As for counts-out, since the private member was ousted from his privileges in June the Whips have effectually prevented that natural relief to the over-wrought legislator. The House of Lotds at its rising to-day will show a record of 95 sittings, of an average .duratioa of 2i hours. Only in three instances during the whole session have they permitted the sacred hour of dinner to be encroached upon. On these momentous occasions the hour of midnight actually saw the Lord Chancellor still on the woolsack, and the members debating the Egyptian and reform policies of the Govern- ment; but such sustained efforts being too mach for their lordships, they were followed by periods of even more than the wonted repose. The session in its legislative aspect has been described as abortive, but while the leading mea- sures referred to in the Queen's Speech have been lost, a large number of useful second-rate and departmental mea- sures have been unostentatiously placed on the statute book. Of 83 public bills introduced by the Government, 54 have received the Royal assent; and of 64 provisional orders under the charge of Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. George Russell, Mr. Hibbert, the Solicitor-General for Ireland, and other chiefs of departments 61 have passed into law. Private members have not achieved much, partly, no doubt, because they attempted too much under existing conditions, as a hopeless block .i 9 the result. No fewer than 148 bills were " introduced by private members, but only 27 have reached the final state. Even the judgment of the House could not be obtained by the authors, for only seven were disposed of by motion, and the great bulk (106) were either withdrawn or dropped, as the session ran its coarse. Together 81 public measures and 61 provisional orders have received the Royal assent. The following figures give the results in tabulated form:—

On Thursday, the two men, Wright and Wheatley, char- ged with shooting Police-constables Snell and Garner, at Hoaton, were again brought up at Worship-street Police Court, London. and further remanded, pending the re- cowry of Snell.

THE IRON TRADE —Consequent upon the depression in the North Staffordshire iron trade, Messrs Robert Heath and Sons have given notice to close their new works at Tunstall in four days. Messrs J Bulland and Son have given notice at their Cliffs Vale Ironworks, at Hanley, to cease all con- tracts with a view to the temporary stoppage of their works.

The polling for ROBS and Cromarty has resulted is the return of Mr R. C. TI. Ferguson (L), who had 717 votes, as against 334 for Mr A. R. Mackenzie (C), and 248 for Dr Macdonald (Land Law Reformer.) The constituency has. uniformly chosen a Liberal representative since 1847, and the present attempt to snatch the seat with the aid of an "independent " candidate has only served to demonstrate its political fidelity. THE ABOLITION OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS. The con- ference at the Westminster Palace Hotel on the subject of the reform of the House of Lords, and the great meeting at St James's Hall, have resulted in the formation of an exe- cutive committee, who have now framed a definite p:an of action. The title of the association is to be ". The People's Leagus for the Abolition of the Hereditar7 Legis- lative Chambor."
