THE REFORM AGITATION. THE PEERS AND THE FeI.ANCHISE.—ENTHUSI- ASTIC DEMONSTRATION AT EARLESTOWN: SPEECHES OF MR. S. SMITH, M.P.; MR. WILLIAM- SON, M.P.; MR. BROA.DHURST, MV.; MR. JOSEPH ARCH, Sec. The most enthusiastic and popular gathering ever held in Earlestown or the immediate neighbourhood took place on Saturday afternoon, when a monster demonstration in cm damnation of the House of Lords and in support of Her Majesty's Government in their efforts to piss the great measure cf reform, known as the Franchise Bill, was held The gathering, or rather series of gatherings, for there were three platforms and three separate lists of speakers, excited an unparalelled interest and enthusiasm throughout the en- tire neighbourhood, and all shades of Liberal politicians entered heartily into the movement, which from beginning to encl was of a most StiCeessful and gratifying character. The programme of the dav'e probeedings was arranged by the joint committee of the county and borough Liberal As- aaciations of South-West Lancashire, and to the hard work- ing otficiels of those associations cordial thinks are due for the success which attended their efforts. Fortunately the day opened auspiciously fine for the demoastration, and as the hoer for the emnmencernent of proceedings drew neer the town assumed a very gay appearanee. Many of the shops and places of business were closed all the fore- noon and afternoon ; and groups of well-attired pedestrians paraded the principal streets. Overhead, notably ia Queen- street, Bridge-street, Merket-street, and Eerie-Street num- berless flails, banners, and Union jacks were suspended across the road, while from almost every window was a pole, fluttering from which were the popular party colours of the Liberate, or national ensigns. This was an evidence of the thorough unanimity and heartiness with which local poli- ticians entered into thole movement, and popular opinion ap- Peered to be tersely expressed in the mottoes " Down with the Lords " and "Up with the people," which were promi- nently displayed across Bridge-street. About noon the hot rays of the sun became tempered with a refreshing breeze; and it was evident that the oft-repeated wish for favourable Weather was about to be fully realised. Between two and three o'clock the streets presented an animated appearance. The local Liberals mustered in strong force, many wearing red ribbons in their coats, while others wore medils on their breasts commemorating the Reform movement. In the vicinity of Fairclough-street, where the premises occupied as the Earlestown and District Liberal Club are situate, everything appeared to be lively. About this time some hundreds of working-men gathered on the Market ground ; and sang a number of national and popular Liberal songs, printed copies of which were die- tributed amongst those present. They afterwards formed themselves in processional order, and, by way of Idaydock- street, marched to the Liberal headquarters in Fairclough• atreet. In quick succession contingents of Liberals from Ilaydock, Ashten, Golf borne, and Newton began to make their appearance, the respective processions being headed by brass bands. Shortly after cards heavily laden special !rains from St Helens, Liverpeel Wavertree, Southport, and intermediate places brought many additional thousands into the town, and a goodly veamber of persons arrived from Warrington, having been conveyed in waggonettes. About four o'cloce one monster 'procession. comprising several thousands of persons from ell pieta of South-West Lanca- shire, was formed in the etreets adjacent to the club. The Procession marched through the principal streets of the town, the Eariestown Liberals coming first, and being me- ceeded by those from Southport, Haydock, Ashton, Col- borne, Liverpool, Werrington, and St. Helens. In all there were Eve bands, among which were the UMW: me brass hand, the Haydock brass 'band, the Ashton brass band, and the Park-lane brass band; the Other band hiving cones from Southport. A large number of banners and bannerettes bearing mottoes and inscriptions werecarried in the ranks of the procession. Ameng the most prominent were: "We demand the vote as cur right," "We respect lawenot privilege," "Lot us have right and not might," " eve tit the Lords defy the labourers?" "Think what the Locele'heive cost the people,' and " Stand to your tights, sit on eePiers," while there were carried, three Loaves of varlotee sizes, the smallest being described as "The Salisbury toe," the next as "The Gladstone deaf, and the largest as " The Franchise log.' The marsh ills were Messrs W Gilmour, D Williams, W Urquhart, M Birkhead, P Hall, and W D Hurdle, and the following rents to the field was tai:en : Down Bridge-street, along Market-street, Legh-strect. Senkey-street, Regent-street, 'Viaduct-street, Earle-street, and again along Market-street to the plot of land opeoeite St. John's Church and near the Haydock She greets along which the procession pissed were densely crowded with spectators, and repeated cheers were given. lldr W J Legh, M.P., 'Lord of the Manor, had kindly rantedinermiseion for the meetings to be held on the land in question, and here three lerge platforms 'hat been erected. In a ifew minutes these platforms—about ;one hundred Yards •sreert—were surrounded by an immense throng, Who iluttily cheered the gentlemen litho cccupied them. Various estimates of the numbers present have been put forth, but there cannot peseibly have been less than B,OOC or woo gathered round the platforms, while perhaps three or four thousands more leiaurely walked about the field. Whateemr the attendance was, however, perfect unanimity and good feeling pervaded the entire compeny, and but one Object, and that to demoneteite their adherence to the present Government in its effort to overcome • class legislation and Party-interests by granting a measure of justice to a large number of Englishmen, appeared to animate the whole. Similar resolutions were submitted from each of the three platforms, and it is needlees to add that they were enthusi- astically carried without any opposition. Reports of the proceedings at the respective platforms are appended. PLATFORM NO.I. The CHAIRMAN said 'he thought the eflret duty they had to perform was to retcrwthanks to Mr Leah, the member of Parliament for East Cheahire, and to Mr Pardey, his agent, ler the use of the ground upon which they were holding thit meeting. (Applease.) Mr Legh and Mr Pardey were both Conservatives, and therefore they ought more fully to appreciate their public spirit in having given them so 'faeourable a consideration to their wishes. (Applause.) He 'sincerely wished Lord Calisbury—(groans)—and the men Who were his immediate allies were possessed of a little of the public spirit of Mr Legh and Mr Perky. (Cheers.) If they had been so possessed they {you'd not in the first in- stance have approved of the Franchise Hill and then en- deavoured to strangle it upon the paltry pretext of waiting +until the redistribution echemo could be peas.d. The.ques- tien of redistribution was a delicate and dirdeelt task, and ho was quite sure a session of Parliament would be the very least that would be received to settle it. He thought the ROLM of Ledo had been ill advised in entering into antag- maim with the people on a false and unworthy issue, but he hoped whatever might be done in the matter would be done in a wise and temperate spirit. At the same time Lee had no daubt that the reform of the house of Lords or at any rate some change in the constitution of the House Weld before long come within the range of practical politics. (Cheers.) It had been o.epected that Sir Wilfrid Lawson would attend, but there had been some mistake in that re- spect, but upon whom the 'blame rested he Was not pre- Pared to say; certainly it did not rest upon Sir Wilfrid hirnsel f. (Cheers.) Mr CIIMILES PILKINGTOR, J.P. (illydoClL), hoped that they would stand shoulder to shoulder in that great fight. (Cheers.) They in Earleetown especially felt strongly on that subject, which was a great and burning quesidon, and recuired careful and considerate thought. The 'town was one .with some 27,000 inhabitants, many of whom had note rote, and therefore that was a very good pl IC3 to fix upon for that demonstration. The Tories said that wee a ques- tion they did not care about, and that there had been no great agitation among the people on it—(" gainrcon," and lagghter)—but he maintained that the great meetings that had been held, and that ens that day, proved that a great amount of spirit had been aroused amongst the people, and that they were determined to have their way in thie matter. (Cheers.) The Lords, in rejecting the Feinchise Hill, had raised a great wave of public opinion, and he felt sore that that wer. e would carry the Franchise Bill on its crest. C" Aye, and drown them," and 'laughter ) What it would do with the House of Lords they hardly knew at present. He hoped it would not swamp 'them entirety—(, swamp them," and cheers)—but he also hoped it would impose some reattaint upon them—each a restraint as would pre- vent them from resisting the will of the people in the future, (Cheers.) The Tories had reeds 3 very great mis- take in rejecting the Franchise Bill, and it was for the Liberals to take full advantage of that by every means in their power, and he hoped they would do so. (Cheers, and a voice : " ei,huck them out.") It was nai the Mist time that it had been said that the Howse of Commons did not represent the will of the people. 'That wee a familiar Tory cry. (Hear, hear.) The Tories paesed a reform Bill with a Parliament vary much older than this one, and their con• tention came to this—that a Parliament when it was four years old did not represent the people. (Leeghte.r.) He .Mtintained that the present Parliament had represented the went of the people, and he had, therefore, great pleasure in reneving—" That tle',3 meeting approves of the course taken tee her Majesty' Government in calling an anthem sesdon -01. Parliament for tee purpose of piecing the Franchise BBL and strongly urges tkem to take all poseible mane to make It law." (Cheers.) ee,, S. K. MuspiaTri (Whines) briefly seconded the resolution. He said ha thought that trerneridens gathering We quite as great as themes he sow in London the other day, and his hope was tleat its unanimity arid enthusiaem would convince Lord Salisbarv—(groens)—by the time Parliamect again assembled ic October, and thee he would repent the tally he had cantnei:ted, and that it would I eid him to pass the Franchise Bill bg an overwhelming major. ' Sty. (Cheers.) He (the speaker) was not surprised at what Lord Silisburg had done, consider-lug how he had gone bead- tong and fooliebLy against every bill that was sent up to the anise of Lords. The members of the House of Lords were net, nor ever had been, representative; but we had, he was glee, to say, a very popular House of Commons which did eepreeent, collectively and individually, the large majority of the people. He hoped with Mr. Gladstone, speaking at Hawareen, that the Franchise Bill would Le passed in a short time, and that the Ler4a and others who had squab- bled over it would rejoice at the granting of the franchise to the people. (Cheers.) nay mutt show not only that day

that they were in favour of the Franchise Bill, but also show it when the general election came by sending really representative men to the House of Commons. (Cheers.) Mr. W. S. ROBSON, of the London "Eighty" Club, sup- ported the resolution in a stirring address. He said it would be a good thing if the Londoners turned out of their clubs and drawing-rooms once a year and met the men of Lancashire. and see how fast public opinion advanced there. (Hear, hear.) A few months ago they were talking of nothing but the Franchise Bill; then they began to talk about the reform of the Reuse of Lords, and now they were beginning to talk about its abolition. (Loud and continued cheers, and a voice "Down with the House of Lords," re- ceived with renewed cheers.) He did not know how far they, as Lancashire men, were prepared to go. (Cries of "AU the way," "Abolish them," and cheers.) He hoped the day was not far distant, and indeed WAS now come, when the abolition ef the House of Lords would be only a half-men- sure, and when they should demand the sweeping away entirely of the hereditary peeraare from England. (Cheers.) They inust consider whet could be mere absurd than that this bill which the English nation, at the last election ap- proved—a bill not only approved by the people, but passed by enormous majorities in the House of Commons, should not pass into law. Oae would think that neder those cir- c'unsstancee it shoeld be law, But it wee net lew, And. why? Simply hecatiee it Must pass In ea-icily the shape desired by Lord Salisbury. (Groans.) The reason for it was that that house Was utterly incapable of reform. He asked them were they content that these men, who cast out the measures passed by their representatives—that men like these should postpone for a day, or even for an hour, the en- franchisement of 2,0D0,000 of their fellow creatures? (Loud cries of " No.") If they valued the liberties which their chiefs thought they had won for them, they would decline to be governed by men whom they had not elected. He, thought he had said enough to justify the meeting in pass. ing the resolution which had been moved, and also the one which would follow, expressing their determination to get rid once and for all of this house of political obstruction, this stronghold of social fetishism—their determination to do away with the system, degrading and demoralising to a free people, of privilege without responsibility, of power without calecitv, and of honour without merit. (Laud cheers ) The reaolution was carried with great enthusiasm. Mr. WILLIAM TYRES (Prescot) moved the second resolu- tion as follows:—' That the electors and non-electors of South-West Lancashire now assembled at E arlestown hereby protest against the obstruction of the Franchise Hitt by the House of Lords, and declare the present constitution and power or that House to be highly dangerous to the good government and welfare of this kingdom." This resolution, he said, followed very naturally after the one which had joist been carried. In considering it they had to consider what was the constitution of the House of Dards. A number of members of the House ef Lords if they had to go back a few years and look among their ancestry, would fled, he wee sore, that they could not boast of it to any great extent. (Hear, hear.) Some of them had their origin in a very ob- scure way, and some of them, perhaps, tn a not very honour- able way —(appleuse)—not as honourable, he WAS sure, as that of most of the men he saw before him. (Cheers.) From the expression of feeling which they bad given he imagined that the remark of Mr John Morley that the House of Lords must be either "-ended or mended 'lid not in their opinion, go quite far enocgh. It struck tim that their feeling was that the House.cif Lords should be " ended." (Loudcheere.) They all knew that the House el Lords exercised ite. powers as strongly nit could do to prevent the Reform Bill of 1832 being passel:, but, although it delayed it for a time, it oould not prevent it being passed in the end. It was obliged to give way, and it would be obliged to give way now. (Cheers.) Mr. S. F.toons, (Miners' Lgent, Wigan), in seconding the resolution, said it had been represented in London, in the House of Commons, and in various parts of the country that the workingmen of England did not at all want the ex- tension,of the county franchise—(A Voice " Hew do they know F"), but he thought Viet that meeting proved that the working men of England, or at least the working men of Lancashire, were determined, whether the Lords considered it half a bill or a whole bill, to have the Franchise 'llxten- sion Lill. (Cheers.) It was a most singular thing that all along the ages one party in the Route of Cornm.os had been deed set against 'reform, while the L'berals had been doireir all they could to enfranchise and benefit the teeming multitudes of people who inhabited the counties and cities and villages of England. (Cheers ) They would have to tats the life out of the hereditary chember, and he believed that by extended eciranchiiement they would secure a re- formed House of Emmons that would more faithfully re- present the people than at present. (Cheers.) Mr S SMITH, Mff", was received with enthusiastic, cheer- ing. In supporting the resolution, he said they were met to supnort Mr Glalstone's Government in c arrying to a suc- cessful issue the third great refori&btll which England had seen in the present century. That bill was the necessary completion of the other two bills, and when they got that bill—as they son. would—there wculd not be the slightest doubt that England would have a thoroughly repre- sentative system so far at the House of Com- mons was concerned. He thought they -might then be able to say that the Huss of Commons would b 3 a true reflection of the sentiments, feelings, and necessities of the people of the British Islands. Cot the resolution went a little further than that. It dealt with the other house. (Cheers, and a voice : "Pull it down.") The House of Lords had brought upon itself e great many very severe strictures which it would have avoided had.it been wisely guided. Had he been in the shoes of the Conservative leader of the House of Lords he should have welcomed the Franchise Bill, and would have given his right hand to help it through. Then the Conservative party might have gone to the now electors and have claimed their votes. But they had been very badly advised and hadrioined issue in what was certain to be for them a disaetroue defeat. They had done their best to cast away what they might naturally have claimed. (Hear, hear.) He pointed out that there was a certain element of true statesmanship and of Liberal progressive ideas in the House of Lords, and said that when they Came to reform that institution —and he quite agreed that the time had come when it must be reformed—he hoped I they would not lose the services of the able men to whom he had referred (Cheers. arid a vnice "Cut aff the rotten branches.") The way of the English people had always been to repair and reform rather than to destroy, and one reason why they had had so little bloodshed and so few revolutions in this country was because they had always gone gradually and steadily forward, trying to carry the great masses of the people with them. When they went in— as they would have to go in—for a change of thanonstitution of the Upper Chamber he lead no doubt they would dose they had always succeeded in doing before—try to keep what was good and throw away what was evil. (Cheers.) Proceed- ing to consider the arguments of the Tory party with re- gard to enfranchisement, Mr Smith said he WAS much puz- zled to know what was the point at which Liberal 3 and Tories were at issue. There appeared to be about as much difference between them as there was between "tweedledum and tweedledee." (Laughter.) Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill had, certainly conceived a very warm aff mtion for the British eleetor—(laughter)—and they were buraing to enfranchise two millions of people, but the tee- rible lion of redistribution stood in the way to devour them. (Laughter and cheers.) The Government had acted with as much moderation and fair dealing as they coeld with re- gard to the Franchise Bill, and had done all in reason to meet their opponents. They might be sure that in Mr Glad- stone's Redistribution Itie there would be us tricks and no rotten boroughs, and that it would be based upon the broad principles of justice. The country could trust the present Government, and therefore they must be kept in power till the great measure of enfranchisement was passed into law. (Loud cheers.) The resolution was then put, and, carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr BROWNBILL, seconded by Mr Alder- man BOOTIIROYD (Southport), a curdled vote of thanks was peened to the chairman.

Mr BROCKLEBINIC, in acknowledging the compliment, ex- presoed his great satisfaction at the orderliness of the im- mense gathering. He could honestly say that he had never before seen a more inteliigent and appreciative audience than he had presided over that afternoon, and he con- sidered it a great pleasure and honour to have been their chairman. (Cheers). PLATFORM NO 2. _

Mr R D Hour presided at the. second platform and was. supported by Mr Henry Broadhurst, M.P, Mr Tomkinson (Liberal candidate for West Cheshire), Dr Wood (Mayor of Southport), Alderman Poulsom (ex-Mayor of Bootle), Alderman Wild, Aldermen Leslie, Mr George Wilkinson (Bootle), Mr W P Clarke, J.P, Mr R Nicholson. J.P, Messrs W it Beckett, W C Rawlins, R Salisbury, J A Dear, II Vaaghan, D Lloyd, T Tyson, F Broadbridge, H Roberts (Warrington), and P HAII arlestow n 1 The CHAIRMAN said that they who CIITio from Liver- pool were anzious that those in the counties should enjoy the same privileges as they in boroughs enjoyed, and they were anxious to support the just claims of those who asked for the extension of the franchise. (Hear, hear.) He must ask them to giwo all the support that t`ley possibly could to the Government of Mr Gladstone under the present very trying circumstances. (Applause ) The House of Com- mons had by a very large majority passed the second read- ing of the Franchise Bill and the last reading was passed I without a dissentient voice. (Hear.) Now they found another branch of the legislature opposing the Franchise and preventing its being granted to them. 'They saw in the very gracious speech that the Queen addressed at the close of FArliament that she herself exprtssed regret that the great measure of the Franchise had not been passed. There- fore, tkey had only to deal with the Lords. (A voice : Down with them.") He would leave it to them to ex- press their own odinions en the resolutions that would be submitted to them. Dr I,Vuov, Mayor of Southport. who was cord' ally re- ceived, said that the Franchise Bill had been carried suc- cessfully through the House of Cornmons, but unfortu- nately the Hacse of Lords hal rjected it. They said that the Bill was tact dead, but yet alive, but he thought that it must be in what was called a state of suspended animation. (Applause.) They know that there was a good deal of sus- pended animation in that gilded chamber. (Laughter and applause ) But they could assure their lordships that the animation would net be suspended outside those walls until the till became law arid until they moved out of the way of the Progress of the nation. (Cheers) The Lords bad rejected the Bill because it was not large ettgugh for them. (Laughter.) They could not pass a measure for the exten- sion of the Franchise unless they had also a still larger measure of redistribution. It seemed to him that the Lords were in the position of a man who had to take a pill—(laughter)—which was too large for him to swallow, sod so be said to bi; wife, "My dear, I

Ilike this pill very much indeed, I am sure it sill do ma a great deal of good, but I cannot possibly take it unless you will get me another pill that is larger than this one, and then I'll try to swallew both together." (Increased laughter and applause.) Were the .Lords afraid that the Liberal party were going to: shirk the question? Could not they trust that party to redistribute the seats? (A voice: They cannot trust themselves) In 1836 the Liberals swept away 53 rotten boroughs—(hear)—ond in 1867, although the Con- servatives were in power, 11 ntore of them were swept, and he tegretted to say that that work would have to be con- tinued, for there were a good many rotten boroughs left yet. He was there not only to join with them in demanding the enfranchisement of 2:000,000 of their fellow•countrymen,but most heartily to express confidence in Her Majesty's Go- vernment. (Applause.) Some people said that they had no confidence in that Government. Why was it ? Was it because Mr Gladstone husbanded the resources of the nation ? (Cheers.) Was it because he had protected trade and commerce? (Applause.) Was it lo2caue the Govern- ment were willing to bring forward the great social question of which there was ro grander advocate in the country than Samuel Smith, who was then addressing another meeting? (Applause.) Was it because they had refused to plunge the mignt remind hitn toot there had country into war? The.; 1?e551 war in F:4ypi, but to the honour of the Government a 'it it be sail that that war was not commenced until patience itself was exhausted, and egiry means had been tried to arrive at a pacific soletion. They might remind him that there WaS war now. Why were they gathered to- gether that day? If it Was not war, it wee a struggle against the House of Lords, (Applause.) That struggle had not been commencEei until every possible means had been tried and every reasonable offer had been rejected. (Applause.) They had nothing to fear had would yield to none in sup- port of the Government, and in admiration of the Right Hon. William Ewan Gladstone. (Applause.) He then moved the first resolution. 'Mr ENOCH EDWA.RDS, Secretary of the Miners' Associa- tion of North Stafford, eecended the resolution as one who had mixed amongst working men front boyhood. Oa every side there was but the one opinion that they should not rest satisfied until the Government of the country gave to every working man who paid rates the same power to vote in the counties that was given to the people living in the boroughs. One thing was certain—that there was no, House of Lords in thie or Ana other country which would prove stronger than the voice of the people, while the people kept themselves together. (Applause.) It they were to succeed they must use every legitimate effort in order to bring that success about. lie hoped that they should press for the measure until every man, whether in county or borough, were put on one common footing Mr ToaranasoN, candidate for West Cheshire, supported the resolution. Tbeir'e he said, was the old struggle of privilege against popular rights, the claim ot the few to govern the country as against government for the people, through the people, and by the people. (Applause.) The House of Lords and the Tory party really feared reform; it Was not an unfair redistribution of seats that they feared,; bat a tar redistribution they were afraid of. They had no I ground of suspecting Mr Gladstone and the Government of unfair intentions with regard to redistribution. Nothieg merelair or generous than the Franchise Bill could be imagined, and there was not a shadow of a pretext for say- ing that Mr Gladstone and the Liberal party desired to un- fairly manipulate the redistribution of seats. The House of Lords desired to raise false issues to put before the country, well knowing that they could not be in a worse position than they were at present, and hoping their position might be improved. The question for they who would be presently esafranchised was as to the use hey would make of the vote when they got it. In considering that point he would con- clude with a verse of a poem by an unknown writer:— We look oa a vote as a solemn trust for a might; purpose , given. And we'll answer the me we make of it to none but ourselves
and Heaven. We have no less stake than the proudest peer In our country
and its laws, And a sinWe vote may Incline the scale to the side of ths good

old cause. (Loud cheers.) Mr Thomas BROCKLEBASK, speaking to the resolution, said that since the meeting at Pomona they perceived a change in their opponents. Now Lords Salisbury and Churchill wore running a race as to which could give the Franchise first. What had caused the change ? These noble lords knew that the extrusion of the Vranchise must be followed by a redistribution of seats, and they wanted to carry that redistribution themselves. Another reason was that they would rather be the party in than the party out.

The resolution was then carried unanimously. Mr T. T. HAVES, J P., moved the second resolution. With regard to the Franchise, they were told by Lord Randolph Churchill that the Tories were competing with them as to who should pass the bast me tsure of reform, but they haid no faith in such promises. When the Reform Bill was pas- sing through the House of Commons, the Tory party found all the fault with it they could, end Sir R. A. Cross and most of the leaders of the Tory party opposed the extension of the Franchise to the counties in Ireland. But the Tories in the House of Lords had done what the Tot ies in the Hones of Commons had not the courage to do. The Tories in the House of Commons were willing to wound,'hutafraid to fight. As re- garded the House of Lords, he believed that the whole hereditary system stood condemned in the light of the nine- teenth century, and the time had come when— Enlightened men shall lead the van, And overthrow this marshalled clan ; This moral learn—that C.sd made man, But never made a Pee..

(Applause.) Mr E. R. RESSELL seconded the resolution. They were agreed, tee said, about passing the Franchise Bill, and they were agreed that the House of Lords must either be mended or ended. The power of veto of the House of Lords was on the eve of going into abeyance, at the least. (Cheers.) it was intolerable that that House ehould interfere with the legislation of the country by spoiling or preventing it. Toe House of Lords had condemned the Government—not on the question of the Franchise, but on a qiestion of general and foreign policy—and if the Prime Minister and his .col- leagues did not think it worth while to mention the matter in the House of Commons next night, or take any action on the subject, they ought from that to understand that their power was a thing of the pest in right and ought to be so in j reality, and, if necessary, in law also. (Applause.) Mr. H. BROADHURST', M.P., supported the resolution. He agreed that they should keep their minds constantly fixed on the passing of the Franchise Bill, but he did not in saying that mean that they should lose sight of that perpotuel block and obstruction to progress that occupied so large a part of their time up to the present, but what ha wanted was tbat they should get that additional leverage with which to ac- complish the great work that lay immediately befere them. The Tories now siid that they had no objection to the Franchise Bill. Well. he did not believe it possible for the most earnest of reformers and repenterrt sinners to be so thoroughly converted in so short a space of time. (Laugh ter.) Having spoken at length on the statements and actions of Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill, he asked was it possible that those men could really be in favour of the enfranchisement of those whom they had looked upon for generations—Day, whom they regarded to-day—as their serfs and slaves belonging to their estates. His experience of labourers, and what he had read of the upper classes, led him to say unhesitatingly on all grounds, on the grounds of political intelligence, patriotism, virtue, and morality, that the men who due ties ditch or trimmed the hedge out- side the [state should leave the same influence and political power as he who lived inside. What the Tories feared was not the ignorance of the people, but their knowledge and in- telligence. If her Majesty's Government might arrange to appeal to the country if the House of Lords would do the some, he should have no fear that they should return to the House of Commons with unthinned ranks, and he very much feared that there would only be a straggling rem:remit of the hereditary chamber assembled at Westminster. (Ap- plause.) Mr Chamberlain replied to Lord Salisbury's charge that the House of Commons was four or five ye us old and wanted renewing. That reply was that if the House of Commons wanted renewing by a fresh touch with the nation, how much more did that other chamber want re- newing. (Applause.) How much more was it necessary that the Lords should appeal to the country, and go and learn the opinime and wishes of the people. He ob- jected to an hereditary chamber altogether, which he , said put a mark of inferiority upon every other section a the community. He refused to bow down to any man because that man was the son of his father. Whether the House of Lords was mended or ended they might de- pend upon it that they were well within a measurable dis- tance of the time when all hereditary right, at least, must cease to exist. Heir, hear.) They must put their hands to the work, for they intended to have the vote. When they had got it they would sea that that perpetual onions of Toryism was thoroughly reformed, if not abolished. (Cheers ) Did they suppose that they would evetlegislate thoroughly while that House existed. He said there was no hope whatever, and he hoped that every man in Lauca- ehire, in England, and in the United Kingdom would pledge himself never to rest from that agitation until they had car- ried triumphantly the Liberal programme of the present day. The resolution was then put and carried. A vote of thanks to the chairman, m wed by Alderman Pote.som (Bootle), seconded by Mr C J CROSTIELD, Jr, and enthusiastically carried, concluded the proceedings. PLATFORM No. 3.

At this platform -th-e--ciiall.;va-s Occupied by Mr. R. Pil- kington, J.P., of St. Helens, and there was also on it Messrs. S. Williamson, M.P. for the St. Andrews Burghs •, J. E,. Johnson-Ferguson, Joseph Arch ; A. Sinclair, St. Helens ; J. B. Leach, St. Helens, and numerous others. The prol- ceediogs were commenced by the singing of "Auld lank syne," after which The CHAERMAN said they had all sung what was so very true that they were not to forget the old achievements nor were they to forget the old leaders. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that they were met together• there, as so many others-of their fellow-countrymen had met together, to pro- test against the actiwa of the House of Lords in connection with the Franchise Bill. Oa other occasions their fellow- countrymen had met in their thousands, and bad expressed their opiuiori in a calm, in a peaceful, and in a determined manner. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had heard their leaders, through the press, speaking to them words of leading, words of encouragement, and words of warning. They had heard their names, and just now had sung their names, and perhaps the greatest name of all—only he should not like to say it was greater than Mr. Gladstone, but for the moment it was more prominently before them— was the name of Mr, Bright. (Loud applause, and three cheers for Mr. Bright, Mr. Bright went to Manchester, an

old man, a veteran with his hair white with 50 years' service in the Liberal cause-50 years' service destroying whit was wrong and in doing what Was right for the people of this country. (Loud applauee ) There was anothee man, too, who went with Mr. Bright to Manchester, aud that was Lord Hartington. (Applause.) Lord Hartington did his duty bravely and well in the Liberal army. (Hear, hear.) In the dark days of Tory rule, from 1871 to 1880, Lord flartington was the Liberal leader. He did his duty and faced those men to the best of his ability, and with his strong sense he showed up their shame and showed up the manner in which they were going to rule the country, and in which unfortunately they did rule it. (Hear, hear.) But there was another man who has rendered great service to the country also, ant that men was Sir He ary James. (Applause.) Sir Henry James his drafted this Franchise Bill, and they were indebted to him for drafting it in such a manner that even now the Peers say they agree with it. (Laughter.) And they all said they agreed with it because it was so well drafted. They c.uld not say otherwise. (Hear, hear.) But what had the people been told in Hyde Park, at St. James'e. Helll and at M in chester. 1. hey were told that a great wrong heel beee jene, that it 0611 passed at its second reareeng by a majority of 130, and after- Wetae a majority of 190, and sent UP from the Coale:lons without opposition, had bean thrown out of the Window. (Hear, hear, and" Dawn with the Peers." Was that true? (" Yes.") There was another set of people came down to Manchester. There were two noble lords c ,rne down- -(hooting)—and one of them said the Home of Commons did not represent the people to-day. (" Oh, oh," and " Who represents them then? ") , Lord Randolph Churchill —(hisses)—said that the House of Commons Was not com- petent. Lord Randolph Churchill said the House of Lords stood between the people of England and the House of Commons, between the people of England and the Govern- ment. ("Oh, oh.") Lord R indolph Churchill said that the Lords could not do with Mr Gledstone's Government, and be should just think they couldn't. (Elear, he ir,'arel laughter.) The fact of it WAS IhoB3 two noble lords did not like the Government at all; they did not like the Liberal party at all; they did not—the House of Lords did not like the Franchise Bill at all, and they did not really want redistribution at all. (Hear, hear, and a voice "Their ways are not our ways.") No ; nor would their paths all end in peace. (Lenghter.) There were many men in the Govern- ment whom Lord Salisbury hated. He hated Mr Gladstone, and they all hated Mr Gladstone. (Three cheers were here crlled for Mr Gladstone and given enthusiastically.) The Chairman then referred to Lord Salisbury's statement at Manchester with regard to the passing of the Reform Bill of 1832, and gave a full and correct account of that episode which materially altered Lord Salisbury's very brief and impeefect version. Had Lord Salisbury, the chairman went on, givew that full account at Manchester he would have told what was really the case. (Heir, hear.) But let Lord Salisbury and the people with him be so mid in the coming session as to send back the Franchise Bill, and he (the chair- man) would venture to say that Mr Gladstone and his Go- vernment would refuse to remain in power unless they hid the same support from the Sovereign as Lord Grey had in 1832. (Hear, hear.) They were certain that if it should be necessary for Mr Gladstone to advise the Queen to make such a necessary creation of Peers that Her Majesty would, as she always has done for the welfare of the people, and in the true interests of the constitution, follow the advise of her great minister. (Loud applecse.) But although these things migeat happen, there was a further question, and that question was, were the House of Lords to go ou year after year refacing measures sent ap by the House of Commons. (Loud cries of "No.") If the douse of Lords would take their prcper place in the constitution and leave off doing these things, and reform themselves, then there might be something in it; but if they would not reform themselves, then they must follow the leading of Mr Bright and other great leaders, and the country must reform them. (Loud appeause.) And if they would not reform therneelves, and the 'country could not reform them, why then their fate was on their own head, and whatever happened would be brought about by the act and deed of the Lords themselves. (Loud applause.) Mr. J. E. Jouersor Fertenson, in moving the first resolu- tion, which was similar to the resolutions paesel at the other platforms, said their Tory opponents had never ven• bared to once meet the ques' ion of the proposed extension of Ithe franchise directly. They had tried to turn the attention l-of the people of the country from the question of reform to that of the foreign policy of the Government. (" We will not have anything to do with the foreign policy question.") At the present time there was no question Mere the eountry save that of reform; and there were only two parties in the kingdom—those who were in favour of reform and those who were opposed to it. (" Well done," and hear, hear.) The Reform Bill of the present session had been passel by an overwhelming majority in the House of Commons, and now the Tories told them that they wished to go even further than the Liberals did. If their opponents were as eager for reform as they professed to be, why did not they amend the Franchise Bill instead of throwing it out. (Hear, hear.) Though Lord Salisbury and his followers said reform was necessary, they might rest assured of this—that during the six yeirs the Tories were in power it was they and they alone who ever;, year defeated the resolution brought for- ward by Mr. Trevalyan in favour of the enfranchisement of I those there assembled. (Cries ef "Cheers for Mr. Trevel- yan," which were given with enthusiasm.) When they re- membered this, they could certainly never believe in the honesty or sincerity of the conversion of the Tories. Did ' they think that any Redistribution Bill which would satisfy Lord Salisbury would satisfy them? He was quit.: 'sure it would not. They were present that day to say that the ' Franchise Bill should not be abandoned, and that the course which the Government had adopted was the only right and possible course. (Hear, hear.) But they were present that day on another and even more important ground—viz, to show their determination to protest most emphatically against the unprecedented and unconstitutional claims which Lord Salisbury had put forward on behalf of the Howie of ! Lords—(hear, leer, and cheers)—to show that those claims ' should be emphatically rejected once and for ever. The I day had at last arrived when not only the power, but the constitution of that house must be seriously modified. (Loud cheers.) Mr STEPHEN WILLIAMSON, M.P., seconded the resolution ! He siel they wanted this Franchise Bill to be passed as it stood. They wanted the principle of it to be affirmed in the first place and to get the validity of law, and then they, would deal with redistribution. (Applause.) He always thought that Mr Gladstone was a very wise man when he kept clear of the shoals and sands and difficulties that will , attach to redistribution, and contended for the principle of giving the St. Helens men a vote. (Cheers.) He hoped there were many St. Helens men there that day. (Cries of "There are) There was another thing in connection with I keeping these two matters separate. He hoped the Govern- , ment wonld never allow the House of Lords toelictate the fornt or the manner in which the legislation of the country ! is to be carried on. (Cheers ) They could easily see that if the House of Lords is to have the power continued to it of upsetting the form and the manner in which legislation is to I be accomplished, they might just as well have a Tory majority in perpetuity, and he hoped the country was not prepared for that. (Cheere, and a voice : "Never will be.") They knew that they 'wanted to force a dissolution of Par- i ment ; but were they to allow the House of Lords, or the the Tory party speiking by that House, to force a dissolu- lion upon the country when a large majority of the people I were represented by a Liberal Government. ("No," and ! cheers.) He would consider it an innovation and a most dangerous thing to agree to, and he hoped the Government t would be firm and not agree to it. (Cheers.) Personally he ' for one would like to mend the House of Lords, but if they I could not mend it then he for one would go in for ending it. 1 (Loud applause.) Mr JOSEPH Ancte, who was received with cheers, said he thought the working clisses of this country had a very dif- ferent idea of legislation to what Lord Seliebury (laughter and cheers); and he thanked Lord Salisbury very I much for the course he had taken with regard to the people's bill. He bad brought out not only the intelligence of two million of his fellow countrymen with his wild action in the Upper House which had so basely insulted the people, but he had brought about the decision of Her Majesty with regard to the autumn session. (Applause.) Whatever might be said by Tory orators their idea of legislation was not by picnic. Oa the contrary, it was by logic. (Applause.) By what right or by what authority did Lord Salisbury call upon Mr Gladstone to resign? He (Mr Arch) considered that was the prerogative of the Crown and of the Crown only, and Lord Salisbury had no more right to call upon the Government to resign than he had. (Laughter, and a voice: 'Not so much.") The people sent Mr Gladstone to Parliament, and had not called upon him to resign. (" We don't want him to resign.") In 1880 there was not a single Liberal returned to Parliament, except Mr Goschen, who was not pledged to his constituency to support an extension of the Franchise. (Hear, hear.) That was made a test question in every constituency in the kingdom in which a Liberal was returned, and if that was not an expression of the opinion of the people what was? (Hear, hear.) Did Lord Salisbury think they were so blind because they were working men as not to know that two and two made four? (Hear. hear.) As a werk- ing man he considered that Lord Silisbury had basely insulted him, and also basely insulted tens of thou- sands of his clase,the aericaltural labourers, and he might rest assured that when the vote was conceded them their Tory lords and sqnires and dukes might put their shutters up. (Laughter and applause.) They knew their business although they were Johnny Hodges. (Laughter.) Lard Salisbury was not so much afraid of the votes of the people as of the way in which they will vote—that is the grand secret of his lordship's opposition to the Franchise Bill. (Loud laughter.) Depend, however, that in the coming struggle the greatest question will be that of the land. (Cheers 1 He would give them no rest while there are 15,000,000 of acres of land, the greater portion of which is of a splendid character, from which men are being driven, whilst it is being converted into game preserves and deer' parks for the privileged few. ("Shame.") As far as he was concerned, the land-grabbers shall pass no more enclo- sure bills to steal the people's land. The fight will be a tre- mendous one ; but tkey should win. (" We shall" and ap- plause.) He hoped to see the day before he was done his work when their land will be free; when landlords shall know the just relationship in which they stand to the people; when the earth which God created for the benefit of mankind shall not be wasted by any man because of the fact that be happens to have title deeds ; when the lords of the soil shall know that the people have rights as well as themselves; and when, though there may be lords and dukes, there shall not be tyrants and slaves. (Loud cheers ) As to the peers, he thoughtit would be a very great mistake to abolish the House of Lords, on the ground that the members of the House have got a tremendous influence in the rural districts, and we want business men in the House of Coot-

mens. If the House of Peers were disestablished, we should have former members of that House cKnpeting for seats in the House of the people. The resolution was then carried with great enthusiasm Mr. W. S. ItonsoN (London) moved the sec nd resolu- tion.

Mr. A SmcLiart, J.P. (St. Helens) seconded this resolu- tion. He thought that they ought all to thank Lord Salis- bury for the curse he had taken. (Hear, hear.) He had for many a year bsen one of those persons whom Lord Salisbury declared to be absolutely insane, who could nver ulderstand why in a self-governing country there should be a second chamber. If they got the hest men in England in the H 0113? of Columns he did not see what they wanted with a second chamber. He had tried for many years to talk to people on the subject and found very unwilling lis- teners, but now, thanks to Lord Salisbury, the hour had struck when the House of Lords must ba mended or ended. (Applause, and a voice : " Ended.") If they could take their power away he did not object to their living in the "gilded I chamber." (Hear, hear, and applause.) The resolution was then caieci, and the meeting con- cluded by singimr, the National Anthem.

DEMONSTRATION AT BOLTON.—The anniversary of Peter- loo was celebrated at Bolton on Saturday with a great reform demonstration, about 20,000 people being present. Previous to the holding of two monster open-air meetings, there was a procession through the town, accompanied by bends, the demonstrators carrying banners and political emblems. Mr J K Cross, M.P, Mr Charles Russell, Q.C, M.P, Messrs Leaks and Agnew, the members for South-East Lancashire; Mr H Lee, the member for Southampton ; Mr Briggs, M.P for Blackburn; and Mr W Summers, 111. P for Stalybridge, were the chief speakers; and resolutions declaring in favour of the Franchise Bill and against the veto of the House of Lords were carried with enthusiasm.—Mr J K CROSS, %Pi said the occasion of their meeting WAS no oralnary one Re hoped that twelve months henee they would have not only the franchise but redistribution wou d be so settled that even the Tories would have no reason to find fault. (Cheers.) The House of Lords had taken a new departure, and claimed what was really only the Royal prerogative, of saying when a Prime Minister should dissolve Parliament. (Hear, hear.) Don't let the issue before them be confu.ed, but keep their minds firmly fixed on the one thing. There were many questions before the public now, but this was not the q ues• , tion of Egypt; this was not the question of the government of Ireland even; it was not a question of curbing the power of Russia, as Lord Saisbury sad ; it was not a question even of the Manchester Ship Canal—(laughter and cheers) —though Lord Randolph Churchill—(groans)—when he posed in Manchester as a somewhat rampageous Radical, wished to point out to them that it was not the House of Lords that had stood in the way, but the House of Commons, forgetting altogether that the Chairman of the Committee was a member of the late Tory Government. The issue was clear and simple. They wanted a full, just, and free reflec- tion of the people's wishes in the House of Commons, and no dictation from the House of Lords. (Cheers.) Mr. W. E. Batoos. M.P., said Lord Salisbury had told Mr. Gladstone to dissolve, but Mr. Gladstone's majority was neither made of sugar nor solt—(laughter and cheers)—and it was not go- ing to dissolve at the bidding of such watery carrannnica- tions as Lord Salisbury's. But the reason why they were assembled there was because they wanted an expression of opinion from the people whether they really were so indif- ferent about the matter as these Conservative orators would have them believe. Did they want this bill or not? (Cheers.) Were they determined to support the Liberal porty ? (Cheers.) Which would they have as the man to whom they would trust the redistribution of political power— Mr. Gladstone or Lord Salisbury ? (Hisses and cries of "Gladstone.") The Conservatives had once upon a time been trusted with a redistribution of political power, and a pretty mess they made of it.l(Cheers.) The time was coming, and fast coming, when the qaestion would be definitely put before them as to whether the day had not come when the power and privilege of the House of Peers ought to be, if not abolished, at any rate curtailed. (Cheers )—Mr ROBERT LEAKE, M.P., said that in 1889 the electors sent Mr Agnew and himself to the House of Coin- mane as their attorneys to save them from their enemies. Now they were to save them from their from their friends— their friends par excellove —the members of the House of Lords. (Laughter ) Lord Salisbury bade fair to be the greatest specimen of the political chameleon that had been seen in modern times. At present he was of a Democratic colour. But how were they to make it wash? His advice was to keep perpetually dipping Lord Saliebary in big meet- ings. (Hear, hear.)—Mr W AGNEW, M.P., asked why had that meeting taken place when they all knew that the Tory party had c opitulated. The Tory leaders said they were eager to give the people the franchise, and they also said they hid always been ready to give it. But his private opinion was that if they gave the Tory leaders an opportu- nity of giving the people the franchise, they would give it in such an emasculated and mutilated shape that it would scarcely be worth having. (Cheers.)

A great meeting of Liberals Was held at Hebden Bridge, on Saturday, and vast numbers of persons attended from all the surrounding towns as far as Halifax and Todmorden. Processions were formed in various parts of the district, which paraded the thoroughfares, a strong procession leav- ing Todrnorden, headed by the local brass band at two p.m., and joining the whole strength in the centre of Hebden Bridge. The mass meeting was held in the open air at Fosterholme. There was an attendance of at least 6,000 per- sons. Sir Matthew Wilson, Bart , M.P., presided, and he was supported by Mr. Isaac Holden, M P., Mr. Chas. Brad- laugh, M.P., Mr. A. H. D. Acland, and Alderman Longbot- tom.—Mr. Joseph Craven, Edgehev Green, proposed the re- solution of the day, heartily approving of the Franchise Bill and that the time has arrived whoa some effective limit should be placed on the power of veto on legislation pos- sessed by the House of Lords —The resolution was seconded by Mr. James Merrill, and was passed amid loud and con- tinued cheering.

A great demonstration of Liberals in the Wakefield polling district took place on Saturday afternoon at Wakefield in re- gard to the franchise question Many thousand of persons carps by rail and road from the country places round about, including Normanton, Morley, Ardsley, Cas.leford, 03sett, Horbury, Shariston, Stanley, dtc. They assembled in the vicinity of the Strafford Arms Hotel, from whence a pro- cession started at four o'clock with several bands of music, banners, and trophies. Th 3 procession marched to Thornes Park, lent by Mr Charles Milnes-Gaskell, chairman of the South-Weat Riding Liberal Association. Here a mass meet- ing was held, over which Mr R B Mackie, the member for Wakefild, presided. Among those on the platform, besides the leading Liberals of the town and district, were Mr W H Leatltam, M.P. for South-West Riding ; Mr R Reid, Q.C., M.P. for Hereford; Mr John B inton, M.P. for Kiddermins- ter ; Mr W C Ithlass, M.P. for East Cornwall; Mr W H Lee, Mayor of Wakefield ; Colonel Mackie, J.P.; and Mr B Pickard, secretary of the Yorkshire Miners' Association. The proceedings were enthusias'ic. An open-air demonstration held at Whitby, on Saturday, was addressed by Sir Joseph Pease, M.P., Mr Arthur Pease, M.P., and Mr Frank Lockwood, Q.C. Sir Joseph Pease said the question before them was one that involved great constitutional issues. It was not brought about by the House of Commons or by the people of the country whom that House represented ; but it was deliberately chosen by the House of Lords. There was but one end to such fights The end must be with that party in the State which demands that which is right, reasonable, and just, and to which no man dare say no.—Resolutions in support of the Franchise Bill, and denouncing the House of Lords, were paaged. A reform demonstration was held at Hinckley, South Leicestershire on Saturday, attended by a large crowd from that place and the adjoining villages. The speakers in- duced Mr G T Paget, M.P., Liberal member for the divi- sion, and Mr James Ellis, the Lioeral candidate at the next election, and resolutions were passed approving of the Fran- chise Bill and the calling of an autumn session to again cansider it, and protesting against the action of the House of Lords in rejecting it. A demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill, re- presenting the counties of Aberdeen and Kincardine was hell in Aberdeen on Saturday. It was the largest poli- tical gathering ever held in the north-eastern district of Scotland.
Mr Burt, M.P., addressed a largely-attended miners' demonstration held on Saturday, at Morpeth, in support of the Franchise Bill.
A largely-attended meeting was held on Saturday at Radernie, in the. eastern district of Fifeshire, when resolu-

lions were passed urging the Government to insist upon the unconditional acceptance of the Franchise Bill, and de- nouncing the action of the House of Lords as unconstitu- tional, obstructive, and arbitrary. The reform of the House of Lords was demanded.

Lord Reay presided at a reform demonstration held at Dunse, Berwickshire, on Saturday. Hav'ng cleared Mr Childcrs' reputation as a Chancellor of the Exchequer from the aspersions cast by Lord R Churchill, he proceeded to state that he was in favour of the reform of the House of Lords. He had voted for Lord Roseberry's motion, and would do so again. What he wanted to see was the House of Lords not working against but working with the House of Commons. Mr MajoribAnka, Ml', also spoke.

„ On S iturday a meeting of agricultural labourers was held at the Vineyard, West floathley. Sussex. The attendance was large, taking into consideration the busy harvest opera- tions now going on, and the long distances which many of the labourers had to journey. The resolution was carried without a dissentient that 6' That this meeting approves of the Franchise Bill as proposed by Mr Gladstone's Govern- ment and pissed by the House of Commons. It regrets and deplores the ill-advised action of the House of Lords with regard to the bill, and trusts that the Government will take such measures as will lead to the speely enfranchisement of the agricultural labourer.” .

A largely attended demonstration was held on Monday at Woodfield Park, Blackwood. Addresses were delivered by Mr Dillwyn, M.P. for Swansea, Mr Warmington, QC., one of the Liberal candidates for the county, and others; and resolutions were passed approving the policy of the Govern- ment. urging no compromise on the Franchise Bill, and advo- cating the Ref. rm of the House of Lords. The resolutions were carried unanimously.'
_ Two Liberal demonstrations were held on Monday even-

jog, one at Girvan and the other at Dalmallington, Ayrshire, in favour of the Franchise Bill and condemnatory of the Ffouse of Lords in refusing to pass the bill. About 5,000 pevle took part in the proceadings, and resolutions were unanimously passed. On Monday an immense outdoor demonstration took place at Brownhills of the dwellers in the Cannock Chase part of LEast Staffordshire, a district where the questions of the ex- tension of the franchise and redistribution have been

Iwarmly taken up, nineteen-twentieths of the householders in the area between S.aiTord and Tam vorth in the one direc• tion and from Walsall to Lichfield in another being without a vote, although numerous little towns have in the last 20 years sprung up there. Contingents were present from 18 or 20 different places, carrying fl igs and banners, msny of which bore vigorously-wcrded allusions to the fl9use of Lords, and at the meeting all such allusions on the part of the speakers were enthusiastically taken up, particu- larly one by the miners' agent, Mr Southall, suggesting a march of 20,000 men upon London to knock at the doors of the House of Lords. Sir M A Rees, M.P., and Mr G W Hastings, M.P., spoke, and at the close Lord Salisbury's effigy was burnt. On Wednesday night a largely attended and enthusias- tic meeting in support of the Franchise 8.11 and the Govern- ment WAS held at Bicup. Speeches were delivered by Mr. O'Connor Power, MP, Mr Leake, MP, and Mr Agnew, M P.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETINGS.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETINGS.

A meeting in support of the action of the House of Lords on the Franchise Bill took place on Saturday, in the grounds behind the Lewisham Conservative Club. Sir J. F. Len- ford took the chair, and about 400 persons were present, in eluding some who frequently expressed dissent from the speakers.—S:r C. Mills, M.P., moved a res)lution cordially approving of extension of the franchise, bet upholding the Rouse of Lords in their refusal to pass "an imperfect measure of reform ;" and strongly urging the Conservative leaders to use every endeavour to procure an early dissolu- tion of Parliarnent.—During the hon. mem e.:r's speech one of the hostile party was forcibly ejected from the woun ls.— Mr. W. GRANTHAM, M.P., seconded the motion, rematking that their opponents rely rarely spoke the tru,b, even by accident,—Mr. Mortaas HOWARD having supported the resolution, it was put to the meeting, and a large number of hands were held up in its favour.—The Caatueraer declared it carried unanimously, but there were several cries of (Es-- sent, followed by a dispute, and the ejection of another of the dissentients. Thereupon some of those present express•Al disapprobation, the result being that another per- son was forced out of the grounds.—Viscount Bury and Mr. J.Talbet then proposed and seconded a reso- luion, which was passed, to the effect that the Government had not redeemed any of their pledges, and had involved the country in a number of unnecessary wars.—Viscount BURT said Radical spouters might spout, and R idical demonstra- tors go on, but it was very doubtful that they would make any difference in the next session of Pa;liatnent. The people had not yet spoken, and until they did the House of Lords would stop the way. (Cheers.)— A vote of confidence in the Conservative leaders was afterwards adopted, on the motion of Viscount Lewisham, M.P., seconded by Mr. Gainsford Bruce.

A Conservative demonstration in support of the House of Lords was held at Bournemouth, on Sturdy, when ad• dresses were given by Mr. Cavendish Bentir.ck, M.P. for Whitehaven ; Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, M.P. for Eye ; Mr. F. Compton and General Sir Frederick Fitzwygrarn, the mem- bers for South Hants ; Mr. C. E. Baring Young, the Con- servative candidate for Christchurch, and others. A large meeting of Cheshire Conservatives was held at Beeston Castle, the residence of Lord Tollcmiche, on Satur- day. Mr H Platt, president of the Crewe Conservative As- sociation, presided, and supporting him were Mr J W Lowther, M.P , the Hon W F Tollemache, M.P., Mr H J Tollemache, M.P., and Captain Cotton (Conservative candi- date for West Cheshire).—Mr J W Lowther, M.P., pro• posed a resolution upholding the action of the House of Lords in postpming the Franchise Bill untii a scheme for the redistribution of seats is introduced. Ile remarked that the Conservatives quite endorsed the principle of the Fran- chise Bill, but they objected to the Liberal party being placed in suc't a position as would enable them to manipu- late a redistribution scheme in favour of their own party.— The Hon NV F Tollemache. 'M.P., seconded. He objected to large masses of people being sent to London to intimidate one of the branches of doe Legislature, and to try to per- suade the people of the country that the Lords were di- rectly opposing the will of the nation.—The resolution was carried.

The Earl of Carnarven on Saturday received some 150 gentlemen, hon. secretaries and secretaries of the Conserva- tive Associations of the metropolitan boroughs and of the county of Middlesex, at his seat, Mem!ere Castle, a few miles beyond Newbury. The gucsts left Paddington Sta- tion by special train at 230 p.m., and ran on to Newbury, whence, by permission of the Board of Trade, it was allowed to proceed over the new line from Newbury to Winchester, which is in process of construction, to a point not more than half a mile from the London-road entrance to the park. Breaks and carriages were in attendance, and the visitors were conveyed, under the guidance of Mr Walter Money, F.S.A., to the Castle, wbeee the Earl and Countess, with the Ladies Winifred, Margaret, and Victoria Herbert, with the juvenile heir, the ROD. Aubrey Herbert, were waiting, their arrival, with a circle of neighboais and friends, including Lord Boston, Sir A. Arbuthnot, Canon Portal, and Mr. Alfred Austin.—After a hearty welcome from the noble host. the avaembled visitors were addressed by the Earl or Car- narvon, who said that for once in four years the Govern- ment had done service in awakening the slumbcring Con- servatisrp. The attack on the House of Lords he declared to be an attack on the Constitution. It was the Franchise yesterday, the House of Lords to-day, and would be the Crown and Constitution to-morrow.--Lord Boston, who fol- lowed, suggested that Professor Thorold Rogers should be sent to the right about with the tagrag and bobtail of the Radical party. The Earl then showed the visitors over the Castle, explaining its art treasures, and next led them to the mist striking points of view in the beautiful park, while a plentiful supply of refreshments was being laid, to which ample justice was done, before the party returned as they had come to their special train, which reached Padding- ton a little before 10 p.m. Mr. Edward Clarke, y.p., Sir Massey Lopes, M.P., and Mr. W. J. Harris M.P., were among the speakers at the demonstration held on Monday at Mount Edgcutnbe Park in connection with the Plymouth Conservative Association. No resolutions were passed. Mr. Gibson, addressing a Conservative meeting at Hali- fax on Monday evening, described the Reform agitation as an agitation with limited liability. The Government asked the nation to forget everything they had done, to accept a mutilated measure dealing with reform, and to condemn the Peers into the bargain. Lord CAMNARVONT, speaking on Monday night at New- bury, denied that the House of Lords had rejected the Fran- chise Bill. All it had clone was to insist upon its being coupled with a measure of redistribution, which is a vast extension of votes meant that what was given should be given jus'ly, and that they should not filch away with one hand that which was given with the other. For what that House had done he claimed the gratitude of every lover ef his country and Constitution. . _

It is proposed to hold on Saturday next, a monstre demon- stration of Conservatives at Hatfield Park, the seat of Lord Salisbury. The Earl of Lytton, G CB. and other well-known leaders will address the gathering on the topics of the day. Arrangements have been made with the railway companies for the supply of cheap tickets. Admission will be by ticket only, to be obtained of the Conservative working-men's clubs throughout the metropolis and the counties.

_ On Monday there was a Conservative demonstration in Hovingham Park, the seat of Sir William Worsley, Bart, when the Conservative Associations of York, Scarborough, Mahon, and Ryedale (including Helmsley, li.mby, Ample. forth, Cox,ve)d, &I), assembled to the number of over 2,000. The Hun G E Lascelles was in the chair—The Hon Guy C Hawney, MP, moved, "That this meeting approves and endorses the action of the House of Lords in declining to pass into law an incomplete measure of reform, unaccom- panied by a proper scheme for dealing with the redistribu- tion of seats." This was seconded by Sir Frederick Milner, M P, who described the recent gathering in Hyde Park as a " puppet show."—Col King-Harman supported the reso- lution, which was carried unanimously.

The Khedive is expected to return to Cairo in about nine days, in order to receive Lord Northbrook in the capital. Enormous refrigerators are being constructed under the London Central Poultry Market, the object being to provide storage for the quantities of frozen meat constantly arriving from New Zealand.

Teta FoIIESTS kND COLLFIELDS OF THE WOULD.—The forests of Europe are estimated to cover 500 millions of acres, or nearly 20 per cent, of the surface of the Continent. In British North America there are said to be 900 millions of acres of forests, in the United States 560 millions, and in South America 700 millions. The total thus estimated for Europe and America alone is equal to 3,600,000 geographi- cal miles, each containing 736 English acres. It is interest- ing to compare this area, so far as the possible supply of fuel is concerned, with that of the coalfields of the world, which is estimated at 134,000 geographical miles. Of this area, one twenty-fifth part is in the United Kingdom, or , 5,360 geographical miles of forest, against 5,000 geographi- cal miles of coalfields in full work. Four-fifths of the known coal-measures lie within Britist and American terri- tory, the forests of Europe and America covering 27 times the area of the known coal-measures of thevorld. In Baden, where the forest statistics are carefully prepared, the annual production of wood is less than the weight of hay that can be grown on an equal area. At that rate—which is low for an average—each geographical mile of forest will yield, one with another, 1,500 loads of timber per annum: But a square mile of coal-measure yields something like 20,000 tons in the year. The latter produce, however, is limited and exhaustible. Extract the coal, and not only is there an end of the fuel, but the soil itself is generally reduced to utter waste. Arrange the forrest according to the best theories of forestry, and its yield is perpetual. Hanover is the European country in which scientific forestry is now probably in the most advanced condition. A forest, under the most perfect regulation, is divided as nearly as possible into six equal areas—one full of trees not exceeding twenty years in age, a second containing trees of from twenty to forty years old, and 80 on. In the latest block, containing trees of from 100 to 120 years old, felling is commenced, the old trees being carefully and successively removed, and care taken, at the same time, to replace them by the growth of seedlings. It is thus endeavoured to preserve, as far as pos- sible, the features of the natural growth of a wild forest, and at the same time to extract a deaaite and calculated harvest of wood from the soil.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

Several interesting matches were played at St. Helens on Saturday. Sutton scored 63 against Pilkington's Plate Glass Work., the latter notching 60. The Groves Rangers beat York-street Schools by 59 runs to 24; and the Eigehill Conservatives scored 84 against 30 by Ravenhead (late Thatto Ileati4), the last-named match taking place at New- sham Park, Liverpool. An exciting game between Dark-lay:le Anchor ant the Parr Evening Star resulted—Anchor, 53; Evening Star, 51. The Albion Amateurs ran up 66, while their opponents, the City Rangers, only scored 56; and the Fingerpost Amateurs notched the big total of 172 runs against the 36 of the Parr Mount Rangers. The Victoria Rangers and Sutton Excelsior match resulted as fol rbws— Rangers, 95; Sutton, 36. Peasley Cross scored 116, against 38 by the Globe C.C.; and Sutton Victoria were beaten by the Sutton Vulcan, the scores being—Vulcan, Victoria, 32. 36; Intone, 32. One of the closeet matches of the semen ended on Satur- day, at Clifton, when Gloucestershire gained their first success this season by a victory over Lancashire by seven I rung. Score :—Lancashire, 188 and 227 ; Gloucestershire, 101 an 321.—0 n Saturday, at the Trent Bridge Ground, Nottingham, the Notts eleven brought to a conclusion their last county match for the present season, defeating Middle- sex in *single inning., with 91 runs to snare. In all they have played ten county matches atid won nine, the remain- ing one having been left drawn altogether in their favour. Such a splendid record speaks eloquently for the all-round strength of the team.—The match M.C.C. v. Gentlemen of Sussex was concluded at Brighton, on Saturdrv, and re- sulted in a draw decidedly in favour of Sussex. *Score : Sues-x, 323 ; M.C.C., 151 and 219.—The match between Somersetsbire and Devonshire was concluded at Taunton, on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for Somerset. Score : Somerset, 300; Devonshire, 106 and 190. On Tuesday Kent followed up an advantage gained over Derbyshire at Gravesend on the previous day, and gained an easy victory over the northern county. Score : Derby- shire, 52 and 182; Kent, 243.—Although defeated in their first match with Hants by a tremendous majority. Somerset- shire on Tuesday had their revenge in the return at Bath, winning by an innings and 63 runs. Score: Somerseishire, 330; Hampshire, 179 and 88. Lancashire beat Surrey at Kennington Oval, .London, on Thursday, by eight wic:iets. The northern side had gone in overnight in the last innings wanting 120 to win, and by the drawing of stumps had lost one wicket for 15 runs, thus 105 were wanted, and as there had been some ram it was thought just possible that the ground would suit the Surrey bowlers. The not-ou.s, however—A. G. Steel and Taylor— hit very finely, and when at last the former was dismissed at 83 the match was virtually over. Hornby and Taylor bit off the remaining runs without the loss of another wicket. The 105 runs had been made in seventy-five minutes. Score: Lancrshire, 252 and 120; Surrey, 149 and 222. Less than an hours play on Thursday was sufficient to finish off the match between Gloucestershire and the Aus- tralians at Cheltenham. Score : Gloucestershire, 183 and 83; Australians, 402.—The return match between York- shire and Middlesex ended at Sheffield in a draw. Score: Yorkshire, 212 and 390; Middlesex, 202.

We bag th offer our s:ncere regrets to our numerous patrons tor the disappointments we have been com- pelled to Inflict on them during the past few weeks. The demand for our Mineral Waters has been on such a scale that we have been absolutely unable, even working night and day, to meet the deluge of orders. Thus many valued customers have, to our deep annoy- ance. been apparently neglected.

For the kind forbearance shown us in this trying time we are truly grateful, and we hope when our New Works in Haydosk-street, St. Helens, come into ope,ation (In a few days), to make full amends for past shortcomings.
We beg those who have lately experienced a seem- ing lack of attention to their wants to accept this apology.

SAD SUICIDE AT ASHTON.—On Saturday Mr Husband deputy coroner, held at.inquest at Ashton Heath on the body of Eliz ibeth Brownhill, 47 years of age, wife of a watch- maker, who committed suicide under peculiar circumstances. It appeared from the evidence of the husband that both he and his wife were drinking together on the Wednesday. He went to St. Helene, where he was locked up for being drunk.. On Thursday morning he sent a telegram to his wife, asking her to forward money to him to pay the fine and obtain his releass. She got the telegram at halt-past eight o'clock on 'Thursday morning, and it is supposed that she deliberately hanged herself then, as when he returned at four o'clock in the afternoon be found lire house locked up. He effected an entrance, and found his wife hanging to the bed-post in their room quite dead. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide while in a state of temporary insanity." FARLESTOWN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB —A general meeting of the members of the Earlestown Football Club was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Monday, when about 40 persons attended. Mr. P. Hastie presided, and gave an interesting resume of the last season's matches. He intimated that matches had been arranged with the first teams of the following clubs i—Northwich Victoria (winners of the Cheshire Challenge Cup for four successive seasons) Crewe Alexandra; Everton (holders of Liverpool and Dis- trict Challenge Cup) Bootle. Liverpool Stanley, Preston Parish Church, Newton Heath, Preston Olympic, Birken- bead, Bootle Wanderers, Liverpool Anfield, Barnes Revers, and Adlington ; in addition to which the club had again entered the competitions for the Lancashire and Liverpool Challenge Cups. Letters were afterwards read from Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P„ Dr. A. Handyside ; Mr. R. H. Wright (Newton), Captain J. L. Wood, and Mr. Thomas Stone (Newton.) It was stated that an excellent field had been seoured at Wargrave from the let September to April stb. Mr. James Whalley (captain) resigned his post, but the members decided not to accept the resignation, and he W 32 re-appointed. Mr. J. Gray was elected ca otaiv, sod Mr, J. Ogden vice-captain of ate flud team.
