South-West Lancashire demonstrated. at Earlestown on Saturday in a way which Was good alike for the eyes and the heart - Englishmen are somewhat phlegmatic. bet when they do get roused there is no keeping them back. They are roused on the question of the Franchise Bill and the Reform of tiW House of Lords; they are "on the job)" and,. it is evident they do not mean to rest untl` it is finished. What a blunder Lord SAMS- BURY made when he alleged a few months ago that the country was indifferent to an extension of the franchise. He did o°l understand what was meant by " power ' repose ; " but he is beginning now to real' se' what is the meaning of energy in action. Bis well, perhaps, that the people should be thwar- ted for a time, if only as a means of putting tp the test the moral force they possess. It.' worth something, at any rate—the oppositin° of the House of Lords—if for no other reason than that of its evpking such enthu- siasm as was witnessed on Earlestown CO mon on Saturday. The Liberal cause Mg, now be said to be advancing by leaps an'', bounds. Not long since the reformer 01 the House of Lords was as the voice of one crying in the wilderness; to-day the voice i 5 the voice of the nation, and the lords then.'" selves are beginning to see that the question is being discussed •as one of practical pol' tics. It is true, taking Lord CARNARVON ag a typical specimen, that they do not she'l , much foresight. Speaking on Saturday to 3 demonstration of "150 gentlemen" had received "a hearty welcome" to clere Castle, he told a tale of "a silly an" ill-conditioned lad" who meddled with 3 bee-hive, and "how for the rest of his life he, learnt a lesson which was never effaced., But what a parody to refer to the " House n' Lords" as a bee-hive! How ..superbly ill; pudent for one of the drones thus to spea", about the working bees I " 111-conditioned c. they may be, and Heaven knows many e` the bees are badly hived, and the they are robbed of the honey the; have produced with so much toil an(' care; but there is a change coming over the spirit of their dream, and let the drones looY. to it that they do not add insult to injury) °r they may receive a-lesson which will shorten their days. Contrast the Tory picnic at Highclere with its 150 gentlemen enjoYing " the beautiful park "—not to mention e "plentiful supply of refreshments "—and the demonstration on Newton Common, whet° ten thousand working-men assembled, corninb from near and fat, at their own expense, after a week of toil, to demand that they shall be admitted as freemen in a land which clalrn.,9 to be free. Can we wonder that these Me" should show some impatience of resistance on the part of a body of men who have been' nourished on Privilege and are inflated witllt' Pride and Prejudice? The wonder is Or they have stood it so long and so tame'Y't But they are now "up and doing with a heat, for any fate." Mr. CHARLES Pilau/vire' remarked at one of the meetings that t.II present great wave of public opiniora had been raised by the Lords Woe', carry the Franchise Bill on its. cres:i upon which one man promptly exclainae t —"ay, and drown them." There-was gre„3o cheering when .Mr. W. S. ROBSON, alladie4 the prospect of abolishing the. House vt Lords, and when Mr. TYRER suggested tllad the feeling was that they should try to enat rather than mend it. Mr. BROADHVRST 110 the case in a nutshell when he said as to t" demand for an appealto the people that thera't could be no objection to such an apPeo if Lords as well as Commoners wwttir submit themselves to the popular vote. 'Tect lordships will, we do not doubt, be horridhey at such a proposal. And yet why should tuco be? What is sauce for the goose is St or for the gander. Whether the Peers like I be no, the Upper House will either have o.bio made representative and directly rspors/1

to the nation, or be so restricted in its power for mischief as to become harmless. But this is not to be done at a stroke. s The first duty is the passing of the Franchise Bill, with a Redistribution Bill close on its heels, and then the people, appealed to as a whole for the first time, may determine what the new Parliament shall do with the House of Lords We must move stage by stage, and some of these stages must be,passed before the Government will feel at liberty to declare themselves on what is now uppermost in men's minds. It is not to be supposed that the PRIME MINISTER is not fully cog- nisant of what is going on in the country, if he does not give it prominence in his speeches at Midlothian. He is above all things orderly and constitutional in his methods of procedure, and, having set his hand to the Franchise Plough, he will not look back or aside until the work is done. But he has faith in the people; he has again and again enunciated the doctrine that a statesman can do little or nothing unless he has the nation at his back. At present his way is blocked, and his first thought is to get it clear. Meantime, taking the question of. the franchise as beyond the region of dis- cussion, there is no reason why the country should not keep to the front the great problem of the reform of the House of Lords and there is no better way of aiding in the solution of the problem than in the holding of such magnificent demonstrations as that last Saturday on Newton Common. When we can fix the Hour, we may rest assured that the Man will be ready.

A WARRINGTON contemporary which is noted for the benevolence of its "neutrality" in all matters affecting the interests of the Conservative party gives especial prominence to a communication which is intended, we presume, as checkmate to the article in our last week's issue on the representation of the borough. As we tiave no desire to be other than fair, and, as we are responsible for what is regarded as the bane, we hasten to give the antidote—such as it is. It is as fol- lows:

"As a report has been somewhat extensively circulated to the effect that Mr. Daniel Adamson, the well-known Chair- man of the Manchester Ship Canal, bad been asked to con- WO this borcugh at the General Election in the Conserva- tive interest, we are asked to state that there is not the slightest truth it it. And, further, that at no Conservative meeting has any gentleman been asked to stand for War- rington, etcept Sir Gilbert Greenall, who, at a crowded meeting in the Public Hall two years ago, was unanimously requested to become the Conservative candidate, and ace oepted the honouratle and responsible position." This contradiction will present itself as a bold one to those who do not examine it; but if our readers will take the trouble to refer to what we wrote on the subject they will see that it is very much beside the mark. The fact as to the main point is that it is nowhere stated that iVIr. ADAMSON had "been asked to contest this bc,rough." That is a lay figure which has been set up in order that it might be knocked down. Our statement was that at the meeting in question " one of the heads suggested Mr. DANIEL ADAMSON, of Manchester Ship Canal fame" It is not for a moment to be supposed that Mr. ADAMSON was fortifying him- self in "the snug " of the hotel—waiting to beasked,and that they popped the question" instanter. We, too, can say that he was not asked, and for the good reason that, before the " askings " were put up with a view t 6 this "unholy 'alliance," it was discovered that his Liberalism was "just catise" of " impediment" of an overwhelming kind. So much for what our contemporary has been "asked to state." We may now go a step further; in another column there will be found two letters on the same subj,2ct—one signed "A Conservative" and the second "Another Conservative." It will be seen that they pretty well dispose of each other, and practically establish the accuracy of our- statement. It may be granted that the gathering which has caused such a stir was "in no sense a public meeting," or "even a representative meeting." That it wasn't either is, as we understand, a serious ground of complaint on the part of some of those who have by their speeches been back- ing up Sir GILBERT GREENALL at the various ward meetings. They naturally ask, "Why was there a meeting at all ?" but as yet they can obtain no satisfactory answer. No one denies that there was a meeting, and, as it is now admitted that Sir GILBERT GREENALL was present during the first part of the pro- ceedings, exception can hardly be taken to our describing it as "influential." The sig- nificant. but by no means unnatural part of the affair is that'. "the the stab in the back" to the baronet—the suggested displacement by Mr. ADAMSON—seems to have been given after Sir GILBERT had retired from the room. It was the •other week only that he publicly said as to the Ship Canal that they "were • sticking it into his vitals ; " and now he Ands there are those amongst his friends who would have him commit political suicide to make way for the Chairman of the Ship Canal. We do not profess to be sympa. thetic towards Sir GILBERT, but we must say that it is too bad of his backers to endeavour to back him into the ditch. But the Tories of Warrington are eividently in a fix, and they don't know what to do to get out of it.

IN our last issue a correspondent (Mr. H. WHITHAAI) drew attention to the fact that, in consequence of what he regarded as the exactions of the Water Works Company, some soo workmen at Messrs. ItYLANDs were, so far as the works are concerned, deprived of drinking water during working hours. • We learn that there is the same difficulty at other firms in Warrington, employers having, for working purposes, rendered themselves independent of the Water Works Company by obtaining water from other sources. They have, of course, a perfect right to do the best they can for themselves in the pur- chase of water as of any other commodity; but we do not see why men who are toiling in heated workshops should be left in the lurch as to drinking water, because there is a difference between the buyer and seller as to the price of supply. Water is amongst the primary necessaries, and is as requisite as air and food for the preservation of life. In such weather as we have had, and are having, it is a cruelty to deprive—if for a few hours only—any person of the opportunity of ob- taining it for the purpose of quenching thirst. It is true workmen may keep a supply by them by conveying it from home, but this, in the peculiar circumstances of the case, is a breach of the law. They ought not to be called upon to run any risk of being brought before a bench of magistrates, and it is to be hoped there will soon be an end of this anomalous condition of things. The Public Health Act, 1875, makes ample provision for deal- ing with a case of this kind. The clause is as follows : Where, on the report of a surveyor of a local authority

it appears to such authority that any house within their I district is without a proper supply of water, and that such • a supply of water can be furnished thereto at a cost not ex- ceeding the water rate authorized by any local Act in force within the district, or where there is not any local Act so in force, at a cost not exceeding twopence a week, or at such other cost as the Local Government Board may, on the ap- plication of the local authority, determine under all the circumstances of the case to be reasonable, the local authority shall give notice in writing to the owner, re. guiring him, within a time therein specified, to obtain such supply, and to do all such works as may be necessary for that purpose. If such notice is not complied with within the time speci- fied, the local authority may, if they think fit, de such works and obtain such supply, and for that purpose may enter into any contract with any water company sup- plying water within their district; and water rates may be made and levied on the premises by the authority or com- pany which tarnishes the supply, and may be recovered as if the owner or occupier of the premises had demanded a supply of water and were willing to pay water rates for the same, and any expenses incurred by the local authority in doing any such works may be recovered in a summary man- ner from the owner of the premises, or may by order of the local authority be declared to be private improvement ex- penses. - We have only to add that the word " house "-is defined as including "schools, factories, and the other buildings in which more than twenty persons are employed at one time" to show that the law has simply to be set in motion by the Town Council, as the local authority, to ensure that there shall be an end of the grievance of which the working men of Wasrington at present so justly complain.

HARTLAND WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The annual sermons in aid of this chapel were preached on Sunday morning and evening by the Rev. Sydney Mess, of Halton, and the collections amounted to upwalds et £5, being £3 less than last year. GOOD TEMPLARISM AT WIDNES.—At the weekly meeting of this lodge, held in the Albert-road Wesleyan Chapel, a discussion took place on "Is it sinful to take intoxicating drink ? " The debate was adjourned, and the members sat down to a coffee supper.—A fraternal visit was made to Widnes Samaritan Ledge by the Star of Widnes Lodge on Monday, when the visitors gave an entertainment. BALL AT WIDNES—Os Monday evening a ball organised hse Mr Mellon, the enterptisinz manager of the Theatre Royal, Widnes, was held in the Volunteer Hall. A good company assembled, and notwi, hstanding the high tempera- ture of the atmosphere, enjoyed themselves greatly, the proceedings being directed by Mr Mellon. Mr C Powell'e quadrille band supplied the dance music, and Mr Harry CraddOck was at the piano. Mr Mellon is about to depart on a six weeks' tour. A BABY SHOW AT WIDNES.—On Monday evening, an entertainment was held in Cook and Grundy's tent, on the Market Ground, the proceeds of which were devoted to the fumed for erecting new schools in connection with St. Mary's Catholic Church. The programine included pudding and treacle eating contests and other similar amusements, the chief item being a " baby show," for which eight infants were entered. The mother of Jane Broon, two months old, was awarded the prize, which was a gilt clock under a glass shade, value e£s. RUNOOIIII RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY-The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr John Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev J Lockwood, Messrs Mclntyre, Derbyshire, Midwood, Rigby, E Aaron, H Linaker (clerk), and W H Lineker (deputy clerk).—Mr Farrington, the nuisance inspector, stated that Dr Gornall, of Warrington, had reported to him the out- ' break of a case of typhoid fever at Wilderspeol. He would attend to the matter.-The Inspector also reported that since the last meeting he had made an extended inspection of the Old Qrtay Canal in consequence of the complaints that had been made with regard to that waterway. Be had also taken samples of the water for analysis, and would submit a full report at the next meeting—There was no other busi- ness. DEPARTURE OF THE REV. G. HACH FROM RUNCORN.— After spending three years in Runcorn as pastor of Halton- road Wesleyan Chapel, the Rev. George Hack early in the present week departed for Pensarn, where he intends to spend a fortnight's holiday prior to taking up his residence in the Manchester circuit. In the autumn of 1881, a few months subsequent to Mr. Hack's arrival in the town, revi- val mission services were organised by the Wesleyan 1 Methodist body, and were attended with great success. The religious enthusiasm of the people was stimulated to a high pitch, and the number of church members was largely in- creased, while the then members reaped benefit in added zeal to the cause. To Mr. Hack must be ascribed no small measure of this success. He showed great powers as a revivalist preacher, and was indeed the most prominent figure at the various meetings. In the spring of the follow- ing year Mr Robertson Wateon conducted a fortnight's mis- sion in the Runcorn circuit, and there is no doubt his labours received fuller acknowledgment and had greater power in consequence of the previous "revival." Mr. Hack also earned the character of a zealoas temperance advocate. Few were the meetings held in the interests of sobriety and order at which his voice Was not heard denouncing in forci- ble language the liquor traffic as the curse of men and a great hindrance to the nation's progress, and no patty will regret his departure more than that pledged to spread the principles of total abstinence. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN AT Rancoux.—Large con- gregations assembled in Runcorn Public Hall on Sunday afternoon and evening on the occasion of the annual ,r- -vices in behalf of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Mis- sions to Seamen. Mr W P Roberts delivered an address at each service, and in company with his wife sang several solos in the pleasing style which causes• them to be wel- comed in any neighbourhood. Unfortunately the collec- tions amounted to about £5 less than last year, only realis- ing £7. On Monday the annual excursion in connection with thrmission took place. About 9-30 the "Fairy Queen," which had been specially engaged, left the Duke's Pier with about 620 persons on board for Liverpool. On arriving at the Indefatigable the party disembarked and looked through that immense training ship for boys, and then proceeded to Princes landing stage, which was reached about noon. During the afternoon the excursionists had the privilege of inspecting that splendid Atlantic liner, Brittanic, belonging to the White Stet. Line, the fire engine station, and the Sailors' Home, and the opportunity was largely taken advantage of. The Sunday school teachers and workers in connection with the Runcorn and Ellesmere Port Branches, at the invitation of the committee of the missions to sea- men, partook of tea at the head missionary rooms, 8, Price- street, and subsequently the Rev T Patrick delivered an ad- dress of welcome. Several of the visitors spoke of the suc- cess of the work being carried on by the MISSIOSS, and a seordial vote of thanks was passed to tbe committee. The trippers reached home safely about 9-30, having spent an enjoyable day. We ought not to forget that Mr W Shaw, the missionary, and the band accompanied the excursion. TAB LATE MR. THOMAS JOHNSON OF RUNCORN. Preaching at Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn on Sunday evening, the Rev W Preston, MA, referred to the desth of Mr Thomas Johnson, J P, in the following terms : We in Trinity Church cannot but feel touched by the removal Ithrough death of one highly respected and well-known as a former townsman. Mr Johnson was known to many of us here. His munificence was widely felt, his generosity was experienced around. To his energy and pecuniary assis- tance this church and the adjoining schools are due. Whilst in Runcorn not alone did he give employment to a large number of hands, but by every effort he sought to promote that which is of more impoitance than bodily comfort— their spiritual welfare. His heart flowed with sym- pathy for the true welfare of the working-man. He desired that he should attain that "glory which shall be revealed" in God's children. He was an earliest supporter of some of our chief societies, and he was an un- flinching advocate of evangelical truth. He sought, as every Christian should, to try and make the world a better one than it was when he came into it. He was faithful to his trust. Up to the last he took a deep interest in this church. I had a letter from him only a few days ago saying he was willing, as a trustee of the church, to fall in with the improvements we contemplate. I little thought I should communicate with him no more. His interest in church affairs did not relax after he left this hewn. He threw himself earnestly into such matters in Wales, and was popular and esteemed in his neighbourhood. Whenever I met him he asked specially after Trinity and friends. His heart was with us, if his body was absent. I have been glad to avail myself of his advice; and I may say that had it not been for this our schools, now so popular and flourish- ing, and giving so thorough and efficient an education, might have been in the hands of the School Board. He was one who was respected by all classes of society. He was the philanthropist, the gentleman, and the Christian. His work is done; his day is passed; he is no more. Death has borne him hence. "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord. Yea, saith the Spirit, they rest from their labours and their works do follow them."

Tatar/3LE ACCIDENd Wmarres.—Mr John Hargreaves, whilst riding on his tricycle along Albert-road, was thrown from his seat to the ground. He wan severely shaken, and one of the bones of his foot was broken. TEN Wasuavartco Dirrom—On Wednesday, about 90 teachers and friends of the Ditton Wesleyan Sunday School had a picnic at Lymtn, being conveyed there in waggonettes belonging to Mr J H Lee, of Widnes. Tea was partaken of in a field belonging to Mr Longshavr, of Cherry-lane. Tnacrtans' Promo nom WinetsB.—About 30 teachers connected with Lacey-street Wesleyan Sunday School had 'heir annual picnic on Thursday, when they journeyed to FrodSharn by train. They were accompanied by Mr B Brown and Mr T Sadler, sUperintetaden.s, and the wives of these gentlemen. A pleasant afternoon was spent on Overton

iIL Exconstott. IttOM WIDNES.—The annual excursion in connection with the works of Messrs Mort, Liddell and Co. took place on Saiurday, when abikut 300 persons went b; special train to Southport. Being favoured with fine weather the trippers passed an enjoyable time at the charm- ing watering place, and returned home safely about ten

o'clock. PRESENTATION AT Winans —Mr and Mrs Fred Harper on Wednesday left Widnes en route for Austrafis, where they I intend to settle. Previous to their departure they were pre- minted with a puree of money subscribed by the teachers of Oakland-street Wesleyan Sunday School. Mr Youd made the presentation, and addresses were delivered by Messrs ki Jackson, T Whitby, and S Springett, general regret being expressed at the departure of Mr and Mrs Harper. Mr Harper suitably responded. COMMISSIONERS BANQUET AT RUNCORN.—Mr R Shaw, chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, in- vited the members of the Board and Messrs W H Linalrer (law clerk), W Brookes (secretary), and M Barker (ser- veyor), to dinner at his residence, The Highlands, on Thursday evening. The following were present :—Messrs J Meadowcrof t,T Norman, S Taylor, J Pritchard, P Briscoe, S Williams, P Speakman, J W Lightburn, and F Fairhurst, and Meiers W Brookes and M Barker. kUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—MI William Chadwick licensed victualler, Greenway Vaults, Runcorn, died sud- denly on Wednesday night. For some time Mr Chadwick, who was 65 years of age, had suffered from bronchitis, and he had been under the care of Dr Carruthers. On Wednes- day he was engaged in his usual occupation at the bar, and appeared in the best of health. About eight o'clock in the evening he went into the yard to obtain some article required by the master of the flat owned by him, and while stooping to the ground he was seized with a severe fit of apoplexy. In spite of the efforts of Dr Carruthere, who was imme- diately called in, Mr Chadwick never rallied, and expired about half-past twelve. SAD ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—OR Thursday morning John Rigby. a labourer living in Oak! and-ztreet, was received in the Widnes Accident Hospital suffering from severe scalds. He was employed at the works of Messrs Gossage and Son, soap manufacturers, and shortly before breakfast time on the day mentioned he had his thumb severely crushed. Be- fore resting and attending to his thumb he set about putting a liquor pan in order, by running off some strong lees and allowing fresh water to flow in.. Whilst thus engaged he fainted and fell forward with his arms and bands in the belling liquid, which splashed up into his face. His eyes, face, and arms are seriously scalded, but fortunately there is no fear of him losing his eyesight. He is under the care of Dr McDonnell and Miss Downie. the matron at the hos- pital. FIRE AT A GROCER'S SHOP AT WIDNES.—About twenty minutes to eleven on Sunday morning, the shop of Mr E J Tucketr, provision dealer, Victoria-road, Widnes, was dis- covered to be on fire by Mrs Lydiard, who lives next door. It the same time PC Lamb, who was in the street, observed smoke issuing from the front portion of the shop, 'and look- ing through the interstices in the shutters saw that the in- terior was ablaze. An alarm WAS quickly given, and a crowd of persons assembled. Water was obtained by means of buckets from the Central Hotel, the atables of Mr J H Lee, and from the shop of Mr M Poole, and the fire was ex- tinguished in less than an hour. Valuable aid was lent by P 8 Robinson and several constables. Just when the fire was extinguished. a hand c irt bearing a reel of hose arrived on the scene much to the amusement of the assembled people. The counter was almost completely destroyed, and large quantities of provisions and the fixtures were seriously dam- aged; the total damage to the stock, fixtures, and building being estimated at about £175. The stock and fixtures were insured in the "Royal." How the fire originated is not known, but it is conjectured that it broke out underneath the counter through the accidental ignition of some matches. P C Lamb states that when he entered the shop be found a box containing matches, and several matches lying on the floor close try, near to the front door. SLANDERING A POLICEMAN AT RUNC MN.—Mary O'Neil, a well known character, was summoned before the Rev E A P Campbell and Mr F Rigby, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mill-street, on the 9th inst.—The defendant pleaded guilty, and P.C. Bason gave evidence.—The ,defendant stated that the charge had been made against her in spite, because she had threatened to report the constable for being drunk and for tossing for drinks with a publican's son.-Superintendent Leah said Since the summons was served the defendant had called Upon him several times and had never made any ac- cusation against the constable before. She bad told him that if he would not bring the case before- the Bench she would put £2O in his way on some future ocoasion.—The defendant reiterated that the constable had some spite against her, and bad used "insane language" to her —Mr Campbell : You plead guilty to this charge. There are 15 other convictions against you.—Defendant : Well, all right. (Laughter.) Mr Campbell: You are capable of lying and slandering as well as drunkenness and disorderly conduct in addition. (Defendant: No, Mr Banks, no.) Both. As a liar and a slanderer, as well as a drunken and disorderly character, we now give you what you richly deserve, 405 and costs, or one month's imprisonment with hard labour. —Defendant: Thanks. Mr Campbell The costs are 9s 61. You are one of the worst characters I ever had before me. (To an officer.) Lock her up. Let's have her out.—The defendant was then taken to the cells. A WIDNES LIFE INSURANCE CASE.—At the County Court at St. Helens on Thursday, Patrick Beehan, a la- bourer, of Widnes, Claimed £lB under a policy of insurance- effected in the Liverpool Crown and Anchor Assulance and Burial Society, by transfer from the Pearl Insurance Office, on the life of his mother, Catherine Beehan. Mr C H Lewin, Widnes, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr Quilliam, of Liverpool, for the defendant company.—Mr Lewin said he believed that his friend Mr Qailliam and he were at

Issue on two points only—v,z, that the age of the deceased was not properly stated at the time the insurance was ef- fected, and that Mrs Beehan was in a bad state of health, which the company allege Twas a bar to any claim upon the funds of the society.—Mr John Urqehart, of Widnes, an agent of the society at the time the policy was trans- ferred, said that when Mrs Beehan was assured she was in the workhouse and was in a good state of health, and was suffering only from blindness. She ap- peared to him at the time to be a woman of about fifty years of age, as stated on the policy. He would be surprised to hear that Mrs Beehan was 70 years of age. In reply to the Judge, Mr Urquhart said that insurance agents often effected policies upon the lives of persons in workhouses.—Patrick Beehan said his mother was in good health when she effected the policy, and that she did it for his (witness's) benefit, in order that be might bury her decently, as she did not want to be buried by the parish authorities. He had always paid the premiums regularly, and there were no arrears. No complaint had ever been made about his mother's health either by the society or its agents until he applied for the money after her death.—For the defence Mr Wilson, the district superintendent, said he recollected see- ing Patrick Beehan, who told him that his mother was liv- ing with him in Widnes, and was in good health. He never told witness that she was in.the workhouse. Had he (witness) known she was there he would not have admitted her into the society.—Dr Hull, medic al officer of the Pres- cot Union Workhouse, said he recollected the deceased being in the hospital of that institution. To the best of his belief she was bedfast until she died. He certainly did not con- sider her to be in a good state of health, and did not think he would have passed her for a life insurance. He judged her to be about 68 years of age. Site was not suffering from any defined disease, but chiefly from blindnesa-His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed with costs, refusing leave to appeal. ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE. AT WIDNF.S —B.POIO Mr H Gaskell, jun., and Mr F H Gossage, at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, Stephe Sculley, a chemical labourer, residing in Water-street, was charged on rem int with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting Police-con- stable Lamb whilst in the execution of his duty.—About a quarter past ten on Saturday night the prisoner was cursing and swearing and acting altogether in a riotous manner.— P.O Lamb, accompanied by P.C. Evans, appeared on the scene, and the prisoner immediately retired into his house. In a few minutes, however, he euurged again, and making use of very violent language he rushed at Lamb, and struck him a savage blow on the left eye with his clenched hand. —The prisoner, who had been several times convicted for various offences, was fined 103 and costs on each charge, or in default one month's hard labour.--Peter Clark, a laboarer, was charged with creatine• a disturbance at the Ring O'Bells public-house, Farnworth, and refusing to quit when requested to do so. He was further charged with assaulting P.C. Heatpn whilst in the execution of his duty. —John Clark and Nicholas Walah, labourers, were also charged with assaulting the cenatable.—Frorn the evidence of John Clare, the landlord, P.C. Heaton, and Henry Mauls- ley, it appeared that about half-rast eight on Saturday night a disturbance occurred at the bar of the Ring O'Bells public-house, in which the prisoners were the principals. The landlord attempted to eject Peter after requesting him to leave, but was unsuccessful, and P.C. Heaton, who was in plain clothes, put in an appearance, having been attracted by the noise. He informed the men that he was a camtable, and they retorted that they "did not care who the -- he was." At length all the men were placed outside, and Peter commenced a savage attack on the constable. He knocked the officer to the gra,end, kicked him over various parts oj the body in a vicious manner, and bit his fingers. The other prisoners also kicked him, and he lost no less than a quart of blood from the wounds they had inflicted upon him. Mandsley and several other persons came to his aid, and Peter, who acted like a " madman," had to be secured to a hand cart with ropes and brought to the police station in that way.—ln reply to the Bench the constable said he was still off duty with the Mange he received.— The Bench fined Peter Clark 103 and costs on eaclacharge, or a month's hard labour ; John Clark, 103 and costs, or 14 days' hard labour; and Walsh, who, the evidence showed, had not taken so prominent a part in the row, was fined 5s and costs.—Maudsley, on the application of Superintendent Batker, was allowed his expenses for attending court.
- , The half-yearly meeting of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks will be bold in the Public Roll, ou

Monday afternoon. TIM SUDDEN DICATH AT 'RIINCORN.—On Saturday, MT T J Ridgway, the coroner, beld an lowa into the cause of the death of Patrick Whelan, 59 •years of age, who died under circumstances previously reported.—A, verdict of " Natural causes" was returten.

_ CIIIISHIRE AGRICULTURAL Socanir.--eThe other .day, deputation from Preston, headed by the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), Attended a meeting of the Cheshire Agricultural Society at North rich, and urged them not to hold .a show next year, when the Royal will be held at Preston, and in- viting their co-operation. Col. France-Ray buret, Captain Cotton, and other gentlemen spoke against the holding of the county show, and the subject was adjourned until the annual meeting of the society. SUDDEN DEATH.AT NnwrowN.—An inquest. MS held at the Bridge Inn, Frodshans Bridge, on Monday, by Mt. Henry Churton, county coroner, touching the death of William Acton, a shopkeeper at Newtown, Frodsham, which took place very suddenly on Sunday morning.—The widow of the deceased stated in evidence that her late husband ap- peared in his usual health-en Saturday night._ and died on Sunday morning at one oclock, after about half-an-hour's illness. The jury returned a verdict of 'Died fromnatural causes by heat t disease." WARRINGTON WATDRWORES COMPANIL—AR ordinary half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of this company was held on Wednesday afternoon in the offices, Cairo-street. The Chairman (Lord Winmarleigh) pre3ided and there were also present Sir G Greenall, Messrs J Marson, J Geddes!, T Barham, Foster (Manchester), W Fairhurst, J Jolley, Neild, Mellor, Rev A Kenwotthy, J S Green, E J Nicholson (law J Ross (secretary), and others. The report of the directors, which Was unanimously adopted, was 89 faIIOWS: —The revenue aocount shows a balance, including the balance brought from the previoas half year, of £2.831 03 61 The preference charges amount to xssilTs 10d, leav- ing a balance of £1..,849 21 Bd, out of which the directors recommend that a dividend be paid at the rate of 5 per cent. per annum (less.tax) on the ordinary share capital of the company, carrying forward a balance of 43r3 23 Bcl to the fol- lowing half year. The reserve fund is increased by the sum of £47 103, beiag the amount of premium received upon the sale of preference stock, and now amounts to the sum of £3,617 10s. - -

- LIVERPOOL AND THE SHIP CANAL—The Liverpool City Council on Wednesday confirmed the proceedings of its special Parliamentary Committee, which had expended £B,OOO in opposing the Ship Canal scheme in two seseions. Sir W R Forwood congratulated Liverpool mem the victory achieved, but hoped- there would be no exulting over Man- chester in its defeat. They had saved the Mersey estuary and an important district of Lancashire from the "greatest possible cilamity that could have befallen them." He as- serted that the interests of the two great cities were identical, and that any effort to remove the real grievance—the ex- cessive railway charges—would have his cordial support. if the scheme were modified so as to include a barge canal available for small steamers the main end would be served, and that could be done by purchasing and deepening the Bridgewater Canal at a cost of about two millions sterling. Sir William was certain that if Manchester and Liverpool I would comperate in securing a reduction of railway charges their common grievance would be removed. Batertezaa, MOND & COMPANY, LIMITED, WINNHIGTON.— An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of Brunner, Mond & Co., Limited, alkali manufacturers, held at the Law Associatioa Rooms, Liverpool, on Tuesday, con- firmed a special resolution to increase the nominal capital of the company from £600,000 to £1,500,000, by the crea- tion of 90.000 new shares of £lO each. The next issue of shares will be of 45,000 ordinary shares of £lO each, and 22,500 7 per cent preference shares of £lO each The half- yearly meeting was subsequently held under the presidency of Mr John Crosfield, of Warrington, the chairman of the directors. The financial statement showed a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half. year ended 30th June last of £69282 3s 41, wlrch, with the amount of £18,676 lae Id brought forward from the pre- vious half-year, makes a total of £87.959 is 51. For the third consecutive half-year, a dividend at the rate'nf 35 per cent per annum on the ordinary capital was declared. The dividend on the preference capital is 7 per cent. A sum of £7 500 was placed to the reserve fund, and the balance car- ried forward was £29,647. The directors reported that .arrangements had been made for the acquisition by the company of two patents recently taken out by Mr Mond, for the utilisation of the chlorine contained in the sett used in the manufactare of so4a ash by the ammonia proc as. The report and balance sheet were adopted.—On the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr H. Coghill, Mr T W Read, eccountant, Castle-street, Liverpool, was re-appointed audi- tor.—A. vote of thanks to Mr Crosield for presiding closed the proceedings. TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT FARNWORTH.—The members of the Farnworth branch of the Church of Eng- land Temperance Society held their annual demonstration on Saturday afternoon. About 120 members met at the National School about two o'clock, and headed by the Star of Temperance brass band and the society's beautiful ban- ner, wended their way in processional order through the lanes of the village, returning to the Parish Church, where the Rev H A. MacNaughtain, M. A., vicar of Prescot, preached en excellent sermon to a 1.1,-T! congregation. Sub- sequently a public tea party was held in the school-room, which bad been embellish* i for the occasion with Minting and plants. In the evening an entertainment was given under the presidency of the Pev G Bond, the vicar, who congratulated them upon the success of the demonstration. The first part of the programme consisted of songs and re- citations, the following taking part :—Miss Bond, Miss Haddock, Miss M Fogg, Mica Hibbert ; Messrs A. Certer, B Thompson, J T Lowe, and A G Davies. The glee party in connection with the society rendered several part songs in good style. A temperance drama, entitled, "The brothers, or lost and found," formed the second part of the proceed- ings: The various characters were represented by Messrs J W Davies, F J Whiteside, Thomas Knowles, Thos. Fogg, J Wright, A Balmer, J Banks, W J Beattie, J T Lowe, and A Carter in a praiseworthy manner, and the incidents of The piece appeared to afford the audience considerable pleasure. At the conclusion of the entertainment Mr J W Davies, the Indefatigable secretary to the society, called for three cheers for those who had aided in making the demonstration and tea and entertainment a success, and the audience heartily responded. TM ESTUARY or THE MERSEY.—The uncertain and

changing character of the estuary of the river Mersey, which formed the principal argument of the opponents of the late Manchester Ship Canal Bill, and that upon which the measure was mainly rejected, is indicated at a somewhat apropos moment by a notice which has been issued by the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board. It appears that the result of the surveys of the bay of Liverpool by Admiral Spratt, the acting conservator, and his colleagues upon the Conservancy Board and in the Marine Surveyor's Depart- ment at Liverpool, is to show that very great modifications have taken place in the channels and banks at the entrance of the Mersey. As a consequence, a rearrangement upon a very extensive scale of the lightships and buoys marking the fair way navigation has been resolved upon, and will be commenced on tha 20th Inst.. or as soon afterwards as the weather mar permit. The chief alterations are the follow- ing :—The Formby Lightship (red flash light) will be shifted 250 fathoms west of its present position ; the Bar Light- ship (fixed white light) will be shifted seven.eighths of a mile to the south-west of its present position, and will be moored in fortv-Sve feet of water at low tide •, and the making of the Crosby Lighthouse (fixed white light) will be altered so as to show the lights or bearings from N. N. W. W. round to west. The changes in the bnoyage of the estu- ary are upon a wholesale scale, so much so that the hitherto existing system will be completely altered. Commanders of vessels and pilots will therefore find it necessary to possess themselves of the details of the new scheme, which may be obtained from the Mersey Dock Office. Tlae commissioners of the Northern lighthouses have given notice that on the 15th September next, a fog signal will be established at the Mull of Cantyre Lighthouse, on the Argyleshire coast. The signal will be made from a fog siren, which, during thick or foggy weather, will give two blasts in quick succession every four minutes, the first blast being a high note and the second a low one. LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN COMPANY. ---• HALF- YEARLY MIETING.—This meeting was held at Easton Sta- tion on Saturday. Mr. Richard Moon, who presided, moved the adoption of the report, which has been published. A year ago, he said, a quarter of the dividend came out of reserve. They then hoped trade would revive, but the coo- trary bad happened, and they had this half-year made the biggest drop that hal ever occurred, he believed, in that company's dividend. The directors had watched the ex- penses most carefully, and had had greater competition than ever to meet for the little trade stirring, and for which they had fought fiercely. The mileage of goods trains had gone down 600,000 miles, and the passenger mileage up 350,000 miles. They had a reduction of about 50,000 first-class passengers and of £16,000 in the receipts, but still the first-class passenger pays us an average of ds 3d each ; second-class passengers, whom some people affected to des- pise, still numbered 2,000,000, and there was very little or no change in that class, 'who continued at about the same number, and they got from them 1s 9d each; in the third- class, however, t iere had been the enorrnous increase in the 'numbers carried of 500,600, but for oarying that extra 500,000 the company had only received £9,000. The amount received from each third-class passenger had come down from 10. l to 141. The profit per train mile on the lino had been about a halfpenny less than a year ago. The increased speed of trains had prevented a saving on the 250,000 less miles run. Since last half-year they had re- ceived from the contractors, Messrs. Laird, the steamer which was intended as one of two more for the mail service, but, in censequence of the Government not being able to fulfil their contract, the steamer was rather a heavy loss, havieg been put on the slow service to which they were condemned, instead of the swift service for which she was designed. Speaking on the " grievons subject "of expenses in Parliament, he said the most serious item was the Man- chester Shin Canal Bill. The ships were never likely to go to Manchester, but they had to oppose the bill, which this year came before the Commons' Committee in its "naked deformity." There was not a more practical man in the House of Commons than Mr. Sclatee-Booth, the chairman of the committee which rejected the bill.—ln answer to shareholders, the Chairman added that they were adopting the vacuum brake, believing it to be the best. The report was adopted.—A special general meeting was next held, when it was resolved—" That, in pursuance of the Mary- port District and Harbour Act. 1884, this meeting authorises the company to lend to the trustees for the district and har- bour of Maryport, on the security of morteages of the bar- bear fund, any sum not exceeding £10,000."

Witness SCROOL BOARD AT WORK—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the following were summoned by :the School Board for neglecting to send-their children :regularly to school :—Joseph Doyle, William Campbell, 'Patrick Walsh, Thomas Dunne, John Mullighan, John Clegg, John Sperke§, Patrick Britt, Elietbeth Delaney, 'Dennis Malone, Mary Davis, Robert Yatese.Edward Taylor, William Burrows, John Finch, John Brannon, Thos. Smith (2 cases), Joseph Shone, James McCann, and John Wall.— Mr G H Denby appeared to prosecute, aeat the cases were proved by Messrs Davies, Joynson, and, Rome, attendance officers.—Each defendant was fined 5s including costs. A Itnerennet MAN IN CANADA.—The "London (Canada) Advertiser" of August 2ed contains the following para- graph :—"ln another column will be found an announce- ment of a change in the personnel of a oity firm, Mr Wm. Littler having become a partner in the piano manufacturing business of Messrs Evans Bros., who are.temporarily located at the manufactory occupied by the late Mr Nitschke. The style of the firm will for the future be Evans Bros. and Littler. The last-named gentleman is.a native of the old country, and has for many years been engaged in journalis- tic work on behalf of the "Liverpool Daily Post," which paper he represented for several sessionsin the Press gallery in the Hense of Commons. He has now, we understand, finally quitted the Press to embarkein the commercial under- taking alluded to. A REFRACTORY APPRENTICE AT. WIDNES —On Wednes- dee, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Thomas Dickinson, a youth about 15 years of age, was summoned by George Lease, tool maker, fee not fulfilling his indentares.—lt appeared that the defendant was an orphan, and. was apprenticed to the cemplainant by the Board of Guardians. About three months ago he ran away, and was found last week working at a bottle house " at Sarleetenvie—rhe defendant said that the cempleinant overworked, him. He used to have him at work train helfepast six in the mornme to half-past sight and flies o'clock at night —The complainant said the defendant had a certain amount of work to perform each day, and he could easily do it in eight hours, but he was leave—The Bench made an order upon the def -ndant to return to work, anelwarned him that be would be seat to gaol if he were brought before them again. DADIAnINO A BARRISTER'S PROPERTY AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednes lay, Margaret Reynolds, a well-known character, was charged with doing wilful damage to the property of Mr T Swift, barrister, St Helens, to the extent of Me—Mr E Medley, agent to the property, proved the damage. Eleven panes of glass were smashed in a house in Sutton's lane, and the window frame was broken. A panel had'also been knocked out of the door.— Mary Treace deposed 04 she saw the prieoner sending stones at the window of the house on the 29± July. The defendant acknowledged that she had taken "tin panes of glass which could be bought for a penny a piece at any glasa works in the country," but denied smashing the wine dow frame and door.—Supt. Bicker said this was the woman's fifth appearance this year, and she had not been out of gaol very long. She was, he added, a dangerous person to be at large.—The Bench imposed a fine of 0s and costs, and ordered the damage to he made good. In default the defendant was sent to gaol for a month. RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY—At the half-yearly meeting of this company to he held on Monday, at the Public' Hall, the directors will present the following re- port:—" The revenue account shows a balance of £453 le eld, including £37 03 id brought from the previous half-year, out of which the directors recommend a divi- dend to be declared at the rate of £3 103 per ceranm per annum, free from income tax, payable on and after the let day et September, this will absorb £4.74 2c leaving a balance of V lfle SI to be carried forward. The ' auxiliary iron tank bee b-en fixed and completed, as well as the bye-pass connecting the inlet and tlet mains at the reservoir, the reflux valve and the relief valve, and 'main to the cooling pond ; these have all been at work land answered admirably during the necessary repairs of the reservoir. The engine-house roof has been thoroughly repaired so as to withs'and the gales of wind to which its elevated position sulajc's it iu wiater. The water in our well has been more than sufficient for all demands during the present dry summer, and it continues to be of excellent quality." RUNCORN • BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Mr. John Ashton prcsided ever the fortniebtly fleeting held on Tuesday. There were present—The Revs J W N Tanner, J Lockwood, Mews Norm in, Wallington, Aaron Midwood, Rigby, Darbyshire, and IlleTntyre.—Visit to the Asylmin : In accordance with the notice he had given, Mr Wallington moved that the Chairman of the Hence commit- tee (the Rev J %V N Tanner), the Rev J Lockwood, Meters Thomas Norman, W Hendley, J Warburton, himself, sod the Clerk ha a committee to v'sit the asvlurn.—Mr Rigby : A nice lot—e nice select lot"P—Mr Derbyshire—The Anibu• lance: The Rev J Lockwood presented the report of the Finance Committee, who recommended the payment of an account of £4O for the ambulance.—Mr Norinan seconded the motion, and observed that the relieving ale .rs ought to he informed that when there was any infectious case, the ambulance ouaht to be sant for. During the last fortnight Mr Wright had sent a person suffering from so infectious disease in an ordinary conveyance, and this ought not to have been done. After some conversation it was decided that the contractor to the WArlchousl (Mr Grounds). be asked to. provide a horse for the ambulance whenever required, at the rate of 51 within three alles redien aml a shilling per mile beyond that radius.

div.head: ALARMING FIRE; TWO lIORSFS
div.p: ALARMING FIRE; TWO lIORSFS
SUFFOCATED.

About one o'clock yesterday morning a fire broke out at ! Warrington which, though not so extensive as to prove des- tructive to the building in which it originated, was the! cause of the death of two valuable horses belonging to a detachment of the 11th Hussars. It appears that on Tnurs- ! day an advance contingent of the troop arrived in Warring- ' ton to procure billets for their or-Al-trades and the horses in question were put up at the White Hart stables in Sankey- street, belengiog to Mrs Brierly, and situated opposite the hotel, the horses being placed in two separate compartments. A sergeant and a private were billeted at the hotel. At one o'clock the following morning a man named Thomas Dykes, who resides at 28, Factory-yard, Warrington, was passing the stables, when his attention was attracted by smoke coming out of the buildings. He at Once gave an alarm, and Police-sergeant Jones, who was at the time near the ! place, ran to the stables and burst open the door. TI was then found that two battens of straw had by some means or another been ignited and were causing dense volumes of smoke. Attempts were quickly made to rescue the animals, but it was found that one of the horses had been already suffocated by the smoke, and that the second one was in a state of great agony. The fire engine arrived on the scene and the fire was extinguished with very lit'le difficulty. Mr. Robinson, veterinary surgeolt was called in to see the second horse, and he ordered it to be shot to put it out of its misery, which order was at once carried out. The two horses are valued at £9O. la a stable immediately adjoining the one where the outbreak oc- curred was a horse valued to be worth about £4OO, but fortu- nately it sustained no injury. The cause of the fire is some- what obscured in mystery, but many rumours have been in circulation on that point, as when the fire was disc evered one of the fir:sears was seen coming from the coach-house adjoining in a dazed condition, as though be bad been !asleep It is said that on Thursday night the soldier re- turned to the White Hart after the house was closed, and went to the coach-house to sleep, but how the fire really did originate is merely g matter of conjecture. . The Hussars, to the number of about 100. arrived in the town yesterday.

div.head: WARINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this body was held at the office in Sankey. street, on Wednesday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr Richard Houghton, J.P., the other members present being Messrs J Hartley, J.P , vice-chairman, J Bridge, W B Kerfont, J Staniar, E Marsh, J Turner W 'Lepton, H Woolff, J Houghton, and J Grounds.—The Surveyor's re- ports on the roads in the district of the Board were read and discussed, and the Surveyor was instructed to submit to the next meeting a statement of what materials and tools he is lin need of, and what further will be required until the end of the year, with a view of obtaining tenders for the supply thereof.—An application was made by the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephonic Exchange Company Limited, for per- mission to erect 51 poles from 'ran-house in Surtonwood to a stated point at Parr Flat. The necessary permission was given subject to an annual payment of Is per pole per annum. --.Mr Hartley made reference to the recent death of Mr Broadhurst, a former member of the Board, and the follow- lowing resolution was subsequently unanimously passed, viz. :—" That this Board desires to express its sincere con- dolence and sympathy with the widow of the late Mr Samuel Broadhurst, at the heavy loss they have recently sustained by his death. The Board also desires to record its sense of the services rendered by Mr Broadhuret during the fifteen years that he was a member of the Board, for three years of which he was chairmen, and four vice-chairmen."—A letter was re- ceived from Mr. Sadler, deputy-clerk of the peace, Preston, forwarding a copy of a reseln, ion pasted by the County Highway Committee disallowing certain items in the main road account sent in by the Warrington District Highway Board for the year ending 25th March. The resolution, be- ing an extract from the minutes of a meeting of the County Highway Committee, held at the County Offices in June last, was as follows Resolved that the following sums be disallowed from the account sent in by this Authority, viz , £136 193 charged under the bead " Materials."'for old materials contributed by the late trustees, and £27 17s lid charged under the head of "Tradesmen's Bills," for costs of working steam rollers, making a total reduction of £164 103 11d, and that the said account be passed at the sum of £696 5s 31, as certified by the County Surveyor and County Auditor." After a discussion the Clerk was instructed to write to the Clerk of the Peace and point out that the whole of the materials thus disallowed, were not left by the trustees of the Turnpike trust, and that therefore the Board claimed lobe allowed the value. The chairman and vice-chairman were appointed a deputation to attend with the surveyor at the next meeting of the county au- thority, in the event of the claim not having been settled before that takes place.—This was all the business of in- ' terest.

Samuel Edwards, a labourer living at Trefoiien, was, on Wednesday, remanded at Odwestry on a charge of shooting D tvid Breeze with intent to murder him. The prisoner had been living with Breeze's wife, an,l uring a quarrel on Tuesday night he fired at the husband with a gun, inflicting a dangerous Wound in his left side.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON,. TIMISDAT. Preparations for the relief of General Gordon are now in so forward a. state that at any time we mar hear that the column is en rtute. To-day news arrives, that renders it doubtful whether it will proceed by. the Nile ropte, at present contemplated, or whether the older Line of march by Sonakim. must perforce be taken. The Nilo instead of con- tinuing to rise as at this period of the year it has done for centuries, is distinctly falling, and the cataracts are impas- sable. This may, however, be the precursor of a further rise, it being within the limits 9f experience that previous to a great rise the Nile has temporarily fallen. There has been another letter from General Gorden marked by the same terseness noted in his firsL It might well be imagined that he would have much to say of the strange life he leads in the desert stronghold. One w.ould suppose that so long cut off from mankind in the outer world he would, finding an opportunity to write at all, even be garrulous. But if he were telegraphing to London from China or Japan, his words costing nine or ten shillings each for transmission, he could uot be more chary of their use. "How are you? I'm pretty well, thank you," is what his anxiously looked for letter amounts to.

The country campaign preliminary to the sharp and de- cisive fight that will lake place at Weatmiester in Novem- ber is steadily going forward. In official circles on the Liberarside there was a.desire to see some lull for at least a fortnight after the rising of Parliament. • it is felt that though it was eminently desirable to have such a magnifi- cent demonstration as that which filled the streets of Lon- don in July no practical good could come of meetings con- tinuously held through August. Ae far as regards affecting the action of the Lords in November it was like firing at a hopelessly long range, and there was, moreover, *the apprehension of popu- lar enthusiasm ineffectually working itself out. Hut the crisis is one in which the people are not to be controlled by nicely balanced calculations. 'they have a strong feel- ing in the matter of the conduct of the Lords, and they are not to te debarred from giving it instant expr,:ssion. There is a general concensas of opinion that the fight will really begin on Saturday week when Mr Gladstone appears on the , old battle-field of Midlothian. The cambined forces ad the newly-allied Leaders is to be marshalled in order to counter- act his influence, and scarcely shall the echo of his voice have died away in Edinburgh when there will be uplifted the voices of Lord Salisbury, Sir Stafford Northcote, and Lcrd Randolph Churchill. The election of Mr Ferguson in Ross and Cromerly is a pleasing kind of preliminary welcome. It is thirty-two I years since the county was contested, and then a Liberal secured his seat by the narrow majority of twenty. In such circomttances it was not without some feeling of apprehen- sion on the part of the Liberals, and with a reasonable hope I on the part of the Tories that an election contest was entered upon. The chance of the Conservatives was vastly im- proved by the local feeling, which made possible the candi- dature of a roving politivan who declared himself in a I special degree the champion of the crofters. It was not likely that, Dr Macdonald wood win the seat ; bet it was certain • he would abstract a good many vaes from the Liberal can- didate, and with a balance of only twenty at the last general election the Liberals clearly cautd not off ,rd to dispense with may support. In estimating the probable results of the general election, Scotland is always regarded as one of the weak points of the Liberal position, and this for a peculiar reason. The feet is that in 1880 Scotland was so completely swept clean of Conservative representatives that there is posi- tively nothing more left to win, and there is of course the probability that some seats gained by narrow majorities amid the enthusiasm of 1880 will be regained by the Con- servatives. I happened to be in Edinburgh at the time of the general election and remember the daily scenes at the club in Princes-street, where, between eight o'clock and mid- night, the telegraph brought news of Tory stronghold after stronghold stormed by the Liberal candidates. div.p: the scepticism which her first minifeetatione created. Miser

-- Hurst, known as "the Georgia Wonder," is quite as wonder- ful as Mr Bisbcp or Mr Stuart Cumberland. Merely pres- sing the palm of her band against a stick, without grasping it, she can prevent its being forced downwards by the efforts of an athlete. Holding an umbrella lightly in her hand it. begins to twist in demoniac fashion finally, ending by being turned inside out. Miss Hurst lifts a chair containing the stoutest available man, by pressing her palms against the side of it. She lays strong men flat on their backs by sim- ply touching them, and performs other apparently incredible feats. It is only nine months ago sinoe Miss Hurst dis- covered herself possessor of this mystic force. According to her own account she was holding an. tumbrel's when the ends of her fingers " seemed to pop" the umbrella underwent. various contortions, ending in its &Ist explosion. fhis is scarcely a clear explanation, and cannot be regarded as satis- factory. Eat the exhibition is certainly wonderful.
