div.p: LUCK, 41ANAGEM ENT ? A STORY OF gATING AND DRENKING.

It was a ban stammer's evening in one of the 'London suburbs. Wrack was over, and all along Noritam-atreet the doors stood open. On the, doorsteps men and women lounged in every sort of,soress and undress, and crow& of children swarmed across the narrow street, and pursued their noisy -games in utter diamgard of the passers-by. There were forty or fifty .Louses all built exactly alike, but there the likeness encletl. Through the °ken doors one could see that some were nearly bare, some so c.rowded with furniture that it axaz hardly possible to get in. One was bright and airy, white the oar; next door revealed a dark gloomy cavity, only made the less inviting by the conttaat with the sunshine oasicle. No: was the contract less re- markable between the people at the &ors. Of all the faces, not one was mare cheerful and happy than Mrs. Tom Wat- son's, who stood with her hand. up to her forehead to shade the sun, looking .dow,c,the long straight road. It was not , often that Mrs. Watson wa.s ictlez found in so convenient a position for a chrt. Souse her, noighboare phrase, Mae was one "who kept herself to herself." So perhaps it was the rarity of the chuncethat induced a woman some years younger than Mrs. Wats= to stcp.and speak to her. 'This new-corner was walking slowly down the road with a -child of about three years old ,dragging at her skirts, and her.urms fully occuoied in the caw of an apron full of potatoes, and a large bag of small parcels with a coupin of zed herrings rolled ia a very small piece of newspaper lying on the top. "Good evening to ton, Kary," elee said, in a high-pitched. querulous tone. "fle worad ,nses your well, as usual. I aleedrift ask how you are." Macy Watson turned round with a friendly nod and smile, but bears she could rerty her questioner went on "I can't think how it is some people have such luck with their children. Mine are always aiiipg. Yours are never ill, Mrs. Watson. Even when yours did get the measles they were up in no tier.e, and mine were ill weeks and weeks, and we couldn't get theirstrengthsip anyhow. Just look at the difference bet weez them, now. None would ever think your,rom was six meath.z-youngee,than my Ted, poor lamb." "Why, he does look sadly, Addy. What's the matter with him, p.ocr little dear? Lie looks more. fit to be at home in bed than welking about the streets. Tom west to bed half-an-hour ago." And Mrs. Watoom took the little fellow up in her arms. He was not a very heavy burden, and her motherly heart was grieved to see the .swhite, thin lips, tiny drawn facc--so different from her own boy's rosy cheeks. "Gone to Wl'''. etacelated Adelaide White. "Well, that's a thing I could floor bring Ted to. All our children are such bad sleepers. And as for Ted. however late it is, he must always sit up 2.r.d have a bit of !swapper with iris father. Very fond of him h. Lather is. Why. if I were to pet him to bed, as soon as ever he heard the rattleof the pl stec he'd scream till you'd think the roof would be off, and th.w.a his father would be sore to fetch him." "You look tired, Addy." Mrs. Watson said. "Core in arid sit down a bit, and.let me give you a glass of my oat- meal drink. It's very goat, though it's so cheap. I boil a table-spoonful of coarse oatmeal for half-an-hoar in a quart of water, and flavour it with citric acid and angst. My John likes it hot or cold." "No, thank you. I must bs moving. My Fred will be home presently, and if I haven't got his supper ready he'll be off to the King's Head. He's out on a late job to-night, but I expect him home in half-ae-boar or so. Is your good man out toe? I thought he always came home early." "He's been in and had his tea long ago," responded Mrs. Watson. "Bat he went oat agile, because he had promised to take the children do wn to the new garden that's been opened. It's l'o;ly's birthday, act: that is her birthday treat." "I should like to zee Fred bothering himself with a parcel of children. Be went a drive out into the country last Mon- day, but I haven't been out for a couple of years. It's all I can do to get my work done, and to find a it of food to put into the children's months. Why, my husband was out of work for a ample of months last winter, and we haven't paid up all we owe yet. There's no money for me and the children to go holiday-making. But thtt's another piece of your luck, Mary. Your husband has never lost a week's work since you were married. Come, Ted, we must be going. Daddy'll be home first, and won't he scold then." Mrs. Fred White went her way down the street, and Mary Watson watched her till she passed out of tight at the corner, and then turned away with a sigh. "Poor Addy !" she said; "I'm afraid she's her own worst enemy." - These two women were acquaintances of many years' standing. They came from the same country village to ser- vice, and had begun by coming to the same house to live with a cousin of Mary's mother, married to a hard-working man of business. Mary had ben the younger of two ser- vants at first, but after some years ths elder servant left to be married, and Mary was promoted to her place; and then it was that she obtained permission to send home for Ade- laide, who had lust left school. But Adelaide did not stay long. She had an acquaintance who was servant in a large house near by, and she was readily persuaded that she could do much better for herself than to stay where she was so strictly looked after, where the wages were not high, and where even the food was of the plainest kind. So Addy left, and s3on, for she had a very good character, she obtsinerla place as one amongst many servants in a a large luxurious house, and she was sure only jealousy prompted Mary to say that someday she would regret having left her old mistress, Mrs. Field. Mary, in her plain woollen gown and neat straw bonnet, who breakfasted off porridge, and want home from her "Sunday out" to dine off the joint that had to serve the family for most of the weekly dinners ; Miry, who did all the work of the house, and was by turns, cook, nurse, housemaid, and laundress, might certainly appear a much less distinguished person than Addy, who was resplen44r3 in ribbons and jewellery, who had her work so carefully ritapvr'd out that she hardly, ever went inside the kitchen; and he'ver etoke More than a ' Chance Word to tha children. But then, not to speak or good store of linen laid by in Msry's box, not everyone knew that Mary had money in the bank, far more than enough to buy all Addy's finery ; and not everyone thought how Nary was able to tura her hand to anything—how she Could market with the least possible money, and cook the most appetising d'shes out of what she brought home; how she was nearly as good as a doctor with all the chil;iren's ailments; and how she kept the house and hers-.?.j as clean and bright as a new pin, and yet never eeeleed to have any- thing particular to do. All these things do not show out- side, and I must confess that Addy, who could not boil a potato, nor nurse a baby, nor go a marketing, and had not a penny piece laid by, oftentimes looked very pretty in her finery. No one will be surprised to hear, however, that one person had found out Mary's good qualities. Before Addy left Mrs Field's service Mary had been for some time en- gaged to John Watson, a young men in constant work at a large factory in the neighbourhood. But neither Watson nor Mary were in a hurry to get married until they hid saved up a few pounds to begin housekeeping with, and so it happened that they were married in the same month as Addy, who becam3 Mrs. Frederick White, and settled down in a house not a stone's-throw from Norham-street. White was a cabman, his work was well paid, and in sum- mer he earned high wag's, but then he was apt to be out of work during the winter. However, the two weddings took place in the spring, and with plenty of money coming in and only themselves to think of, you may imagine what a good time Mr. and Mrs. Fred White had till the following au- tumn. White often said that no gentleman's table was better supplied than his own, and on Saturdays, when wages were paid, and Sundays when he had a whole holiday, there I was nothing too good or too expensive for him to buy. But autumn came, and slick work; and then winter, .and for some weeks work ceased altogether. They had not one penny laid by, aud of course they had to go on credit at the shops where they were known. There was no more, feasting on Sundays nor on any other day in the week, if they could only ot on credit enough food to keep them from hunger they thought themselves fortunate. To do Adelaide justice, she tried to bear all the brunt of the battle herself. She did her very best to make things comfortable for her husband, and to get a piece of meat for his snpper, though she fed herself day after day upon bread, or a potato with a little weak tea. She, psor child, looked ill and worn, and if Fred White had used his eyes or his sense to good parpose,he would have seen that his wife grew more wan and weak every day; but he only noticed that home we:oft as comfortable as it once had been, and that she wasn't as pretty, nor as good-humoured, nor as rosy as she used to be in the old courting days, when she had lived on the fat of the land and worked little. Before spring was round again a tiny white-faced baby had come to glad- den the home, and brought a new smile to Addy's worn face. But though work and wages were again to be had, and food was once more plentiful, Addy's strength would not return ; and before the roses blossomed the baby•face was white in d-atb, and the poor young mother was broken-hearted. Such a sad, stern lesson it was! And, after all, I do not think that she learned it, for the next year, and the next, and every year until this time, White had earned large wages in the summer, and feasted; and had earned nothing in the winter, and starved. The only difference was that as years went on ether children claimed the loving heart that th

first baby had left so^denelate, so there were fivemouthe in- stead of two, and thesammer feasting was somewhat cur- tailed, and there werefive to starve in the winter, and it was not Adelaide alone who grew wan and thin on ,tea and bread. White did not. Tea he diet not care for, and as there was nothing to drink at home bat tea and water, and he qiked water even less *ma lea,•ke had gotinto the habit of sending his eldest child to the public-house for beer, if he did net go I to fetch it himself, when he usually stopped to drink:it, and I often drank far more than tee conld afford either for his Ihealth or his pocket. After a night or two spent like this, when Saturday wages wore paid there was a tong-score to be settled, and not mach mosey came to the poor wifeeeveka sat waiting at home over the.dying fire, to bay the children's food for a week. Thingseeemed so bad that it was. useless trying to make them better, and as they were not made better they grew, as things do, from bad he worse. Mrs. White said quite traly that her children were always If they took any ckildish ec=plaint they never picked up Itheir strength like the selghbour's little ones. ic they .went to school they never were in theaame standards astheir companions. If there wasear_ything about in the rev the little Whites were sure to be the first to catch ih. She saoke -the truth, too, when she told Mary Watson that -Fred liked better to sit in the publio-house than to takethe,children to the parks; that I think esheeoctild hardly havedorgoteen how he had once upon a time ,taken his boy on a half-hollday stroll with John Watson and John's eldest little girl, who strode along bravely and merrily. Poor little Freddy was knocked up directly, and, crying for weariness, had to be carried all the way home. Ee was such a pretty boyoreith his mother's eyes, and long,. fair curls hanging ,down his back. But proud though A delaide was of her darling's ,beanty, she would have given it all to see him a hit -stronger, , running about on a pair of sturdy straight limbs Like little Polly Watson, for Freddy's legs were as crooked as a .couple of bows and the baby's bid fair to match them. "Itiajnet .my Luck! " Adelaide eigehed to, herself. alac Whites' home hod net, yet become like the most wretched of the neighbourhood.; yet, turning from it to-the Watsan's cheerful cottage, yoawsuld certainly have thought that yen had turned from poverty to wealth. And so -in truth you would, if you agree that poverty depends not on the amount of a men's peeeessiona, hut on the use lee makes of them When Adelaide spoke of the many weeks her husband %ME , short of work and of John Watson's luck and constant -em- • ployment, she sorely forgot that, raking the year through , White's income was the larger, and that if he had had the sense to spread out his income throughout the year, even his weeks oat of work were good opportunities for improving himself And fitting himself to occapy a better position.. John Watson was no teetotaler whenhe married. But Karr had learnt la service to do withe at been, and teeing what temp- tations to drink fall in the way of working men, she da- *to:lined ths4, if John ever took to c mach,' tshould be by no f salt .e 4 hers. She was far too wise a woman-to feed. her husband ,are cold salt ,fod because it 111.1 E less trouble at the time. !That is one of the ways in which lazy ~people save a few ,present pains at the expense of untold ntare sorrow. If a man is fed on .Cairst-producing food it is .only natural that he should drip, and if he can get nothing-to drink but beer, heo-aill go to the public-house to fetch-it. Ceohn's can when- he went to work was always filled oval-same wholesome drink, cold in swelter, something to heat le winter. land at night when :Jchn came home it was a rare thing if Mary had not some borfood for him soup era savoury stew, or even a eubstantial pudding. John was neverdarned out in a morning with only a breakfast of cold baconand bread, or bread and cheese, washed down with weak tea, but he started to his worleaeell warmed and comforted with a good basin or porridge, or a steaming cap of tocoa, o: ,eocoa and oatmeal, or good coffee. And as for the childree, running ; to school after such a good breakfast, they were alert and had began their lessors in no time, while some of their schoolmates, who got /lc thing better than bread with a scrape of treacle and a little cold tea, were shivering and incapable half the mocning. "Don't area find it a,deal of trouble, Mrs. Watson-' the I neighbours often asked. I'm sure I find the day all too short for what I'm obliged to do, let alone undertakinga lot of extra work." "The little tronble I . take at the beginning saves Me a great deal in the end," Mary always replied; "nit that d'm unwilling to do what makes erly good man and the children so much healthier and happier, even if it does cost use some pains. But it's like a good many other things in the world. A stitch in time, you know. Lazy people always give themselves the moat work in.the long ran. What trouble is it to pour a little b dling water over to-morrow morning's porridge? I shouldn't do anything else if I didn't do that. Aud if I do get up ten minuteseetrlier to boil the porridge next morning, isn't that much less worry than to hear the children fret and cry, or to have the teachers complain that they don't get on in srhool It's jut the same with my good man's supper. Wouldn't I rather, a thousand times over, take a little pains to cook for him, to have something hot and comfortable that we can both sit down to, than see him get his meals without a bit of comfort about the place, and then perhaps to go off to amuse himself like many men do. Even for myself it's worth while to take a little trouble. Why, I've known scores of women grunolde because they had got indigestion so bad that life was jaat a misery to them, and when you come to inquire, it's always the same , tale-: 'I can't touch a bit of anything till Poe had my tea.' They take their tea, and have taken it for years, four and five times a day, and hardly another bit of hot food week in and week out, just because they were too lazy to cook for themselves, and it wasn't much trouble to set the kettle on. 1 There's no accounting for taste, but I'd rather, if I am to be I plagued with a thing like indigestion, not have myself to thank for it. Bo you don't catch any kettle en the hob all day long." It was a favourite topic of Mrs. Watson's, and she was apt to "run on," as her neighbours put it, if once she were started. Another of her favourite practices was always to pay ready-money. "It's only a case of getting just one week before-hand," she frequently declare-I. "The money that's paid on a Saturday night ought to de for the week that's coming, instead of the week that's gone." _ .
----- - ,- Strangely enough, few of the neighbours could see that. - - --

_ "We ain't all so rich as you, Mrs. Watson. It's lucky for you you can," they would reply. "We can't hardly pay for what we have had, and it'll be a long time before we find- money for what we're going to have." One might have thought, to hear them talk, that if they waited long enough the bills paid themselves. Mrs. Watson had also a reputation for getting wonderful bargains at the shops where she dealt. "It was just like her luck," folks said; "she was always a lucky woman." To peep one moment behind the sures, her " luck " con- sisted in this: she was known at the shops as a regular cus- tomer who always paid ready money. No one had ever lost a penny by her; on the contrary, she was a customer well worth keeping and paying some attention to. On the other hand, there were people in the street who were always run- ning in for penn'orths of this' and ha'porths of the other, taking up 118 mach of the shopman's time to serve them as Mary's groceries for the whole week; there were others who ran up bills, and were months before they paid- there were others worse still, who begged for credit and never paid at all. If all these had taken their custom to another shop, the grocer would have been rather glad than otherwise. Be certainly would take no pains to keep them. But Mary's custom was quite another thing, and if anything specially good came in, or if a bargain was to be offered, or if any- thing could be sold at a little less price, it was Mary Watson who got the chance, and it was quite natural and fair that she should. We left Adelaide White trudging weariiy home with her bun4W her boy, ylq bt'r two herrings. It was late, and she t, was tired, so she just blew up the nre, touted the Pan, mane tea out of the kettle that had simmered all the afternoon, took one dish out of the cupboard with a few cold potatoes, another with some pieces of bread, and set them both on the table with a third plate of very warm butter, and the sup- per was ready. Milk there was none, for what had b:en left from the morning had been put in a dirty jug and had turned 8011 T. Fred White came in, hot, dusty, and very cross. Be tossed his coat into the nearest chair, threw his hat into another, gave one ill-satisfied glance over the table, the soiled cloth, the unappetising meal, and sat down without a word. Little Ted looked at his father's face, and having learnt wisdom by experience' slunk out of sight. Adelaide gave her husband his cap of tea, took another for herself, with one of the crusts of bread and a potato, and the supper proceeded for some moments in silence. Both the herrings, with the least dry bread and the lion's share of butter, fell to White's share; it was an arrangement he was accustomed to, and doubtless thought quite natural and right. But to the poor wife, whose crust was very unappetising, it seemed hard tbat Fred should begin grumbling over his food. Lie had looked in at Watson's on his way home, and had found such a cheerful family group gathered round a supper-table so different to his own, that he could restrain his feelings no r longer. And when at last even the weak washy tea came to an end, and there was nothing to drink but water, that had been warmed in the sun all day long, he started up with something like an oath on his lips, and muttering that "When afellow did mean to do his best he didn't have half a chance," left the house. No one need ask where he was gone. His wife knew only too well. No need to warn her what she has to expect when White's heavy, uncertain steps are neard along the street. This sort of thing happens often—every year more often. He is only a good deal worse tonight than usual, for the weather is hot and thirsty. and the stuff he drank was prepared not to quench thirst but to excite it. Next morning, as Mrs. Watson was locking her front-door, preparatory to starting on her weekly day's shopping, the doctor, who was an old acquaintance of hers, stopped on her I threshold.

"Thank you, ro, Mrs. Watson, I'm busy and can't come in to-day," he said. "I want you to go round and see Mrs. Fred White. She's a friend of yours, I think. White's met with an accident at his work this morning, crushed one of his fingers and sprained his wrist. I'm afraid he won't do much work far some time to come. From all I hear he'd been drinking heavily overnight, and then this morning he was muddle-hesded and clumsy. What he did no one seems to know, but he got wrong with the chaffcutter or something, and there he is, poor fellow. I'm afraid he has not a very comfortable home. I wish you'd teach his wife a lesson in housekeeping, Mrs. Watson. You'll go in and see what you can do, I know." And the kind-hearted, busy man drove off. Of course, Mrs. Watson would go in. Poor Adelaide was sitting in the midst of an untidy room, the remains of break- fast on the table, the week's in just begun, sitting help- less, crying, with her head n her hands. "It's just my luck !" she sobbed out. " It would have been bad enough if it had happened when work was !lack, but just now, at the best time of year, and we not paid up

for tasty/deter:yet ! What shall I do? Whatthall do?" MarrWatson was much too kind-rs woman even to re- member at such a moment that possibly it was not all a question of luck. It was a time for work, nct talk, and Mary tock off her bonnet and set the 200111 straight in less than no time. Then she took Ted's hand and moved to the door. "I'll clrae back before long, and lookin again, Addy." she said. wßcn't you bother about Ted; he shall-stay with my youngsters for a bit till you're straight. Can I get any- thing feryou at the shop? Mr. White 'll be wanting some- thing presently, and there'll be the children home from school atrhalf -past twelve." Addy's cobs broke out afresh. There was nothing in the house. ',Fred would eat nothing hat meat. He hated slops. The doctor had ordered him broth, and how was she to get broth,ette'd like to know? That was all very well for rich folk. -As for the children, they'd get a piece of bread and a serape of dripping, and think themselves lucky to get as mach. She didn't know where oven bread was to come front , afar.: this week. She hadn't a shilling.in the house. and Oleg wouldn't trust her in the Arms any more. It wasmoarly half-past twelve when Mrs. Watson came back, with little Ted by her side,,carefully holding some- thing date up in brown paper. "I've brought you a drop of potato-soup for Mr. White, Addy. I,eltanced to have just a cupful left.from last night, as mach-ac he'll eat, and you haven't much time.lor cooking yourself. .And Ted's brought you a present of one of my pasties. .it's nothing but a bit of crust, with potato and onion, and-sweet herbs inside, and a mouthfal.of bacon to ! give it a relish ; but the children like it better, than bread- and-dripplug, and I don't know that it costs anymore. And , as you were out of groceries, I thought maybe the children r could havac. dish of porridge when they come in, as it doesn't take long to make, so I brought a pen'orth of meal with me." _

....- -- 1 Who could refuse presents so kindly meant? Belem Addy could deterae:ne what she should say, there was -a. saucepan on the fire, and Mary was stirring the meal into the boiling ' water. An&then, when the children came, they were so pleased with the nice hot porridge and treacle; and father , came down to see what was going on, and delighted Td by • eating a .niens of the pasty he had brought. ButALe soup Iwas the best success; for White (as may be supposed) had not a fine appetite after his accident, and onion ,pasty, ! though excellent in itself, was not quite to his taste just then. The potato-soup—though it was made only of potato and turnip,and.a scrap of onion, with water, and pepper and I.and salt and dsipping, with a little sago and milk.added- 6tasted,first-rate, and, served up with a nice piece of toast, it iaaft nothing to.bn desired. I Many•days after that, Mary Watson's eheerful•face ap- .4:eared,at the ,Whites' door; and if she came empty-handed, i.she brought a.pair of hands that could work the most won- . derf al transformaCons. She would take scraps of vegetalles that Addy thought only fit for the dust-bin, peelings of turnips, half a carrot, with a small bone from a chop and a bite: bacon-rind, and beforeyou knew where yen were, there was a teacupfulci broth ready to be thickened with flour,or Image, and to make a capital dinner for Fred, who wasn't allowed too much sold food all at once. Another time the would take the pieces-of bread, and, soaking them in water, would add the dripping and treacle that might have been spread on them, with a halfpeenyworth of currants, and there_ was a pudding fit for asking. One day she persuaded Ade-, laide to take in half-alemartern °Ulant instead of a loaf, an with nothing but baking-powder and cold water, she boiled big light dr.mblings for ,the family supper, to be eaten with treacle or hot dripping. She never preached, or appeared to think herself any wiser than other folks; but if -tUre was anything she knew that I was likely •to be useful to anyone else, she took as much pains to tell them as if it were some benefit to herself. And every day Addy found herself wondering at the number of cheap foods she had never thought of buying, had never even heard of. 141 the house where she had lived before her marriage, everyone believed that meat was the only thing to do you any good, and that the more you ate the batter you were. Addy kept that belief still. Only, as meat was not always come-at-able, she did not.eat mach, and she fell back then on white bread and butter. As for vegetables; she never thought of theirbeing anything better than luxuries— things you bay to eat with meat when you've a few pence to spare. It was quite a revelation to her when Mary first made her a present of two-pennyworth of dried haricot beaus, and told her that they were really more nourishing than meat. She would nqj have believed it, but that she found the children's appetites were satisfied with so little, that she began to think it must be true' though at first she considered that quite a point against beans—that you could only eat so very few. Of coarse, Adelaide White did not become a good cook and manager all at one bound. There were many difficulties to o.vereome, and cooking, like most other trades, needs a long apprenticeship. But she did leave off laying all mis- I fortune: to the door of her ill-luck, and she began to under- ' stand that many of her misfortunes had come beeline of her I own ignorance or indolence, and that they would come again It she did not work hard and learn how to avert them. Many a time when she was inclined to stay in bed of a morning she got up, rather than that her children should go 111-fed to school. Many a time, when she was solely tired, she resisted the temptation to sit idle or to gossip on the doorstep until her husband's supper was ready. Very often, indeed, money was short, and it would have been easy to run up a bill, or to carry something to the pawnbroker's; and yet, somehow, Adelaide planned and contrived to do without one or the other. And she had her reward. All these things happened some years ago; and now, if you were to go down that suburb, you would find neither Mrs. White nor Mrs. Watson. John Watson save money enough to buy a donkey and cart, and a cow, and a few pigs, and he has gone back to live in the country village where Mary passed her childhood. It has been the dream of Mary's life; and just as in London she had always done her very best, so now, in the country, her cottage is the prettiest, her butter the best, and her husband the happiest for miles round. The Whites have not done quite so well as that. They began too late, perhaps, when the Watsons had the start of them. Fred White is one of the steadiest, soberest men in his yard, though, and has managed to get his own horse and cart, and has insured his life in the post-office and belongs to a sick club; so that there is very little /ear of their coming to want again, whatever the 'olive may hold in store for them.
Eat to live, not live to eat. Plain living means high thinking. To know that which before vs lies in daily life is the prime wisdom.

IThe two men, Wright aid Wheatley, charged with shoot- ing Police Constables Suell and Garner at Hoxton, were again brought np at Worship-street Police Court on Thurs- day, and further remanded pending the recovery of Snell. FATAL ACCIDENT WITH FIREWORKS —During a display of fireworks at Bournemouth, on Wednesday night, while some rockets were being seat up from a steamer, a bomb or signal rocket WS by mistake exploded, and several persons were injured, one, a grocer's assistant, so seriously that be died on Thursday mrmning in the hospital. It is stated I that the captain of the steamer received terrible wounds, and that between 20 and 30 persons were injured. IMPRISONMENT OF A CLEROYMAN.—At the Preston Ses- sions, en Thursday, the Rev John James Lang, curate of Therm on-in-Craven, was found guilty upon an indictment charging him with having as- saulted two girls at Resegrove, near Burnley. The prisoner formerly held curacies in Salford and Annotate, and evidence was given that hitherto he had held an unblem- I Mei character. The Chairman, remarking on the pain- Vol nature of the case. sentencrd Lana to twelve months' imprisonrcent, with hard labour. . ITHE BISHOP AND THE SPORTING PARSON,—This last tribute to Mr. Fronde's memory will remind many a West Icountryman of a story which, among the hundred and one related of him, described the reception he is said to have I given to his diocesan, the late Lord Bishop of Exeter. Week after week sundry nevapapere had been publishing articles , of the most scurrilous description, headed " Rnowstone ! again ;" the burden of which reflected on Froude'e mode of 'life and the lawless acts perpetrated in that parish. These, of course, never failed to reach the Bishop's eye ; conse• • quently the stout-hearted prelate, always a friend to be de- pended on when his clergy were, as he thought, unfairly assailed, summoned Mr. Froade to appear at the palace, and explain the grave charges thus publicly brought against him. Bat neither did Froude obey the summons, nor would he give the Bishop a chance of wigging him by at- tending hi a visitations; so, like Mahomet and the mountain, the Bishop determined to go to him ; a course which, short of legal proceedings, WAS the only one now open to him. Accordingly, on a bitter winter's morning, the Bishop, con- veyed by a poet-chaise from Tiverton, arrived at ICn mono Vicarage, and having inquired if Mr. Fronde were at home, was told ha was, on hearing which he entered the house. After a short delay in the cold guest chamber, the Bishop was shown into another apartment, where sat Mr. Frauds before a comfortable fire, his head muftl.d in flannel, and his voice apparently as hoarse as that of a carrion crow. "I've come to see you. Mr. Fronde," commenced the Bishop, "to inquire if —" " Oh, yes, soy lord ; 'tie cold work, sure enough, travelling over our moors; but do 'ee take a glass of hot brandy and water, 'twill I,eep off the ehivers when nought else will." Then, in spite of the Bishop's protestations that he needed no alcohol, especially in the morning, From% rang the bell and ordered a glass of brandy and water to be mixed forthwith, "hot and strong for the Bishop." Again his lordship positively declined the stimulant, and endeavoured to explain the object of his visit; but Froude, apparently not hearing a word he had uttered, cut him short by saying, "It's my only doctor, my lord, is a drop of brandy; and if I had but taken it when I got my chill I shouldn't now be as I be, deaf as an haddock, and nursing this fire like an old woman." The Bishop would hear no more; but, making a grave bow, took his leave, entered his carriage' and returned whence he came. In ten minutes from that time, so goes the story, Fronde was seen to mount his horse and trot away in com- pany with the hounds.—The Out of-Door Life of the Rev. Jno. div.head: XAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 23, 1884
div.p: THE XAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 23, 1884
FOREIGN NEWS.
EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN.
THE KHARTOUM EXPEDITION-LETTER FROM GORDON.

Demo, SATURDAY —The Mudir of Dongola has collected a nurrater of boats, 500 camels, and 1,200 men to assist the Government steamers up the cataracts. Five hundred more men will be ready to help in a few days. CASCO, SUNDAY NIGIET.—The Mudir of Dongola tele- graphs the receipt of a letter from General Gordon, dated the 20th July. Khartoum was safe. General Gordon asks for news of the expedition. He says he intends to remain at Khartoum harassing the rebels by his steamers until the ex• peditior arrives, but that the cataracts are very ,rapid and dangevcus at present. He acids that the troops are well. Col. Chernaside telegraphs that Osman Digma's followers are deserting. Three thousand are said to have retired at Hatpe's. An Arab has just arrived from Berber. .I.Te de- clares ti,at the town was taken by a horde ef hungry Arabs, not undo: the direction of the Mabdi's lieutenant, as sup- posed.

MONDAY.—The following troops will start up the Nile for Wady Haifa as soon as transport is provided :—The 2-td Battalion Essex Regiment, the 2nd Battalion Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry, the Litt Battalion South Suf. fordshicetraegiment, a squadron of the 19th Hussars, and a corps of mounted infantry (British). Official telegrams from Suakin: gate that Osman Digma's following is much reduced, 3,000 of his followers having left for Athai, and that he makes demonstrations to keep up appearinees. Deserters from his camp report that the rebels suffered some loss every night from th 6 fire of the troops. A Portsmouth correspondent says :—Four hundred boats, each to accommodate twelve men, have been ordered by the Admiralty for service on the Nile, and the type of boat .was, on Monday selected at Portsmouth by Colonel Butler and several naval officials. Each boat is to weigh 1,200 pounds and to carry; C.,700 pounds, including camp equipments and ammunition, each of the twelve men being allowed .25C pounds. Several contractors have received orders to be completed wiain 27 days. At the experiments on Monday a boat was loaded with nearly three tons of commissariat stores, it beine,latended that each boat shall carry 100 days' provisions, and when the ammunition was placed on board the cargo wetgbod 31 tons, and the boats answered so well for stability and buoyancy that the pattern was at once accepted:_

The Barrow er.laipbuildinz Company have received an order from the CoTernment for a number of ()oats of SOft each, which are to form part of a large flotilla intended for the Nile, to be,r.eed in the expedition to Kkartotan, for the relief of General Gordon. The order is to be completed in a month. Mews Waterman, of Devonport, have re- ceived instructions -to build within one month ten boats, each to carry three ;Gas, for service on the Nile in connec- tion with the Gordon Relief Expedition. Messrs Henderson and Company, of Pa.trick, Glasgow, have secured on order for thirty-three laoatz. Each boat is to cost £7O. Another Clyde firm has tendered for a smaller number. Very few Clyde shipbuilders woAld undertake to construct such small craft.

Drafts from the Mounted Infantry for the Nile Expedi- tion are now being prepared at Aldershot and Winchester, and drafts from the Mb •Eussars, Royal Artillery, Royal Engineers, Commissariat and Transport Corps, Ordnance Sera ice Corps, Royal Sussex,Legiment, South Staffordshire Regiment, Royal Highlanders, and Cameron Highlanders, numbering in all 1,150 men, wlll be conveyed from Ports- mouth to Egypt in the hired transport Poonah during the first week of Septemher. A large proportion of the Mounted Infantry will be furnished with camels; the remainder, as well as the cavalry, being supplied with horses recently purchased abroad. A number of officers of the Intelligence Department and Commissariat and Transport Staff left Woolwich on Wed- nesday morning for Khartoum. They lake out maps showing the whole route of the relieving expedition. The Admiralty have chartered several hired transports far the conveying of the boats to Alexandria. The voyage from Wady Ilalfa to Old Dongoll will occupy about 21. days. A route across the Bayuda desert will then be taken to avoid the fourth and fifth cataracts. One route available is from Debbeh direct to Kh artouna, and another from Arnbirkel to Shendy, and thence by river to Khartoum.

div.head: LORD NORTHBROOK'S MISSION.
div.p: LORD NORTHBROOK'S MISSION.

SIMLA, TUESDAY—Lord Northbrook having expressed a wish that a Mabommedan gentleman for India should be attached to his staff in Egypt, Maulvi Stmiula Khan, Judge of Aligarh., bAs ben selected for the post, and leaves for Egypt on September 2nd. WADY flacra, WYDNESDAY.—A detachment of the 35th Royal Sussex Regicaent has arrived here. Lieutenant Ingle- field has teen appointed staff officer of the railway trans- port service at this place.

Orders were received at Woolwich on Wednesday for the 9th and 11th C mipanies of the Comrnissiariat and Trans- port Corps to embark for Egypt during the first week in September. They will proceed to Assouan for service in the transport of war stores, thence going up the Nile, crossing the Baynd Steppe, and onwards to Khartoum. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR.

TAMATAVE, SATORDiY.—Owing to the difficulties of transport, the French commander in Malaeasy waters has hesitated to advance against the Hovas. Mules, however, arrived a week ago, and a forward movement is shortly ea- pectA.

div.p: FRANCE &ND CHINA.

PARIS, SATURDAY—The Senate met this morning at nine o'clock, when the CAnte de Saint-Vallier, reporter of the Committee upon the Credits demanded by the Government for the operations in Tonquin. speaking on behalf of his col- leagues, recommended the House to vote the sum required, and to defer the debate on the Tonquin question until the reassembling of Parliament after the recess, when the Sup- plementary Credits would be discussed. The Due de Broglie declared it to be impossible to give a vote of confidence to the Ministry. M Jules Ferry accepted the postponement of the debate, and declared that the Government would regard the passing of the credits 29 equivalent to a vote of confi- dence. The Ministerial bill was then adopted by 183 against 1 vots. M Martin Peallle, Minister of Justice, subse- quently introduced the Revision Bill passed by the Ver- sailles Congress,after which the House adjourned until three o'clock this afternoon, when the decree closing the session was read.

SUNDAY.—There is no news from Pekin con- firming the announcement made yesterday by a London morning paper thxt the Chinese Government had declared war against France. On the contrary, the Taring-Li Yamen on the 14th inst addressed a note to the members of the Foreign Diplomatic Bodies protesting against the action of France, and invoking their mediation, with a view to effect- ing an amicable settlement. The official communication was couched in a pacific tone. TOULON, M3linay.—ln anticipation of war with China, orders have been issued that all naval officers away on fur- lough shall return to Toulon. ALGIERS, MONDAY—The ste liner Rio Negro left here this evening for Tonquin, having on board 1,300 troops, besides war material. PARIS, MONDAY —The Minister of Marine has received the following despatch from General Millot, dated Hanoi, August 17th :--'‘ The coronation of the new King of Annam took place this morning. I am about to publish the French ultimatum in reply to the pretensions put forward by the Regents, and also my proclamation to the people of Annam. The French fig has been displayed on the citadel of Hula for the last two days. Colonel Cruerrier conducted the ne- gotiations with the Annamite Government with great zeal and intelligence" PARTS, MONDAY.—A desptch of to.diy's dee, from Thusian, reports that Colonel Guerrier has left Hue with troops on his return to Hanoi. The success of his mission was cunplete. It is sfated that orders have been sent to Admiral Courbet to take nossession of the arsenal of Foe- chow: but not to clrry mnilfta operations further. gIIINOTIAT, TIiEsITAY.—Teo Tsung Tang and Shu Tseng Chen, the Chineseplenipotentiaries, have left Shanghai in accordince with instructions from Pekin. Thirty-five members of the Board of Censors have presented a memorial to the Empress opposing the conditions de- manded by France and strongly urging hostilities. The Empress is reported to have decided upon declaring war against France, The Central News is enabled to confirm the telegram from Foochow, which states that a Viceroy has been ordered to return to Nankin. The Viceroy thus mentioned is not, however, Lihung Chang, but Tseng Kuo Chuna. His recall would appear to show that the negotiations with M. Patenoke have failed.

PARIS, Tat-usual-, 9 P.M.—The time allowed for the ac- ceptance by China of the French ultimatum expired at one o'clock to-day. The Chineal Government having refused its assent, Li Fong Pao, the Minister here, received his pass- ports this evening. • THE CHOLERA.
MausEILLEs, SCN-D—AY—, official bulletin gives the number of deaths during the last 24 hours as 38, of which 16 werelrom cholera.

TOULON, SUNDAY.—In the last 48 hours ten deaths. At a hamlet situated between Cuers and Sotteville, where there are only 37 inhabitants, 20 cases of cholera, five of which proved fatal, have occurred in one night. PARIS, SUNDAY —The return of mortality from cholera during the last 24 hours gives the number of deaths as fol- lows :--in the department of Eastern Pyrenees two, in the i-fo•au!t 12, in the Aude five, in the Gard three, in the Van- close one, and in the Basses Alps two. There were nine fatal cases in Italy.
MARSEILLYS, MONDAY, 8-30 P m —The official bulle'in gives the number of deaths during the last 24 hours at 45, of which 14 were from cholera.

TOULON, MONDAY, 6 P.M —There have been six deaths from cholera here since 10 am. Two occurred in the town and four in the suburbs. The nv.mber of serious cases is in- creasing. Three more deaths have occurred in the little hamlet of Lessimes, near Solliesville, and the people of the latter place are panic-stricken. One death is announced from La S .yne, and a nother from 13: ignoles. The record for the hospitals is :—Ben Rencontre, 3 admissions, 2 patients discharged, 1 death, and 17 cases under treatment; Saint Mandrier, no admissions, 6 discharged, no deaths, and 44 under treatment.
Pants, MONDAY.—During the last 24 hours there have been thirteen deaths from cholera in the department of Psrenes Orientates, five in Herault, four in Gard, and five in Aude.

ROME, MoNDAY.—The official sanitary bulletin to-thy states that there have been three fresh cases of cholera in the provinces at Bergamo, Lombardy, two proviug fatal. At Carnpobisso there have been five fresh cases, two of which we-e followed by death. There have also been two deaths among pitients already attacked. From Cosenzt two new cases are reported, two others at Garfagnana, six in the
province of Parma (one being fatal), one at Seborza, and one at Colas°.

TOULON', TUESDAY, 10 AM.—There were two deaths from cholera in the city last night, one case beiEg that of an inhabitant who retuined yesterday. In fatal cases death now follows more rapidly than at the outbreak of the epi- demic. A slight change for the better is noticeable among the .pitients under treatment.

MARSEILLES, WEDNESDAY, 9-20 A M.—Four deaths from cholera occurred here last night. TOULON, WEDNESDAY, 10 AM.—One death from cholera occurred here in the suburbs last night. The state of the public health shows an improvement this morning. MARSEILLES, THURSDAY. 8-50 A M.—Only one death from cholera occurred here last night. TouLoN, TELUIZSDAY, 10 AM —There were four deaths from cholera here last night, two occurring in the Bon Recontre Hospital, and two in the suburbs. 'Three very serious cises are now under treatment in the Bon Recontre Hospital.

THE GREELY EXPEDITION. NEW YORK, MoNDAY.—Lieut. Greely stites that as far as Lieut. Lockwood went towards the north-eastern end of Greenland, the coast continued. Lieut. Greely does not think the North Pole can be reached, unless every circum- stance hitherto found to be unfavourable should prove to be favourable to any party making the attempt. If the Tole is ever reached, he is of opinion it will be by way of Franz Josephland. He states that the existence of an open Polar sea is well-nigh certain, and that this is proved by the ice drifting out of Mussel Bay and Spitsbergen in mid-winter, and by the narthern drift of the Polar ptck experienced by Dr. frlvy and Lieutenant Lockwood in lat. 82 deg. 33 min. N. Lieutenant Greely adds that his party suffered much in the retreat to Cape Sabine. The temperature on the warmest day in Lady Franklin Bay was 52 deg. above zero, and the coldest 65 deg. below zero. Lieutenant Greely states he distinctly saw his shadow cist on s one occasions by the aurora borealis. Referring to the alleg itions regard- ing the Grwly expedition, the World says that Dr. Parry I committed suicide, and that .his flesh was eaten by his coal- rades.
THE INSURRECTION IN ARABIA. VARNA, SUNDAY.— Three more tribes have joined the in- surrection at Yemen. All the available troops are being des- patched from Syria and the Arabian ports.

THE CONGO. VIENNA. SUNDAY NIGHT.—The European Cabinets have, aocording to the Political Correspondence, agreed in princi- ple to the proposal to convoke a Conference upon the Congo queation, in which Germany is to take the initiative. GOVERNOR CLEVELAND AND THE PRESIDENCY. NEW Yon, WEDNESDAY.—Governor Cleveland's letter accepting the Democratic nomination for the Presidency is published to-day. It favours an amendment to the conga- tu.ion disquali,ying the President of the United States for re-election to that office. Governor Cleveland reiterates his former declaration that working-men should be protected in peacefal efforts to assert their rights when endangered by aggregated capital. He believes that American workmen are not recuesting unreasonable indulgencies, but as intel- ligent, manly citizens seek the same consideration which those demand who have other interests at stake. TURKEY.—MUTINY OF CONVICTS. CON&TANMICOPLE, TllESDAY.—lntelligence received here from Malta states that on the arrival there of a Turkish steamer bound for Tripoli, with GO convicts on board, the latter mutinied and attacked the Turkish guard. In the con- flict that ensued three of the convicts were killed and one woutieled, while four Turkish sole iers were hurt. The Go- vernor of Malta claimed jurisdiction in the matter, but the Turkish Consul opposed this claim on the ground that the steamer belonged to the Ottoman Government. GREAT FIRE AT ATHENS.

ATREN6, TRIMS (Told -in-a-r-kel:c. 305tr0cte4 of wood, situate in the centre of the city, has been completely burnt down. A large quantity of provisions stored in the market was also destroyed by the flumes.

div.head: PRI4',SCOT.
div.p: PRI4',SCOT.
THE BREWSTER SESSIONS.—The annual brewster sessions for the Prescot police division was held in the Cl)urt House on Thursday, but owing to a pressure of news our report is held.over until next week.

PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was to have been held on Monday night, but as there was not a quorum present no business was transacted. The members present were Messrs W L Evans, and T P Hewitt, and H Cross (clerk). THE SANITARY CONDITION OF PRESCOT A WARNING TO HOGSEIIOLDERS.—Tne Local Board of the Prescot town- ship are actively bestirring themselves in order to put the town in a better sanitary condition than at present exists, and the following notice has just been issued :—" Whereas the bye-law of the Board, prohibiting the throwing out of house refuse and other noxious or offensive matter, upon the surface of the streets and water channels in the district. has been continuously evaded by persons occupying houses adjoining such streets. Notice is hereby given, that such bye-law will hereafter be strictly enforced by the Bard, and that all persons so offending are subject to a penalty of £5 on conviction."

GARDEN DEPREDATIONS AT RATNITILL AND HUTTON.— At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Richard Ball, a young man, was summoned for trespassing in search of mushrooms in a potatoe field at Rainhill, is the occupation of William Strettle. The offence was committed on the 2nd instant, and the damage was assessed at dd. The defendant was fined 2s GI and costs, and ordered to pay the damage.— A lad named Richard Ball, with two others named Frecik. Crompton and Joseph Eccleston, were also summoned for trespassing in the same field, and were mulcted in a like penalty.—John Thornley Underwood and John Swift (lads) were summoned for trespassing in a wheat field at Huyton, belonging to Thomas Rimxter, on th 3 2nd August, and were each ordered to pay the costs and the damage, assessed at Heyes, William Lewis, John Jervis, and Edward Percival (lade). were summoned for stealing turnips from a field at Fluyton, belonging to John Rimmer. The defendants pleaded guilty. The prosecutor stated that in all upwards of £1 damage had been done, but he did not wish to press the case ; he only wished an example to be made for the sake of others. The parents of the lads pro- inised to look after their lads in future; and Reyes (who had been previously convicted for a similar offence) was ordered to pay a fine of Sc and costs, and the others were ordered to pay the costs. PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—The fortnightly meet- ing of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held on Thurs• day, at the Workhouse. Whiston. Mr Meadows presided. The ViFiting Committee, it was reported, had had under con- sideration the desirability of excluding strangers from attending Divine worship in the Workhouse chapel.—The Rev T Chambers moved that persons outside be allowed to attend the service in the chapel.—Mr Newsome said that persons really came to go into the house to see inmates. It had been found that the privilege had been abustd —The Rev Thomas Chambers said he had nothing against the com- mittee; but he deprecated any mystery with regard to those services. He would withdraw his motion.—The Workhouse I Master reported that there were 418 inmates this week. against 432 last week and 422 in the corresponding week of last year. Boys and girls in Kirkdale School and Pantasaph Orphanage, from the Prescot Union, 154; vagrants relieved, 41; corresponding week of last year, 54.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the perma- nent appointment of Mr Henry Kay as school attendance officer for the No. 3 district at a salary of £7O p::r annum, met a further suns of £lO per malm for his services as inquiry officar.—The following were selected to visit the various asylums in the county in which lunatics belonging to the Prescot Union are con- fined :—Messrs Dobeil, Leatherbarrow, and Meadows, with the clerk (Mr Hartley).—The Clerk submitt:d his half-yearly estimate of expenditure to the 25th of March, 1885, which amounted to £21,274, against a total last half-year of £22,908. The estimate was adopted —The Chairman drew attention to the fact that several letters had been received from children who formed part of the seventy that were sent out to Canada a short time since. The children ex- pressed thanks for the kindness shown to them throughout their journey, and stated that they were settled in comfor- table and good homes.—This was the principal businese.

div.head: TOOTH DRAWING EX rRAORDINARY.
div.p: TOOTH DRAWING EX rRAORDINARY.

A case which appeared to excite considerable interest was heard before C spt. Willis and Mr A R Gladstone, at Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, when Daniel Murray O'Hara, of Church-street, Prescott was summoned for assaulting a young woman named Ann Moore, residing in Brook-street, Whiston.—The defendant pleaded not guilty.—The com- plainant stated that on the 9th inst she went to defendant's place of business to have a tooth drawn. She sat down, and the defendant attempted to pull the tooth, but occasioned her very great pain. She was compelled to scream, where- upon the defendant seized her by the arm, which he severely twisted, and he put her outside.—The defendant cross- examined the complainant with the object of showing that on the day in question the air was very sultry and close. He afterwards asked her if she was not delicate and subject to hysterics.—The complainant replied that she was not sub- ject to hysterics—The defendant:• Ob, yes, yes, you are, my girl ; I could see it.—P.S. Bull slated that on the Satur- day night in question the defendant came to the police station with P.C. Bennett, the latter having the complainant and her mother in charge. The defendant, however, at the police station refused to give a charge against the two females, and they were liberated.—The defendant said that there had ly:qin a conspiracy in the neighbourhood ; and the complainant with her mother and one or two other women had visited his surgery with the object of preferring a serious chirp against him. He accused the women of having crested a disturbance in his house, and said that P.C. Ben- nett, who was on duty in plain clothes at the time, had witnessed the dieturbince, and took the women into custody on his own ace ird. He alleged that the complainant screamed to an alarming extent, and said that he mhy assisted her to the door in order to let her have a little fresh air. He called his housekeeper, a Mrs Evan', who gave evi- dence to that effect, and the Bench ultimately dismissed the case.
An explosion occurred on Thursday morning at Pigou's Gunpowder Mil Is,'llartford. No ono was injured, but much damage was done.

- Mr. P.. 1. Power, Nationalist, was on Thursday returned Without opposition for the county ok Waterford, in succes- sion to Mr. J. A. Blake, resigned. Lord Salisbury's visit to Glasgow is fixed for Wednesday, the Ist October. Sir Stafford Northcote will address a meet- ing in Edinburgh on the 10th September. The Bolton trfigistrates en Thuradly committed for trial a youth of 18, named Hewerdine, who was charge 4 with having perpetrated a large number of burglaries in Bolton and the neighbourhood.
GENTFHAL NEWS.
- - The wearers of the blue ribbon in Australia and Tasmania number 75,000.

, Mr Joseph Lavesey, of Prestoa, founder of the temperance movement, is reported to be seriously ill. There was a disastrous fire on Saturday night in the oil mills of Mr W Gray, at Sculcoates, Hull. The damage is estimated at £lOO,OOO. • Mr J W B Lee, an Edinburgh solicitor in large practice, was arrested on Mcniliy clurged with misappropriating £l,OOO intrusted to him for investment. Mr Boehm has modelled two bus's of the late Duke of Albany. One is said to ho intended for the Royal Mauso- leum at Windsor, and the other for Balmoral. Great alarm was caused in Birmingham, on Tuesd ly, by the death of a man nam-d Ralph from what was at first sup- posed to be Asiatic cholera, but which is now reported to have been English cholera. Earl Manvers has nude a return of 4B per cent on their rent to his agricultural tenants, and the Earl of Yarborough a reduction of 15 per cent for fiye years to those of his tenants who have paid their rents. The Queen presented new colours at Osborne on Satur- day to the Ist Battalion of the Seaforth Highlanders, Ross- shire Buffs, Duke of Albany's, of the 3rd battalion of which regiment the late Duke of Albany was colonel. PENNY TRAM FARES.—At the half-yearly meeting of the Southwark and Deptford Tramways Company, held on Mon- day, it was reported that " there is no doubt that penny fares are the mainstay of the traffic, and it may be desirable at no distant date to consider the propriety of establishing a uniform penny fare to and from any points of the company's system."

1 ERRIBLE DEATR ON TLIE RAILWAY.—A railway porter namen Kneedon, aged about GO, met with a shocking deate at Low Moor Station (near Halifax), on Tuesday. He was ailing some points on the main line, when a train came upon him unobservectly until too late to escape, and the poor fellow was literally cut to pieces. Death was in- stantaneous.

ROYAL COLLEGE OF MUSlC—Alderman Whitcombe, of Portsmouth, has presented the Prince of Wales with a cheque, value £3,000, to found a Portsmouth scholarship in the Royal College of Music. £2,000 of this is Mr Whit- combe's own money; the rest has been subscrioed. The Prince, in repiy, slid he trusted other towns would follow Portsmouth's example. FRAUDS ON Girms.—William Lloyd was on Monday re- manded at the Liverpool Police Court, charged with haying fraudulently obtained .E 5 from Margaret Walker. It was alleged by the prosecution that this was only one of a num- ber of cases to be brought against the prisoner, in which he had pretended to be carrying on a business simply to obtain deposit money from girls whom he engaged to assist in the shops.

TRE BIGGEST CUSS The EVER KNEW."—At a coroner's inquest at Fulham, on Saturday, it transpired that a boy eight years of age having fallen into a pool of water on the Thames three feet deep, several men stood near looking on while the lad drowned. A witness described the men as being the "14gest curs he ever knew," and said he wanted to fight them, upon which they walked away. Verdict "Accidental death."

CONSERVATIVE EXPERIMENTS IN BIRMINGILAM.—It is stated that the Conservative executive in Birmingham have decided to contest most of the wards at the November elec- tion. This movement is believed to be in consequence of the desire of Lord Rind°lph Churchill to obtain some tan- gible test of the strength of the party in the b)rough. When a similar experiment was made six years ago all the Conservative candidates were defeated. rgE DEFALCATIONS AT WIGAN.—FURTHER DISCLOSURES. At Wigan, on Wednesday, William Holt, late borough trea- surer, was charged with embezzling certain Bums of money belonging to the Corporation, and John Caldwell, stock and share broker, and professional auditor to the Corporation, was charged with receiving two particular sums knowing them to have been embezzled. Formal evidence wis given by the burgess auditors as to Holt's defalcations, and as to their finding letters and papers from Caldwell in his office. A witness named flampson, a former clerk of Caldwell's proved the passing of money from Holt to C tldwell in the borough treasurer's office, that this money was taken from the Corporation safe, and that Holt had told Caldwell that he knew it was not his (Holt's) money, but belonged to the Corporation. Both prisoners were reminded for a week. Mr Ackerley, who prosecuted, rated that the examination of Holt's books so far disclosed defalcitions amounting to over £7,000. The court was crowded, great interest being taken in the proceedings. THE INTENSE HEAT.—MANY DEATHS—The coroner for Central Middlessex, on Saturday, held inquests on the bodies of six males, aged 5, 41, 52, 56, 60, and 02 respec- tively. In each case verdicts of death produced by the ex- c ssive heat'affecting either brain or hearts were returned. On Saturday, JAMB Pullen, aged fifty, a potman, of 50, Shakespeare-road, South Hornsey, was taken suddenly ill, and on going into the surgery of Dr. Tickler, of King Henry's-walk, Islington, he expired in a few minntes, death deing due, it is believed, to the intense heat. Two deaths from sunstroke occurred in Bolton, on Monday. In one case a young man, who was carting for the Corporation, was suddenly taken ill and died; and in the other an old man dropped down dead, after drinking a glass of ginger beer. At an inquest held at Halesown, on Monday, respecting the death of Thos. Roberts, labourer, it was shown the deceased was employed by Major Smith in harvesting in the fields. He partook of a very hearty dinner, and upon resuming his work be complained of the excessive heat, and whilst medical aid was being obtained he died. The jury were of opinion that death had been caused by inaction of the heart, pro- duced by excessive heat.

EXECUTION OF PETER CASSIDY.—At eight o'clock on Tuesday morning Peter Cassidy, aged 54, described as a Unman, was executed at Kirkdale prison, Liverpool, for the murder of his wife. The crime was brought about by think. The prisoner and deceased lived at Bootle, and on the 25th June deceased returned home after a long absence. She was suffering from the effects of drink, and Cassidy himself was in a similar condition; they quarrelled, and the prisoner, described as a very affectionate husband when sober, smashed in her 1431,1 with a cleaver and a wooden mallet. He was recommended to mercy by the jury, but the recommendation was not acted upon. He was tried before Mr Justice Day at the Liverpool assizes on the 31st July. Reporters were admitted to the execution. The executioner was James Berry, of Bradford, who performed his office with dexterity and skill, contrasting with the shocking exhibition by Binns at the last execution at Kirk- dale. He gave a drop of nine feet, the weight of the cul- prit being 9 stone 4 pounds. _ Insensibility was instanta- neous, and the action of the heart ceased in five minutes. The culprit bore himself with firmness and resignation. A general opinion prevailed in Liverpool that he should not have been executed, his crime having apparently been committed owing to the exasperation caused by a bad wife. The usnal inquest was afterwards held. ROYAL VISIT TO NEWCASTLE: NARROW ESCAPE OF THE PRINCE OF' WALES.—Newcastle and the banks of the Tyne presented the gayest appearance in view of the Royal visit on Wednesday. The weather was magnificent, and the elaborate street decorations looked brilliant in the bright eunlight. The streets (which were stoutly barricaded) were crowded, and excursion trains packed with visitors arrived every half-hour. On Tuesday night the city was brilliantly illuminated, and enthusiastic crowds blocked the thorough- fares. Bonfires were lit at various high points. The Prince and Princess of Wales, accompanied by Princes Albert Victor and George, left Rothbury by special train on Wed- nesday morning, and arrived in Newcastle at noon. A pro- cession was formed, and the Armstrong Park ex- tension was opened. The Royal party was enthu- siastically cheered by immense crowds of people. During the Royal progress through the city an alarming ac- cident occurred, On entering Grey-street the horse ridden by Colonel Young, in commend of the Newcastle Artillery Volunteers, became restive, and backed between the horses drawing the carriage in which were the Prince and Princess of Wales and their two sons. The cheering immediately ceas3d, and great anxiety was manifested by the crowd. The horse was got out, but it then became entangled in one of the wheels of the Royal carriage, and the party seemed in no little danger. The horse wheeled round rapidly, and the Prince of Wales had a narrow escape of being struck by the colonel's sword, only avoiding it by stooping hurriedly. As it was, the sword passed within a few inches of his hat. The horse was then got away, and the Prince raised his hat to the people, who responded with a vigorous cheer and waving of handkerchiefs. On Thursday, the Prince of Wales, who was accompanied by the Princess, performed the ceremony of opening the new dock at the Coble Dene, near Newcastle, which has been constructed by the Tyne Com- missioners at a cost of nearly three quarters of a million sterling. The dock was, at the request of the Commissioners, named by His Royal Highness the "Albert Edward Dock." At the luncheon which followed the Prince spoke of the vast improvements made in the navigation of the Tyne by the enterprise and pereeverancE of the local authorities. THE ARTILLERY MEETING.—The northern artillerymen in camp at Shoeburyness commenced actual operations on :Monday, when the practice with shell from the 131 pounder Palliser mumzle-leading gun took place. The first prize was won by the 4th detachment of the Ist Shropshire, with a score of 45 out of a possible 48. The second prize fell to the Bth detachment of the 4th Lane ishire with 33. Reposi- tory drill was carried on all the afternoon, and the best time was recorded by the 3rd and 4th detachments of the 2nd Lancashire. At the artillery meeting at Shoeburyness on Tuesday the shot competition with 40 pounder Armstrone,,s took pleas at 1,600 yards range, and the first prize of £3O was won by the 3rd detachment of the 2nd East York, with 42 points, in 3 minutes 40 seconds. The second prize was Wien by the 2nd Durham, the third by the 2nd East York, the fourth by the Ist Forfar, the fi th by the 6th Lan- e eshire. The Western Davenport detachment took the first prize in the Royal Artillery competition with 42 points, in 6 mins. 55 secs. On Wednesday, theresults werelmade known in the important competitions which extend over a fortnight. The first prize of £lOO, given by the Queen, was secured by the 2ad Middlesex, with 81 points, the metropolitan county thus securing the highest honours here as at Wim- bledon. The 3rd Middlesex took the Prince of Wales's prize, while the third, fourth, and fifth prizes tell respec- tively to the 2nd East York, 2nd Durham, and 2ad Lanca- shire. The 2nd East York won the Association prize for the highest aggregate with the 40-pounder, their score being 63. The week's repository competition fell to the 3:d Kent. The Bth Lancashire were second, and the 2nd Lancashire third. In the 40-pounder competition carried on during the day the 4th Lancashire, 3rd Kent, Ist Lancashire, 2nd East York, and a third detachment of the 3rd Kent won the five prizes in the order given. On Thursday the repository badges were won with the greatest ease by the 3rd Kent men, this being the sixth time the honour has been secured by I the Woolwich corps.
Lady Carberry died oil Tuesday at Pimle County Court, Cork.

The Maori Kin,' and his attendant chiefs embarked at Gravesend on Wednesday, on their return to New Zealand. James Malloy, a betting man, Wa 3 on Wednesday fined £2O and costs for betting at Oddfellows' sports at the Aston Lower Ground. The International Medical Congress, which concluded its sittings at Copenhagen on Saturday, m?ets next year at Washington.

A Greek sailor, who in a public-house nu trrel, was stabbed by another Greek in Liverpool, now lies in hospital in a precarious condition. Two pleasure boats carrying eight persons came into col- lision at Stratford on Saturday. Both boats sank, and a yoLng, man and two young women were drowned. On Tuesday the annual show was held of the Lytham, Kirkham, and Blackpool Agricultural Society, and was es- pecially strong in the heavy horses for which the district is no'ed.

The Home Secretary adheres to his original resolution to close Chester Castle prison. The castle will now be exclu- sively used for military prisoners, and for short-time and remind prisoners. Four bandsmen of the Royal Irish Rifles, who hired a boat for the purpose of rowing about the harbour at Guern- sey, are thought to have been drowned, as nothing has beep heard of them since Tuesday afternoon. A cottage in Beswick-road, Norwich, suddenly fell dowh on Wednesday. Eight persons by whom it was occupied just got out before the building collapsed, the cracking of the timbers having warned them of what was coming. The Mayor of Accrington has opened a subscription list for the relief of the widow and family of Police-constable Brown, who was killed by being run over by a wagonette on Sunday. The funeral of the deceased took place or. Wednesday. GORED TO DEATH GY A BULL—An old man named Wil- Hain Burdett went out, near Hinckley, in Leicestershire, on Sunday to bring in some cattle. A young bull attacked hiror • tossed him into a ditch, and gored him so terribly that he died en Mond GREAT SCULLING MATCH IN AUSTRALIA.—HANLAN DE- FEATED—Sydney, Saturday.—The sculling match between Beach and flanlan, for the championship of the world, was rowed on the Pararnatta river to-day. Brach was the win- ner by seven lengths. SUICIDES IN Gaol, —A man named Barrett, undergoing a short term of imprisonment for robbery, hanged himself in his cell at Galway Gaol on Saturday night by a chain MS' pended from the cell window. This is the third suicide ig the same gaol within three months. A woman named Rafter has been admitted to Mercer's Hospital, Dublin, suffering from terrible burns on the head and face. It is said she was chased from the street upstairs into her own house by a woman named Murray, who throw a bottle of vitriol over her. Murray is in custody. SUNDAY DRUNKENNESS IN VALES—The way•in which Welshmen evade the Sunday Closing Act was illustrated at Chester on Saturday, when the landlord of a public-house , at Shatwick was charged with permitting drunkenness on the previous Sunday. The police found 20 men drunk in the boos, aid a police-sergeant said that 50 or GO other men, chiefly Welshmen, were lying drunk under the church • walls. The magistrates fined the publican and two Of the men.

SHORT TIME AT OLDHAM.—A meeting of cotton Spin'ners of Oldham, including both limited companies a d pri- vate firms, was held on Saturday to consider the question of adopting short time. About six million spindles were re- presented. It was unanimously resolved that the returns - obtained were so satisfactory that the committee recom- mended the trade to adopt abort time at once. It is under- stood that the mills in Cldham and the neighbourhood will run four days per week. FALL OF A MILL CHDINEY. While the Town- field mill chimney at Oldham was being repaired on Wednesday the top part of it fell, smashing through the roof of a machine shop. Robert Nelson, who was working on the scaffold, observed by the falling dust that some coping stones bad given way, and saved his life by getting on a ladder. A piece of stone fell on a mechanic named Rincheliffe, in the workshop, injuring his forehead and arms. The adjoining street was blocked. MANSLAUGHTER IN HALIFAX.— Ou Monday evening a serious affair happened at Booth Town, Halifax. A man named James Ri.lgway, a labourer for the Corporation, re- turned holm about six o'clock. A woman with whom he lived, named Mary tipnley, aged 26 was, he says, in drink, called him a drunken pig, and struck him with a poker on the shoulders and knee. He states that he then raised his fiat, with which he struck her on the head, breast, and arm. She fell at once, and died shortly afterwards. Ridgway has been apprehended.

DISTURBANCES AT DURGAN.—SERIOUS CHARGES.—AI Lurgan Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a number of charges were heard arising out of the recent party disturbances. Two men named Bailey and a man named McSteay, Catho- lics, were committed for trial for severely bmting George Creany, a Protestant, on Monday night; and a Catholic, named Wilkinson, was remanded on a charge of dangerously stabbing a Protestant, named O'Rorke. Two Protestants, named Wright and McArtney, were also remanded, charged with causing the death of a Catholic named McEvoy. Several p,rsons were sentenced to varying terms of impri- sonment for assaults and inciting disturbances. MR. GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO MIDLOTHIAN.—The Premier, according to present arrangements, will leave Hawarden to visit his constituents in Midlothian on the 213th or 27th inst, most probably the latter date. After fulfilling his Midlothian engagements he will remain for a short time only in Scotland, paying same social visits. Some hundreds of visitors drove into flawarden on Sunday. Mr Gladstone at- tended both services, and was accompanied by Mrs Glad- stone, Mr and Mrs W H Gladstone, Misses Helen and Mary Gladstone, Mr Herbert Gladstone, and Mr Henry Gladstone. The Premier did not read the lessons. He looks remarkably well. A crowd assembled at the entrance to the castle, at the rectory, and along the pathway lead- ing from the rectory to the church, Mr Gladstone being everywhere respectfully saluted.

ROT CEN FISTI AT ST. HELENS : HEAVY PENALTY. —At the St. Helens Town 1-1,11, on Monday, John Kelly, of Windle, was summoned for exposing unsound fish for sale on the sth itest--The defendant did not appear.—Mr J 0 Swift appeared on behalf of the Corporation, and stated that Mr Thomas Coughtray (sanitary inspector) was near the railway station on the sth August, when he saw the defen- dant with a mats named Rourke. They had a handcart, upon which were a barrel and a box containing herrings. The fish were unwholesome and putrid, and Coughtrey told Kelly that they were not fit for food and must be taken away. Kelly appeared to acquiesce in this suggestion, and returned to the station where he unloaded the cart. Cough.' trey thought no further attempt to sell the fish would be made, and went away; but from what he was after wards told he went in search of Kelly, and ultimately found him with the ruin Rourke at Gerard's Bridge. They had then the box upon the handcart, and about 60 or 70 of the her- rings left. They were quite rotten and putrid, and were ante rly unfit for food. They were covered with salt to take away the bad smelt; and he (Mr Swift) thought that after those illegitimate endeavours to get rid of that rotten stink- ing stuff the case was one calling for the highest penalty— three months' imprisonment It was utterly useless for local authorities to keep down epidemic disease and dis- eases with which they appeared to he threatened if that sort of thing was to be allowed.—Mr Thomas Coughtrey was then called and gave evidence in support of Mr Swift's state- ment, adding that be had the fish destroyed by order of Mr J.F., after the fish had been inspected by the medi- cal officer.—A man named Rourke, employed as an out. porter at the r til way station, deposed that the defendant en- gaged him to wheel a handcart for him through the day. The defendant after being cautioned by the inspector sold about half a barrel of the herrings.—Dr McNicoll stated that the fish were thoroughly black and rotten, and were likely to elm diarrhoea and colic if eaten.—The Bench commit- ted prisoner for three months with hard labour. THE DUBLIN NC ANDALS. —lt is rumoured that one of the clergymen who left Dublin when it became known that the authorities were instituting prosecutions in connection with the scandals has returned to the city, acting on professional advice. The police have procured the evidence of two addi- tional witnesses, who will be examined against Captain Kir- wan. They were discovered in London last week by Chief Superintendent Mallon, with the assistance of Scotland Yard officers. On Tuesday, at the Dublin Commis- sion Court, before Baron Dowse, the trial of the pri- soners who are charged ire connection with the above was commenced. County Inspector French, of the Royal Irish Constabulary, was first indicted with having Com- mitted a felony in May, 1883. On the application of his counsel, who stated that he was not of sound mind, a jury were empanelled to try whether he was competent to plead. The constables who had been protecting the prisoner before his arrest, and two doctors swore that in their opinion he was insane, while three medical men who had been deputed by the Crown to examine him, deposed that he was only feigning madness. The jury, after a lengthened delibera- tion, were unable to agree, and was discharged. James Rater, aged 79, merchant, was indicted with the same crime. He pleaded guilty, and sentence was deferred.—Mr Cornwall, Secretary of the General Poet Office, Dublin, was indicted with .the like offence, and pleaded not guilty. A cooper, named Clarke, gave evidence against the accused, after which the Court adjourned. The Dublin felony trials snore resumed on Wednesday, when it was an- nounced that the Crown would adjourn the case against French because of the conflict ef medi- cal evidence as to his sanity. The trial of Mr Corn- wall was then continued, and three further witnesses having been examined for the prosecution, counsel addressed the jury for the prisoners, contending that no conviction could some as a consequence of the evidence of such odious scoundrels as those who had testified against him. The evidence for the defence was to the effect that at the date fixed for the felony by the principal witness for the Crown, Mr Cornwall was in Scotland, the re/ihi being proved by Sir R Dalzell, his brother-in-law, Miss Periet, and Mr Higgins, of Bedfordshire. It was also proved his beard had been white since 1880, whereas two of the Crown witnesses had sworn it was black.—Baron Dowse having summed up, the jury, after three minutes' consideration, returned, amid ap- plause, a verdict of not guilty.—The prisoner was put back there being another charge against him. On Thursday, Fowler was tried for keeping an improper house. All the frequenters of it were called by female names, Malcolm Johnston being Lady Constance Clyde. The Judge said one of the men who frequented the house was Lieutenant Sankey, of the sth Dragoon Gutrds, who was known as the "Baby." He understood a warrant was out against him, and he hoped he would be caught Fowler was foiled guilty, and sentenced to two years' imprisonment with hard abour, the Judge being sorry be could not impose a heavier penalty,
