The town-clerk ot Tralee has vindicated his nationality. tater referring to an Act about stray dogs, he states that "any dogs caught offending will be liable to be seized by the Police and prosecuted and fined according to law." Row To CATCH FISH.—" Boy, how much do you want for that string of fish ?" asked an amateur fisherman on his Way home from a day's sport." The boy named his price. 'All right; there's your money. Now just throw the fish," and he dexterously caught them. "Talk about catching fish !" he said, as he pursued his way. "Is your sister at home ? " asked a St. Louis young Irian of the little brother who answered the bell. "Yes, She's at home," said the boy; " we're goin' to have cocoa- nut pies for dinner to-morrow, and she's out in the kitchen helpin' mother to make 'ern." " Indeed ! " replied the Young man, evidently very much pleased. "And what part of the pies does your sister make ? " 't She cracks the cocoa-nuts with her teeth," answered the little brother. Balzac, being asked to explain an abstruse passage in one Of his books, frankly owned it had no meaning at all. " You see," said he, " for the average reader all that is clear Seems easy, and if I did not sometimes give him a compli- cated and meaningless sentence, he would think he knew as inuch as myself. But, when he comes upon something he can- not comprehend, he re-reads it, puzzles over it, takes his head between his hands, and glares a, it, and, finding it _impossible to make head or tail of it, says, Great man, zatzac ; he knows more than Idol GENTLE CRITICISM.—Mr. B. : "These biscuits remind me Of mother's." Mrs. B. : " Well, I declare ! Have you gone crazy P " Mr. 11. " Crazy, my dear? Of course not I " Mrs. B.: " Well, I never expected to hear you say that any Of my cooking resembled your mother's! She was a won- derful cook, I have no doubt, for you have said so thou- Bands of times." Mr. B. : " Yes, she certainly was. In fact, there was only one dish that she ever failed in." Mrs. B.: " What was that ? " Mr. B. : " Biscuits." Madame D., in Vienna, was a very careful sort of person. Elhortly after Christmas she met Madame S.' who asked her What present she had made to her husband. Madame D. replied, "You see, I find it very difficult to save anything from my housekeeping-money these hard times, and I had to set my wits to work. My husband, you know is an in- veterate smoker, and passionately fond of a good cigar. boring the last three months I have every evening taken a Cigar out of his and stowed it away in a box. On Christ- mas Eve I presented him with this box as a surprise, and You should have seen how delighted he was ! " WHAT LOOSENED HE/3 TONOTIE.—A stylishly-dressed WO- was brought before a magistrate recently for stealing Some ribbons in a shop. The chief clerk had observed her talking freely with her counsel, and was puzzled because she looked at him blankly when he asked her name and residence, and replied with a shake of her head, "She is French," ex- plained the lawyer, " and doesn't understand English. Put it down 'Marie Latouche.'" The clerk frowned incredu- lously. " What age is she ? " he asked. "Twenty-two," replied the lawyer. Then the clerk's eyes twinkled as he said softly, " Thirty-two ? " "No, twenty-two! " snapped the fair prisoner ; but she clapped her hand to her mouth in a moment, and began laughing. Umph !" said the clerk. " You can speak English if you don't understand it! In a certain class in an American university, some twenty Years ago, there were two students of the same name, one a ,Youth of leisure, the other a man of study. They sat side by side in the Greek section under Professor Sophocles, who Was, as is known, a better scholar than instructor. The mark-lists at that time were made out monthly, and Jones the student was surprised one morning to find that his marks Were low and the other man's were high. The professor had evidently mixed up the names, and Jones remonstrated. An adjustment was promised; but next month occurred the same mistake. For the third month the marks were correct; the fourth time brought round the same error. When an- Other remonstrance was made, Professor Sophocles was rather nettled, and, turning fiercely on Jones, said, "Your name is Jones, sir, and you must abide by the consequences ! " The late President Garfield once said that he was obliged to see an average of about thirty persons for every office to be filled. If the question was one of removal, the number Was much greater, including the friends of the incumbent as Well as the candidates for the place. There is an amusing story of the method Mr. Lincoln adopted to settle a contest over a post-mastership which had greatly annoyed him. There were two candidates in the field, and petition after Petition had poured in upon the weary president, and dele- gation after delegation had rushed to the White House to argue the claims of the rival aspirants. Finally, after he had been bored for half an hour by a fresh delegation, Mr. Lincoln said to his secretary, "This matter has got to end somehow. Bring a pair of scales." The scales were brought. " Now put in all the petitions and letters in favour of one man, and see how much they weigh, and then weigh the Other candidate's papers." It was found that one bundle Was three•quarters of a pound heavier than the other. " Make out the appointment at once for the man who has the heaviest papers," ordered the president, and it was done.

FRlDAT.—Before Mr John White and Captain Reynolds. ALLEGED ASSAULTS.—Harriet Broadhurst was summoned by Mary Sinnett for assaulting her on the 16th inst.—Mr P Davies appeared for the defendant, and the complainant said that she was only represented 131 God.—After hearing the evidence, the Bench dismissed the case.—Thomas Dolphin and Arthur Hymn were summoned for assaulting Alice Oxley, on the 16th inst.—Mr A Browne defended.— There was a considerable amount of hard swearing in the case, and the magistrates dismissed it. PROVOKING LANGIII.OI3.—Esth,r Williams was summoned for using threatening language to Alice Oxley, on the 16th Angust.—Mr. Browne defended.—She was bound over to keep the peace for six months in one surety of £5.--Clara Horton and Margaret Stringer summoned each other for using provoking language on the 18th August. —Mrs. Stringer was bound ever to keep the peace, and Mrs. Horton was ordered to pay her own COW. NEGLECT OF CONTRACT.—WiIIiam Garrett summoned a girl named Rose Mary Dickinson on a claim of £2 16a 7d, alleged to be due as compensatation for her having on the 26. h July left his employment without notice.—lt appeared that part of the claim was for money paid by Garrett on her behalf to other persons.—The Bench ordered ' her to pay 12s, the amount due in lien of notice, and told Mr Garrett he must recover the remainder in the County Court.--Martha Whittle was summoned by William Gar- rett for disobeying an order for the payment of an amount due.—Ordered to pay Is a week.

The jubilee of the Boiler Makers and the Iron Ship, Builders' Association was celebrated in, Manchester on Wed— nesday. In the morning a procession was formed in Albert Square, and the men—some 3,000 in number—marched to Belle Vue Gardens, where they had dinner, Mr. William Mather in the chair. There are about 28,000 members of the association, and the funds in hand amount to £lOO,OOO. THE COUNTESS AND HER CArs.—At a special court of the Kensington (London) bench of magistrates, on t'atur,lay, the case of the Countess de la Torre again came on.— The countess had been ordered to get rid of a number of dogs and cats that she had sheltered in her house, thereby causing a nuisance to her neighbours. She now declared that she had -only three cats under her-care. An officer of the court was, howevef, sent to the house, and reported on his return that there were eight cats and a kitten on the stairs, one in a room on the first floor, three in the front kitchen, and another (dead) in the back yard. There were also seven dogs in the heuse.—The bench confirmed the order for the abatement of the nuisance, and ordered the countes! to pay 10.1 for each day since the .2nd inst, when the original order was confirmed by the general court at Westminster.

MORE BATHING ACCIDENTS. - At Chester, on Monday evening, a young man, named Charles Evans, a striker in Messrs Wooil's anchor works at Saltney, near Chester, was bathing in the Dee. The water was vary low, and Evans was trying to walk across, when he suddenly sank into a hole, and was drowned before assistance could be rendered.—On Monday night Henry Beeton, a boy, was als9 drowned in the Dee, near the Dee Mills, whilst bithing.— A young man, named Edwards, was drowned in Llandudno Bay whilst bathing. Professor Reddish, who was near at the time, made several attempts to recover the body, but without avail —At the Mumbles, near Swansea. on Tuesday, two young ladies, named Batchelor. were bathing when one got out of her depth. The sister went to assist her, but in the meantime a gentleman swam out and rescued her. After she was brought in it was discovered that her sister had been carried out to sea. She was drowned in sight of friends.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY—Before Alderman Burgess and Captain Litton. The only case of interest is reperted in another column. MONDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the chair, Mr Ziba Armitage, and Mr John Fakelough. DnuNNENNEss.—James Cummings, lark from Northwich, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Bank-street on Saturday afternoon.--John Quincy was charged with being drunk and disorderly at 12-25 that morning.—He was dismissed on payment of the lock-up fee, la.--Catherine Hankinson was fined Sc and costs for being drunk and disorderly on Cropper's•brow.—John Platt, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Merkur,- street on the 9th met, was fined 53 and 6s costs.--Joseph Bibby, for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street on the 9th lost, was fined 103 and costs or 14 days.--Edward Griffin, for being drunk and disorderly at the same time and place, was also fined 1013 and costs or 14 days. A Row AT THE Rosa—Harriet Hayes, a young woman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Rose-yard on Saturday evening.—lt appeared that she went to the Rose Inn and smashed nine panes ef glass with a stone that she threw at the windows.—Prisoner, who aid that she was assaulted by the landlord and landlady of the Rose, was fined 105 and costs, and ordered to pay the damage or go to prison.for 14 days. INnEcENce.—Mary Ann Bate, an elderly %Yemen, was sent to prison for 14 days fer being guilty of indecent be- haviour in an opening off Brown-street. "As GOOD AS CAPTAIN WEBB." A Ulan named Wil- liam Price CM charged with being drank and indecent in River-road, Latchford, on Sunday night. PC 16 deposed to receiving complaints about the prisoner's conduct, and a man named John Coyne said that between five and six o'clock on Sunday evening he saw the prisoner bathing in the river near Capner's boathouse, daring a time when a considerable number of respectable people were passing on the side of the river. The prisoner said be would be "as good as Captain Webb," --Fined lOs and casts, or 14 days. Sego= ..ATTENDANCR —Matthew Curley, for neglecting to send his two children to school, was fined Sc in respect to each chin—Several persons were dealt with for similar offences. A NUISANCE. Joseph Shaw, charged with allowing a nuisance to exist at his slaughterhouse by an accumulation of garbage, was dismissed on payment of costs. STONE TataowlgG.—Thomas Weyinan, an elderly mane was charged with throwing stones in Wilderspool-road, on the 9th August.—He explained the circumstance on the ground that it was a joke.—Dismissed on payment of costs, Ts. CHIMNEYS ON FlRE.—Walter Roberts and Thomas Woods were each fined is for allowing their chimneys to be on fire. Funious Datvigo. Henry Rodhel, a German, was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart, and with furiously driving in Lythgoes-lane on the 9th August. —Mr Jenkins defended.—Defendant was fined 103 and °casts for being drunk, and 20s and costs for furiously driv- ing. TUESDAY.—Before Councillors Monks and Broadbent. DRUNRENNRS" —John Mannion, Dolman's-lane, for being dna% and Jerly in Batterrnarket-street the previous evening, was L led 5s and costs, and a similar penalty was imposed on Wm. Philips, Rosa-yard, for drunkenness. A PIANIST IN TnouncE.—Thomas Blake, of Bakehouse- yard, was summoned by his wife for an assault committed on Saturday evening.—It appeared that the prisoner was en- gaged as a pianist at the Borough Arms, and after he had left there on Saturday and goee home be quarrelled with his wife, and committed the assault complained of.—Pri- eloper, who said that he had thrashed his wife because .she was under the influence of drink, was bound oyer in his own recognisances to keep the peace for six months. A Flour ABOUT A Dui/ex.—Patrick Noon Was charged by John Higgins with assaulting him on Sunday. The parties live near each other, and it was alleged that Noon assaulted Higgins because the latter refused to give him a share of a b3ttle of "pop."—The Bench dismissed the case.

WEDNESDAL—Before Mr. John Fakelough and Captain Litton. DRUNKENNESS.—Joseph Smith, a travelling hawkar, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on the previous morning. He was discharged with a repri- mand. .

WIFE BEATING —John Clare was charged by his wife, Ellen Clare, with assaulting her on the previous Saturday. —A quarrel arose in consequence of the prisoner accusing his wife of rifling his pockets, and, complainant alleged, the prisoner struck her several blows when she bad the babyin her arms and knocked her down. Ea then got hold of her by the hair and dashed her head against the floor.—Mr P Davies, for the defence, contended that both sides were equally at fault —Prisoner was ordered to be bound over in his, own recognisances of £lO to keep the peace for six months.
THURSDAL—There was no business.

div.p: _WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WRDNESDAY. —Before Messrs Bleckly (in the chair), S Rigby, R Houghton' T Manion, and Tinsley. DETVENNESS.—Patrick Flannigan, labourer, Peter Bat- ten, and Michael Charles were each fined 53 and costs, or seven days, for being drunk at Houghton Green. ASSMILT.—WiIIiam Taylor was dismissed on a charge of assaulting Frederick Heywood, at Glazebrook.

OBSTRUCTION.—WiIham Armstrong, for leaving a lurry on the highway at Houghton Green without having proper control over it, was fined Is and Costs. DAMAGING WHEAT.—Charles Campbell and James Maloney, soldiers stationed at Orford Barrack, were sum- moned for damaging wheat standing in a field in the occu- pation of John Bates, and situated near Marsh House.lane, on the 14th inst.—They were fined 40s and costs. PnovotriNG LANGUAGE—Mary Sinnett was charged with lasing provoking language towards Harriet Broadhurst.—Mr Davies appeared for complainant.—The Bench decided to bind the defendant over to keep the peace for six months. DANGEROUS NEGLIGENCE.—WiIIiam Jackson, for not hav- ing three persons employed in the care of a locomotive under his charge, on the highway at Poulton, was fined 103 and costs.

FATHER AND SON—Charles Harrison was charged with using malicious threats to John Thomas Harrison, his son. Mr A Bro vne appeared for the complainant, and Mr Jenkins defended.—The case was adjourned until next court day, both patties being bound over to keep the peace in the mean- time.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before the Rev E A P Campbell and Mr F Rigby. A Wommq's WRANGLE. - Annie Shaw, a well dressed young woman, was summoned for having on the 11th inst. made use of defamatory and abusive language towards Mary Ann Page' wife of a dock labourer, living in Handley-street, calculated to provoke a breach ot the peace.— Mr Hitchen appeared for the complainant.—After hearing the evidence, the Bench said it seemed to have been a vulgar women's wrangle and dismissed the summons.

r, AGGRAVATION.—Peter Cliff, a young man, pleaded guilty to assaulting Thomas Newton, 13 years of age, on the 11th instant. Inspector Atherton stated that the boys teeth were loosened with the blow. The defendant alleged that the complainant and other boys werecontinually aggravating him by shouting at him and throwing stones.—Mr Campbell said the Bench so disliked the practice of boys teasing those upon whom they thought they could impose, that they would only fine the defendant 63. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr Holbrook Gaskell, jun. DRUNKENNESS —For this offence a fine of 53 and costs was imposed upon each of the following persons :—Patrick Graylisb, William McMillan, John Dagnall, Henry P Mather, Benjamin Hudson, Walter Bushell, John Riley, Henry J Woodwa,d, and Catherine Farley. BREACH GE THE PEACE.—William Slater was convicted of committing a broach of the peace, and was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, in his own recognisances of £lO and one surety of £5. SLEEPING OUT.—John Finnity, 17 years of age, was sen- tenced to seven days's hard labour for sleepicg in an out- house in Caroline-street, on Saturday night. WEDNESDAY.— Before Mr H GaskeTh sen, and Mr F H Gossage. CONFIRMED DRUNKARDS.—Rose Kelly, who made her 39th appearance in the dock, and who has this year served two terms of a month each for drunkenness, was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with bard labour for being drunk. As she descended the steps into the cells, the prisoner said she hoped that their worships would provide her with a good dinner before she left for 'good."—Ann Rollinson, who made her 10Ch appearance, was fined 10a and costs for similar offence. HIGHWAY OFFENCES.—Robery Hoey, for allowing his donkey to stray in Warrington-road, on the 9th Diet, was fined 5s and costs.—John Fairclough pleaded guilty to be- ing asleep on his cart on the Bth just, and he was fined 2s Gd and costs.

"THE QUEEN AND CONSTITUTION." Sir,—Most of your readers have, I dare say, heard the above given as a toast at the various convivial meetings Englishmen delight to attend. Were any of them asked to give a definite and concise answer as to what it meant. I feel confident they would acknowledge their bewilderment. The Queen exists as head of the State. As an individual the is supposed to be the emMdirnent of the Constitution After her Majesty, we have the Lords and Connoting. These, 4ra:their turn, are followed by the various Courts of .I.aw; The whole of the governing body may be fairly given as what we term " our glorious Constituion." flow much of this is gloriou it would again puzzle our wise-acres to say. It le well, of course, to be careful how we criticise the acts and doings of a reigning, Sovereign; so many personal and selfish interests are centred in the continneace of Royalty, and as Lord Tennyson tells us, "the fierce light that beats upon a throne" is apt to dazzle the beholders and make it unsafe for the unwary critic. The suggestion made by Mr. Henry George that we allow the Qaeen a "a widowesernario £4CO per annum has my hearty support. That we should centioue paying her £600,060 is neither more nor less than a gigantic piece of foolery. VVe paid the Prine aCansert £630,000 for m arryinig her, and now what the brood of German paupers cost the British taxpayers it is hard to say. Not a Garman princelet -comes to this country but what we are called upon to pay his fare, and place a yacht at his deposal. The bill for keeping yachts in repair, and. furnishing and refurnishing mansions in which these Germans may inereaee and multiply, is 80:11e- -Mail; enormous. Tae money so wasted would go a (-long way towards freeing us of these fearful "Bitter Cricm" that we periodically hear, Even when the country is relieved of the further maintenance of one of these paupers, the :bill for funeral expanses is sent in to the nation, as in the case of the late Prince Leopold. Bat what do we get in reenrn for all this? Simply nething. Monarchists tell as that-we are saved from the periodical disturbances that Republican- ism inflicts upon France and America. This is mere moon- shine. Setting out with the pecarliar advantages Englandlo posseesed of, she need imitate no other nation. At once vepeel the Act of Setttleinenr, and the rest will be easy. 4lereditary royalty, like hereditary legislators, must be done away with; they are based upon hereditary poverty, and carry nothing but corruption an I misery with them. We are paving a million per annum to sustain that which giver Ms nothing in return.

"When f gaze .oa,the proud palace, and behold one man In the blood purp!ed robes of royalty, Feasting at ease. arid lording over millions; Thee torn me to the hut of poverty AR see the wretched lab'rer warn with foil Divide his scanty morsel with his Wants, I sicken, and. indignant at the sight. • slush for the patience of humanity " It is well known< that the Queen is now saving enormous sums of money yearly, and that she, or those around her, seiz 3 told of the emoluments intewled to be saved to the nation by the abolishment of sinecures, and this in defiance of Acts of Parlienteet which expressly state that all moneys not ap- propriated ,to the privy purse shall be expended in maintaining the dignity of the offi:s of the Chief of the State. Our eloriocs Constitution unfortunately has saddled on to its back something fateworse than royalty. With this Old Man of the Sea we might manage; if it does no good it does eno active injury. But we have also to bear the divinely ap• pointed House of Lords. During.the present agitation vari- ous efforts have been made to prove that the peers have at -tee time or anotinr been of some use. For every ounce of .gain a ton of loss can be placed against it. During the pre- sent Parliament their chief occupation has been rejecting hills. Measures that take up night after night of anxious thought, are rejected by these Lord Tom-Noddies, who -usually meet at fon; and after deep and anxiose thought retire at a quarter Past. How happens it that the Tories ibave always a majority in the House of Lords.? Laying the pestilential spirkual peers ont of the question, it seems very strange that privilege should always be ablo.to count upon a majority of temporal peers. Perhaps this i.e a con- stitutional secret known only to the wire-pullers of the dordly caucus. , Their .lordships have always been strong supporters of Parliamentary corruption, and every .effort elute by the House of Commons to clear iteelf of this foul and corroding influence ha s b ten persistently rejected by the House of Lords. They raise stand in the way of.con• stituencies sending working-men to P trliarnent, by insisting that all the election machinery shall be of an expessive character, and. refusing to paSS Bribery Bills, they make it impossible to send any but rich men to Parliament. This sa question that working-men should ponder deeply upon. To send one of their clas3 is almost imposaible, and yet until this is largely done, they must never expect their case to receive due attention in the Hears of Commons. We have ones nodic efforts to reform the land laws, yet bow is this possible so long as the Lords retain a vetoing power. Even the 3impfest measure for allowing farm labourers the right to till charity lands has been rejected and muti- lated by these lordlines so that it remains a dead letter. Look at the Irish land question, an there cannot be a doubt in the mind of any one that the whole of Ireland's misery dies at the door of the House of Lords. On their heads rest all the Irish blood that has been spilt ; and now clever writers are engaged to pr we that the lords require compen- sation. Look through the history of religious equality ; not one measure has ever been passed by the C 01131130119, but hag been most strenuonely opposed by those in another place." Burial laws, Jewish emancipation, Catholic emanci- pation. reform of every description was obnoxious to their lordships refined taste. At the Warrington Borough Palice Court yesterday, be- fore Captain Reynolds and Mr John White, a respectable looking man named Peter Thompson, was summoned on a charge of obtaining LIO by means of lale pretesces from Christian Bower, a Warringtoc butcher. The charge arose in respect to a. horse transmtion between the parties.—Mr Jenkins appeared for the complainant, and Mr Yearsley for the defendant —Mr Jenkins said that the case was of a somewhat unusual character. The defendant resided at Lawton, and was air-Taber. and the prosecutor carried on husinise as a butcher in Warrington. On Wednesday, the 13th inst, the incidents relating to the chirgs took place. Ho should prove that the d4,ndaot mule the followin,g asser- tions when endeavouring to sell a horse to the complainant: that he had the bailiffs in his house, was in trouhle and wanted mon.y, was a farmn and lived at Manor ROLM, Lowton, and that the horse in ques- tion was sound. If his (Mr Jenkins) instructions were Cor- rect, he was prepared to prove that the whole of these state- ments were falsehoods, which, he cantended, was a false pretence.—Cloisian 'tower, the prosecutor, said that he met the defend int and a man named Shaw on the day in ques- tion, and in consequence of what Shaw sail he went with them to see a horse in Horsemarket•street. Thmce they went to the King's Head Inn, where the defendant made the assertions enumnatel by. Mr Jenkins, and atid that Bower could have the horse examined by a veterinary sur- geon, or could take it.oa trial. Defendant said that he wan- Led £lB for the animal, but it was well worth £3B. He wan- ted to sell it because he must have some money. The horse, defendant said, was quiet, and had been driven by his daug's- ter. Ultimately wltness bought the horse on trial on the assurance that it was sound, and paid £lO on account. Cross-sxamined, witness slid that he thought the horse was lame, and Mr Yearsley then submitNal that there was no case.—The magistrates' clerk (Mr H II White) said that there might have been a very dish meat transaction, but he did not see how the false pretences was made out.—Captain Reynolds was it opinion th it th.re wan no ease.—Mr Jen• bins contended that there was twiee wetence4 as the horse was found n)t to be sound —Mr Yearsiey : He admits that the horse was lame when he bought it.—Mr. Jenkins: Ater he bought it —Prosecutor said that he dis• covered that tbe horse was lame the Thunad ty mo.n.imt after the transaction took place.—The Clerk: The prosecutor said In reply to Mr. Yearaley that after ho had tad rde horse in the afternoon he smirked that the ho.se was lame.—pro- secutor : T thought it was lame, but the dlendint wdull not have it so and said I could hive it exanained or have it a week on trial.—Mr. Jenkins: 163 y that the assertion that that the horse was sound was a false pretence.—ln answer to the Clerk prosecutor said that he asked the defendant for tie money back before he took out a su munns.--Tlle Clerk did not think the case should ha sent t 4 the Sessions, but said that if Mr. Jnakins took it up as ono of conspiracy amongst a number of men to defraud, be might Succeed Mr. Jenkins said that it was his intention to ask the Bench after the c,s-, had been heard if that would be the best cnurse.—The Clerk sail Mr. Jenkins could scarcely expect the time of the court to be taken up for that purpose.—Mr. Jenkins said that be had a right to ask the court to assist him in providing the ends of jtistice.—The Bench decided tie dismiss the case.—Mr. Jenkins: I will bring the case be- fore you in another form.

LYTAL MEET ACOIDENT. DRIVER CENSURED.

On Tueeday evening Mr Brighouse, couaty coroner, held an inquiry at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-steeet. Warring- ton, relativelo the death of a child named Elizabeth Mil- liegton Penaherton, 14 months old, which occurred on Satur- day morning .under circumstances detailed in the evidence adduced. The deceased was the daughter of Joseph Pem- berton a boiler inaker, living at 129, Dallam-lane, and on Saturday moraine, she was run over in Dallam-lane by a horse and tarry tat at the time were not under the control of the driver. Mr A Browne, solicitor, Warrington, watched the case on behalf of George Whalley, the driver of the , horse and Larry in question. The following evidence was given :—Janet Pemberton, wife of Joseph Pemberton, and mother of the deceased, deposed that she last saw the child , in good health a few minutes before the accident. About ten o'clock on Saturday morning the child went down the lobby of the house to the street, and about three minutes after. wards witness heard a ccream, ard, going outside, saw ti girl named Clara Whitelsouee holding the deceased in her arms. One of the deceased's legs had been cut off, and she was taken to the Infirmary. Witness saw a lorry and horse opposite a shop next door to her house. The lorry was I loaded with iron, and the horse was going at a good speed. The child died on the afternoon of the same day. By Mr Browner There was a deal of shunting going on about the gate where she Was told the horse and lorry came from. She had often noticed horses and lurries standing outside the gate. The street was a very narrow one. By the jury: The horse seemed to be going at a good trot.—Clara White- house, aged nine, an intelligent looking girl, said that on the day in question she was going on an errand to a shop next door to Mrs Pemb3rton's when she saw the deceased stand- ing in the roadway just off the parapet, laughing at a horse that was coming towards her. The horse knocked deceased down, and the wheels of the furry went ever her. Witness did not see anyone in charge of the horse and lorry. By Mr Browne: The child was standing about two yards from the footpath. There was an engine shunting on the line near by.— Sarah Rtybould, 170, Winwick-road, deposed that she saw the accident when just past Oh, brewery in Dallatn-lane. She saw a baby aleout a Yard from the parapet and a horse knock it over, a lorry that the horse was dragging also go. log over it. Witness saw no one except the deceased in the street, and did not see anyone who appeared to be in charge of the horse and lorry. She went to the child and did not see anyone who appeared to be in charge. By Mr Browne: The horse, which was on the right side of the road, was walking —Daniel Macintosh, Stamford-street, a labourer, said that he was in Dallatn-lane on S tturdey morn- ing and saw the deceased directly after the accident. Ile saw no one in charge of the horse and cart. There was a check office inside the gate near the railway line, and it was usual for carters to get their checks there. Witness had seen horses and carts standing inside the gate while the carters got their checks—Charles William Howell, 13G, Bat- tersby-lane, spoke to seeing the wheels of the Wry run over the deceased. Ile did not see anyone in charge of the horse. Afterwards witness SAW George Whalley in change of the horse.—Thomas Downey, a fitter, said. that on Satur- day morning he saw Whalley washing his face ir the engine house at Dallam-lane. Witness had previously seen him take a horse and lurry over the line through the north gate leading to the line. That was labia three minutes before 1 Whalley washed his face. Whaliey -emained about three minutes in the engine house, and witness did not afterwards again see him. By Mr Browner lie hid heart that the man was Whalley, but did not know of his own knowledge. The person he saw was washing paint off his face.—Dr Joseph gave the result of a post mortem examination of the body of the deceased. The clue° of deafh was collapse and shock to the nervous system due to the injuries to the right leg and thigh. &c —George Beckley, Church-street, son of the owner of the horse and lorry driven by Whalley, was celled by Mr Browne, and s aid that Whal ler had been engaged by his father for six years, driving between Dellam forge and How- ley-quay. Whalley was a temperate man and as steady sons as ever they had. He had often known drivers leave their horses and carte in Dallam-lane during the time that they were getting checks at the office. Witness had often gene into Dallam-lane and left his horse and cart there, and then gone back to the check office.—The Coroner: What I control could you have over the Ii tee should a train come up P—Witness : He would have to take his own chance. Continuing, witness said a coal train generally came down the line in question at about eleven o'clock in the morning. ' —Lawrence Gilooter, cheek taker at the north gate of the Dallam Forge, who had not been sub-pcened, was then sent for by the po:ice, and in answer Is questions put by the coroner, stated that a man named Whalley came to the office on Saturday morn- ing with a load of hers, and witness checked him. Witness was not aware that drivers were hound by any regulations to take their carts to stand in the line whilst getting the checks. Inside the works were three or.four lines. There were no trains coming from the main line at the time wit- ness saw Whalley. Shunting on the web lines might take place at any atm.—This was all the evidence. Numerous questions were put to witness as to the action of the driver in leaving his cart in the lane, and as to the custom of drivers when delivering their checks at the office.—The Coroner summed up at length, and after a consultation in private the jury returned a verdict to the effect that the child met its death accidentally. They also found that the driver Whalley, though not guilty of criminal negligence, had been guilty of negligence that called for the censure of the jury. The jury ales made a presentment to the effect that better provision should be in tde at the Dellam Forge to allow carters to have absolute control over their horses dur- ing the time that the " checking " Was being carried out.— After the jury had returned this verdict Whalley was called into the room and censured by the Coroner, who told him that the jury had taken a most merciful view of the case in not Committing him for manslaughter.—The irquiry lasted about four hears.

iiIIOIiND:DEAD AT STOCKTON HEAT El. About noon on Toursday, a gardener, in the employ of Mr. Tinsley, of Stockton [Leath, discovered in a field in close proximity to the police station the dead body of a man, apparently about SO years of age, lying on his face dead. There was found by lais-side a bottle labelled " Laudanum," and there were indications that he had swallowed a portion of the-contents. and had afterwards vomited. He was respect- ablidressed, but there were no marks on his clothing by which his identity could be recognised. Yesterday after. noon Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inqeest at the Mulberry Tree Inn, • Appleton, Stockton Heath, relative to to the death, when the evidence given below was adduced. =Joseph Corey, Chapel-lane, Ap2leton. gardener to Mr. Tinsley, said that about 945 on Thursday morning, he found the hotly of the deceased in a field belonging to Mr. Tinsley. He was lying on his face with his hand under his forehead, and vu dead. Witness gave info-m ttion to the police.—Edwin Jones, labourer, Stockton Heath, said that on Monday evening he saw the deceased in the London Bridge Inn. He said that he was in trouble, and was goistr, on the road. He also said that he had paid lOs for rent, and had left ZS on the rent book for his son. Afterwards he contradicted that statement, and said that the money was only £5 odd. Deceased appeared sensible, and• witness understood him to say that he lived at Crouton, or something like that. He said that he had left word with his ecn that if he was not at home at six o'clock that night he need not be ex- pected. Witness only saw deceased have one glass of beer. Deceased said that he did not care if he never saw his son ag du. He further said that he did not know Or care where he was going to.—P.S. Alfred Booth, stationed at Stockton Heath, said that on Thursday, from information' received, he went to the place where the deceased was found as described by Corey. 11l removed the body to the Mul- berry Tree Inn. Near to the body witness found the bottle ' produced, labelled" Laudanum—poison," and had the name of I? J Machin. pharmaceutic al chemist, 83, canning-street, Liverpool, and Horton Pharmacy, Huyton. The bottle was almost empty and the cork was out. Witness found on re- m-wing the deceased that he had been vomiting. Witness should think that the deceased bad lain there about two days, as the head was discolouring. There were no marks of violence on the body. Three halfpence were , found on the decetsed. The body was that of fa man about 60 years of age. He was sft. 71n. k height, of &ender build, pale complexion' grey eyes, bald, grey whiskers and moustache. He had no front teeth in the top jaw. He was dressed in a dark tweed coat, black cloth vest, nearly new moleskin trousers, a grey mixed woollen shirt, grey worsted stockings, blucher boots with iron tipped heels, and a soft him& billycock hat. There were no marks on the clothing. Witness had not been able to learn anything as to the identification of the deceased.— The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was found dead, the Corener remarking, that the jury a ouid martely think that a post mortem should have been held, as from the position or the bottle when found, and the fact of the deceased baying vomited, they might reasonably pre- sume that he died from poison, but whether administered as medicine or not !redid not think that thercould tell. The police would no doubt make every possible inquiry as to identification.

Bachannon, on Saturday last. —The,prisoner. it appeared, had been rect rested in coniequence of his being drunk and disorderly to go hems, and bad then become violent and kicked the officer. div.head: FASEIIONABLE WEDDING AT LYMNI.
div.p: FASEIIONABLE WEDDING AT LYMNI.

the Thursday the marriage of Miss Josephine Battereby, second daughter of the late Mr W Battersbv, of Lymm Hall, to Mr J F Walthow,ef Galveston, Texas, U.S., was celebra- ted in the Parish Church, Lymm. The bride belonging to a family deservedly popular in Lymtn, and having by her own amiable qualities won the regard and esteem of the in- habitants, the marriage, as might hive been expected, ex- cited an unusual interest in the village and neighbourhood. For an hour or more prior to eleven o'clock, the time flied for the ceremony, the roads and lanes leading to the pic- turesquely situated church were alive with people making their way to that place of worship, the bulk of the femi- nine portion of the population being apptrently bent on taking patt in the interes.ing proceedings, if not as actors, at least as spectators. A suitable display of decorations had also not been neglected. Tue road which leads from the hell to the Church was spanned by a large arch, with two smaller spans to allow feet passengers to pass along the 'pathways, the materials chiefly used in ths censtruct- don being everkreens and various eelonred flowers. A num- ber of pendant floral festoons hung from this arch, whilst it was appropriately surmounted by the floating banners of England and the Uuited States. Just shove the Central span the kindly wishes" We wish you joy " and " God be with you " were prominently set forth. This arch was designed and erected by Mr W. Brazendale, builder, Lymin, on whose artistic skill it certainly re- flected no discredit. A. somewhat similar em- bellishment, made by Mr. F. Simpson, bead gardener, sur- mounted the gateway leading from the park, aed within the ; park several smaller arches had been constructed. From various vintage places near the church banners were float- ing, and within the sacred edifice the chancel had been very tastefully decorated with flowers and ferns by Mn. Morris, Mrs. Callender, Mrs. Gaut, Miss Williamson, lad other ladies. The path from the entrance of the church was Icovered with ecirlet cloth, which was also laid down at the main entrance to the hall. Besides being favoured by the presence and efforts of well wiahers, the weather was every- thing that could he desired for such an Occasion, and if there j be anything in Herrick's prognesticetion that "Blest is the ; bride on whom the sun doth shine" this nuptial ceremony j was acccenpanied by happy auguries. By the time fixed for I the arrival of the bride the chute!' was well filled by an ex- pectant congregation, and the path through the church-yard was lined on both sides by a considerable company. The ; bride, who leant on the arm of her brother, was preceded by her bridesmaids and two prettily attired pages, Masters H. ! and W. Duckworth, who after getting within the church , stood on each side of the en.rance, and afterwards followed 'up to the chancel. The bidal party was preceded up the ! aisle of the church by a piny of choristers I who sung "The voice that breathed o'er Eden" j The service was full choral, the organist being Mr. I Theodore Ardern, and it included besidee hymns an Andante Iby Lemrnens ; Offertoire, by Salome; Invocation, by Salerno; and an Andante, by Batiste. The officiating I clergyman was the Rev. G. W. Guest, the rector, who was aisistell by the Rev. Mr. Lrnax, crate. The bride was dreseed in a frieze velvet bodice and train, the front being of satin with:pearl trimmings. She also wore I diamond ornemente. and a peril and diamond bracelet given by the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Miss S rtattersby, Miss Rose, Mies L B ittersby (Wolverhampton), Miss Nor- man, and Miss Duckworth, who each wore bangles pre- sented by the bridegroom. The groomsmen were Mr Ziegler, Mr Warthon, Mr Bretherton, and Mr Battershe. After the service the party were driven back to Lymm where a beeekfast, provided by Messrs Parker and Son, Manchester, was partaken of by about sixty guests. In the afternoon the newly-united pair drove to Bank Quay Station, Warrington, whecce they departed for the Cumber- land lakes, where they ietend to spend a few days prior to sailing for America. Besides private presents to the bride, she has been presented with a large marble clock by the ball servants, half-a-dozen apostle spoons and sugar tongs by the out-door servants, a silver sugar basin by the teachers of the Church Sunday school, and a flower stand by the members of the Lymm drum and fife band. In the evening the village was paraded by the local bands in honour of the occasion. Daring the day, Mr T Birtlee, photographer, Warrington, took a secceseful group of the wedding party, and a smaller group of the bride and Bride- groom and bridesmaids.

LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE POOR RATES.—The follow- ing are from papers just made public, howing the amount of rates collected, and the amount expended, in this and the adjoining county :—Lancashire: The poor rates col- lected amounted to £1,506,976. The sum of £32411 was received from the Tretsury in aid thereof, and £56,676 ob- tained (rem other sources. The expenditure amounted to £1.592,381; the expenditure out of this towards relief was £753,057, awl the sum of £838424 for purposes entirely unconnected with relief.—Cheshire: The poor rates col- lected in this county amounted to £292,516. The sum of £1.0,892 was received from the Treasury, and £9993 ob- tained from other sources, making a total of £313,406. The expenditare for the county amounted to £323304, while a sum of £137,173 was expended upon the poor, the re- mainder, £186,131, being expended for purposes totally un- connected with relief. THE PROPOSED SCHOOL BOARD FOR GREAT SANKEY.— The 28th instant is the date fixed for the election of the projected School Board for Great Sankey, and it is thou tilt by many that it will not pass off without a coetest. SALE OF MACHINERY.—On Tuesday the fixed plant of the Scotland Bank Ironworks. Warrington, was sold by public auction by Mr Tuomas Whitehead, auctioneer, Warrington. There was a good attendance of local buyers, and also of buyers from Manchester, Sheffield, Liverpool, and Leicester. Good prices, it is stated, were realised at the sale.

TEMPERANCE MEETINGS. —A Gospel Temperance Mission wilt be conducted on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday evenings next, by Mr William Forbes, of London, in the Workmen's Club-room, Market-place. At noon on each of these days a public prayer meeting will be held. On the evening of Monday, the Ist -September • a public .farewell meeting to the Rev Thomas Rippon will be held, at which the Mayor will preside. Me RYLANDS AND THE LIBRE= COMMITTEE.—OD Tues- day the members of the Liberal Management Committee, Burnley, who, with the Mayor (Alderman Baron, J P.), had received an invitation from Mr Rylands to spend a day at his country residence, p oceeded by train to Thelwall, near Warrington, and afterwards went to Massey Hall. Here they were entertained at lunch by Mr Rylands, with whom they spent a very enjoyable day.

CURIOUS FLND AT EIATTON.—WhiIst repairing property at Hatton, near Warrington, some time ago, the brick- layers found in one of the walls a chest, which contained documents having reference to the Daresbnry and Thelwall estates. Mr. Woods, of Hatton, who is the present landlord, received them from Mr. John Smith, bricklayer, Hatton. The papers found are deeds relating to the property owned by the late Squire trough, of Thelwall and Dareebury Hall.

Tug Ltvma OF ST. BARNABAS.—We understand that the Rev. George Anton, who has recently been licensed to the living of St. Barnabas, Bank Quay, Warrington, is a mem- ber of St. Bee's and also of the University of Durham. He was ordained deacon in 1878 and priest in 1877 by the Bis- hop of Durham, and after serving the caracies of St. Barn- abas, Sutherland, and Barnopfield, in Northumberland, he was instituted, in 1881, to the vicarage of Cold Coniston, near Leeds. SHAMEFUL OUTRAGE : MAIMING HORSES.— The War- rington police are now engaged in making investigations into a shameful outrage that has recently been committed, two horses that were put out to graze in a field off Marsh- house•lane, naving 'aeon shockingly mutilated on the haun- ches by Some person or persons as yet unknown. Clean cuts of considerable magnitude are said to have been inflicted with a knife. A reward has been offered, and it is much to be desired that the offender or offenders will be brought to r justice.

RUMOURS OF Examen Crtormta —Daring the past few days many rumours have been in circulation to the effect that English cholera had broken out in Warrington and the neighbourhood, but on making inquiries we learn that there have been no cases attributable to that malady. It is pre- sumed that the rumours have been caused by the .fact that there have been cases of acute diarthcei—a natural consequence of the intensity of the heat of the past few weeks. We have medical authority for stating that there is little or so probability of an outbreak of English cholera in this neighbourhood, but it would be .well that at present careful attention should be paid to the subject of a proper diet.

THR BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, August 16th, 1884. The mean temperature was BLS Fahrenheit, and therefore 3 degrees warmer than preceding week. The maximum temperature 86 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 12th inst., and the minimum temperature 34 Fahrenheit on the 15th inst. 'The rainfall measured C 8 inches. The general direction of the wind was westerly. During the week, which was the 33rd of the current year, 31 births and 18 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 2i per 1,000, against 24 3 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 153 the correaponding week of last year. Tne d,aths included 5 from diarrhoal, 2 from old age, 2 from heart disease, 4 from brain disease, and 2 from lung disease. —Some IL GORHAM, Ededictl Officer of Elealtb.

PADGATE Ciduacrt Scaoor.s. Yesterday week, the annual treat was given to the scholars of the above schools. The children net at three o'clock, and proceeded to a fie Id which was kindly lent for the occ talon by Mr Jacksou, of Fearnbead. After indulging in various games and amuse- ments, they partook of a substantial tea, the arrangements for which had been admirably superintended by Mrs Turner and Mrs Granger. Several interesting games were then played, the larger buys juining in cricket acid football, the little ones amusing themselves with "cap and bells" and other juvenile delights. Thanks are due to the esttemed Vicar of Padgett) (the Rev W El Williams, M.A.), Mrs WU- Mime, Mr Granger, Mr Mines, and Mr Jackson for their etTarts to make the treat a success. A vary pleasant evening was terminated by the singing of the National Anthem.

"Fux O am BtatsvoL."—Mr. Henry C. Jarrett's original Fun on the Bristol" company has, during the week, oc- cupied the boarde at the Public Hall, appearing in that most smelling piece before good houses." Fan on the Bristol " is calculated to keep an audience in roars of laughter, but in- termixed with the hilarity and jokes is 'some excellent music, which gives a welcome variety to the entertainment. The first act opens at the house of the Widow O'Brien, wealthy but vulgar, where coasiderable flirtation Is carried on by her two charming daughters, who have had the ad- vantage of a fashionable education. The Widow's " bulls " In her attempts to speak as befits her improved condition in life are as ludicrous as the candour with which she occasion- ally admits her humble origin is charming. The second act is laid on board the S.S.Bristol: and includes a mock sentimental elopement and an Inc:dental introduction of a musical entertainment of a high order. A burlesque upon the " L idy of Lyons" is irresistibly Comical and the bravestie on "II trovatore "is also very laughable. The piece is well staged and the various characters admirably sustained.

FIRM AT A RIXTON FAIL:1—.011 M mday Afternoon a fire WAS observed to have broken oat on the farm of Mr George Caldwell, of Riaton near Glizebrook, a larga stack of clover hay stacked in yard adloining the homestead having become ignited. The flames were first seen issuing from the roof of the stack by a labourer employed at the farm, who at once gave information to Mr Caldwell. About two score men who were working on various farms in the neighbourhood lent their assistance with the permission of their respecilve masters, and every effort was made to subdue the outbreak by pouring water on the flames by means of buckets, a run- ning stream near by affording an ample supply of water. Fortunately a stack that was situated very near to the one on fire was preserved from contagion, but it was found im- possible to save the other, and as it continued to burn through the night a mountei'messenger was despatched to Warrington to summon the fire brigade. The alarm bell was rung at about nine o'clock on Tuesday morning, and a contingent of men soon arrived at the scene of the fire with the engine. The fire was then speedily eatig- guished. The damage done is estimated at about £l2O, but the property was insured The firemen played on the remnants of the bu-ning stack for several hours.

ANOTEEE STABEHNO CASE.—At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Har- rison) and Mr John Fakelough, Charles Jackson, alias Josiah Gleave, was charged with unlawfully wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm, Michael Mannion, a fus- tian cutter and a single man, residing at 68, Cockhedge-lane, on Sunday morning at about 12-15.—Mr Hunt (Chief-con- stable) said that the prisoner hailed from Sankey) bat for some time had been workia.; for Messrs Naylor Bros. at Howley-quay, and was !Aging in Greenell-street. About 12 o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner was in company with the sister of tha prosecutor. Man ion would tell them that he saw his sister add the prisoner together in Fennel- street, and found fault with it, saying that his sister should not be out so late at night. Shortly afterwards Mannion felt something strike him in the left side and then the trick- ling of blood, He said "I'm stabbed" and found a wound in his side. The prosecutor went to the infirmary, where the wound, which was not a dangerous one, was dressed. When prisoner was apprehended a clasp knife with blood on it was found in his pocket.—Mr John Turnville Smith, as- sistant surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary, deposed to dres- sing the prosecutor's wound, which he described as a slight one, on the left side, just below the armpit. It was about half an inch long and an inch in depth, extending inwards and slightly backwards. It was not a dangerous wound ow- ing to the direction it thok.—Prosecutor and his sister Mary Mannion then gave evidence.—The defence was that the prosecutor ran against the knife with which the prisoner was cutting a piece of cork, and thus accidentally inflicted the injury upon himself.—The Bench decided that there was not sufficient evidence to commit, and the prisoner was dis- charged. SALE or Sri:Errol PROPERTY An important sale by auction of a freehold farm and lands in Stretton, and free- hold and leasehold dwelling-houses, land, and premises in Warrington, took place at the Lion Hotel, on Wednesday evening, the auctioneer being Mr Thomas Sutton. SHOCKING ATTEIRPr TO BERN THREE PERSONS,—At Shrewsbury, on Friday, Jane Jones, of Pontesbury, near S irewsbury, was remanded by the county mar,istrates on a charge of amen. The evidence of the police showed that prisoner went to the house of a tenant named Mary Morgan and onthe latter declining to pay rent or leave the premises, prisoner locked her and her two grandchildren in and set fire to the tha'ch. Some men rescued the inmates, but the cottage was burned out. TtrE HALLEY WILL CASlL—Edward Mundell and Chas. div.head: EXTRAORDiNARY SCENE AT A FUNERAL.
div.p: EXTRAORDiNARY SCENE AT A FUNERAL.

At the St. Helens County Court; on Wedaesday afternoon, a case of an extraordinary nature was heard before Mr T P , E Thompson, judge. Mrs Mary Astiall, a widow, and aMr Joseph Finney, a wheelwright, sued Mr John -Thomas Flet- cher. undertaker and coach proprietor, of Bickerstaffe.street, for £2 18e, in respect of the burial of the husband of the first-named plaintiff. Mr J P Mearns appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr John 0 Swift defended. From the open- ing statement of Mr Mearns, it appeared that Mre Ashen lives in Elliot-street, and Mr Joeeph Finney in Doulton-st. The husband of Mrs Ashen died on the 17th July last, and Mrs Ashall asked Mr Finney to attend to the funeral arrange- meats, and to hire a hearse and two mourning coaches on • the most reasonable terms he could. Mr Finney went to the establishment of Mr William Garton Dixon, in Bicker- staffe-street, almost adjoining the defendant's and ordered , the hearse and coaches, the cost being £2 18s. As he was returning he saw Mr Fletcher' and, in the course of conversation, told him whet he had been to Mr Dixon's for. Mr Fletcher add lie could do it as cheap as anybody else. ' Finney said it was too late as he had given the order. Mr Fletcher said he would go and see Mrs Asball, and invited Finney to go in a gig with him, but Finney declined. When the latter arrived home he sent his wife to tell Mrs Ashall what he had done, and was surprised to leart that Mr Flet- cher had been up, got the order, and Mrs Ashall had paid , him £3. They went to Mr Fletcher and demanded the money back, but he refused, saying he had got it and would i stick to it, but would not mind returning 21, which was the difference between Dixon's !Wee and his own. The strange thing happened next day, Mr Mearns said, when one pro- cession came and took away the body and some of the rela- tives, while the other rival procession of coaches was almost empty. As a fact, Mr Dixan carried out the funeral arrange- ments, and they asked that the money shoeld be returned. , Joseph Finney was the first witness called. He said Mrs ! Ashen asked him to get her a hearse and two coaches, 'the best and cheapest he possibly could, as she was poor." ' She did not mention any money. He went to Mr Dixon's I place, and saw Mr Shaw, the manager, who quoted £2 18s, I the body having to be taken to Rainford, a distance of four miles. Witness gave him the order. On coming away be ' saw Mr Fletcher. and entered into conversation about the matter. He told Mr Fletcher it was no use going to see Mrs Ashall, as he bad given the order to Mr Dixon. He did not Igo straight home, but when he found what had occurred, Mrs Ashall accompanied him back to Mr Fletcher, and be ! explained that the money had been paid, becenee Mrs Ashall believed lie (Finney) had sent him down. IFletcher Laid he should not refund the money.— His Honour said he did not see how the plaintiffs could, after the evidence of their own witnesses, go on with the case. Finney had proved that Mrs Ashall authorised Fletcher to pond the coaches. It would have been more reasonable, however, if, when Fletcher found that both he and Mr Dixon had been employed, he had offered terms.— Mr Mearns: We are willing to come to some arrangement, but the other piny won't.-11r Swift: I certainly won't be a party to any arrangement.—Mr Mearns: Your honour will see that Fletcher's order was countermanded on Sunday morning.—His Honour: Fletcher got the order.— Mr Mearns: But how did he get it, your honour ?—The Jodge : It seems reasonable that they should employ the man who had got the money. I can't understand them employing Dixon after that mistake they had made in enarloying Yletcher.—Mr Me3rns : The fairest way, I think, would be to divide the money, bec.use they both went to Itainford. The One went full and the other empty.—Mr Swift : As a matter of fact Mr Dixon's men went an hour before the time , arranged. They juggled for the coffio, leaving the mourne:s behind. They got to Reinford as best they could or not at all: -Thomas Shaw said be was manager for Mr. Dixon. On the 19th July Finney came to him and said he was wanted in the Royal Alfred Hotel, next door. He went, and a man named Joseph Craven said, "I told you I should bring you an order some time; this men hes got it:" and Finney gave him the order.—The Judge said it seemed to him to be a waste of time to go on with the case. Somebody or other seemed to have behaved very cruelly towards Mrs. Ashall, but he did not see how she could recover the money, whether it was got by a trick or not. She told Fletcher to send the best notches he had, and having paid the money she could not get out of it. At the request of Mr Swift— who said he should be able to prove that Mr Dixon's name was not mentioned to Mr Fletcher at the first conversation with Finney, and that Finney had no authority to engage Mr Dixon—Mrs Ashall was called. She said she had not authorised Finney to engage Mr Dixon, but had asked him to ascertain what he could get a hearse and two coaches tor. She bad given Mr Fletcher the order.—Judgment was given for the defendant, with costs a eainst Finn.v. -

SOUTHWORTH•WITII•CROFT &I:TOOL BOARD.—There not being tha reqnired number of members to form a quorum, no business Was transacted on Tuesday evening. Tan SERVICES OF DEMAND Norse —At the County Ses- sions at Warrington on Wednesday, before Mr. Ii Blackly (chairman) and other magistrates, Mr. Peter Worthington, a retired builder, was summoned by Mr. Tunstall, assistant overseer, for non-payment of rates.—Mr, Worthington said that he paid a large sum yearly in rates, and always did so before the time fixed for camposition. In this instance he complained that he had never received the demend note, and that under these circumstances he should not have been sum madly summoned before the conre—Mr. Tunstall then called a clerk, who swore tint he pasted the demand note. It was not delivered pars many because defendant lived out of the township.—The Cttair.nan thought that the note should have been delivered in person. He did not know what authority Mr. Tunstall had for posting the notices.— Mr. Tunstall replied that that was the usual custom adopted in such cities —The Bench said that they were not satisfied that the demand note had reached Mr. Worthington, and therefore the cola must fall through.—Mr. Tunstall said that he had served Mr. Worthington with another demand note, and should summons him for the next court.

div.head: DUBLIN SCANDALS.
div.p: THE DUBLIN SCANDALS.

At the sitting of the Court on Friday, Gustavus Corn- wall and Captain Kirwan were put on their trial for con- spiring to procure young men for felonious practices: Dur- ing the swearing of the jury, there was a scene of excitement in court. The Crown largely exercised the right of ordering :jurors to stand aside, and, as these jurors were well-known citizens, defendant's counsel taunted the Crown with being actuated by fear of "United Ireland" owing to the article in Thursday's issue. THE MURDER OF A LONDON CONSTABLE.

Thomas Orrock was again charged at Bow-street on Fri- ; day with the murder of Constable Cole. Evidence was . given as to prisoner's name being scratched on a claisel found on the scene of the crime, and a fellow workman of ' Orrocks, named Miles, deposed to °crocks asking him to help him to take away the plate from the Baptist Chapel. ' Another fellow workman, named Ames, now under sentence at Coldbath Fields, said the tools produced were similar to those Orrocks used. Orrocks told witness he knew them in : who did the murder. Some further evidence was giver., and the case was adjourned. THE GORDON RELIEF EXPEDITION. 1 The Central News learns that the number of troops to be employed in the approaching expedition will by no means ' reach the figure of 5,300 as reported. It will on the contrary, probtbly not exceed 2.500. The statement that no boats will be sent out from England is also incorrect. The boats will be shipped to Alexindria in four or five steamers, the fist portion going early in September. A sheerness tele- gram ssys the Admiralty have ordered the armour-plated ship Ajax, attached to the Medway steam reserve, to be completed for sea with all possible despatch.

div.head: CHINA.
div.p: CHINA.
SHANGHAI, FRIDAY Mort-ti7rin'.---M de Semal le, the French representative at Pekin, his !owered the French flag at the Legation, and started immediately afterwards for this plaee:

PARIS, FRIDAY —Admiral Courbet'e instructions were to c mmence to bombard the arsenal at Foozhow ; yesterday evening, which would correspond to sunrise in the far East. After the bombardment the troops will land to destroy the war mate- rial and stores, the value of which is estimated at about a thousand million francs. This operation will constitute an act of reprisal on the part of the French Government against China. The French troops will then proceed to occupy the port and mines of Kelung as security for the payment of the indemnity claimed by France. PARIS, FRIDAY ArrEasooN.—Li Fong Pao has delayed his depalture. It is believed that he is waiting for fresh instructions from his Government. The Government erg-U:1 at Paris published this afternoon a leader violently attack- ing England.

A Central News Berlin telegram says that the Chinese Government intend notifying the French Government thit any attempt to repeat the Kelung incident will be considered as A declaration of war. The Treaty Posers will then be called noon to discharge their duties as neutral. The Times, in its second edition, publishes the following telegram dated Pekin, Friday :—The French Lagation left here yesterday. Tne telegraph station in this city was opened to•day, and this is the first message despatched thence.

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.

TOULON, FRIDAY, 10-10 .c.x.—There were two deaths from cholera here last night. The state of the public health to- day is less satisfactory on account of the east wind which has prevailed since sunrise this morning. Measmuts, FRIDAY.—Five deaths from cholera occurred here last night. The Prince of Wales has sent a subscrip- tion of £4O to the Prefect for the relief of the sufferers from the epidemic.

A stowaway named Kennedy who, with three companions, was put ashore at Kilmanthemas, near Waterford, from the barque Oranmore, is lying mu in the Workhouse infirmary. The doctor in attendance believes he is suffering from Asiatic cholera.

GARDEN PARTY AT THELWA,LL.—On Saturday afternoon, Mr W Long, of Thelwall Heys, Thelwall, gave a garden party at his residence, to which were invited the head teachers and thelr assistants of all the day schools in War- rington and the various surrounding villages About 121 male and female teachers were hospitably entertained by Mr and Mrs Lung, and partook of tea provided in a tent erected on the grounds by which the residence of the host is picturesquely surroanded. Amongst the guests were Major and ‘lrs Pickmere. A. band of music was in attendance, and during the afternoon various games were enjoy 4. . After tea short speeches were delivered by Maj sr Pickmere, Mr Finney, and Mr Dewhurst ; and Mr and Mrs Long were heartily thanked for their hospitality. The party corn- menced about three o'clock, concluding about 8-30. Mr Long takes a warm interest in educational matters and a , recognition of the efforts of the teachers by which they were eaabled to have a say's enjoyment in the fresh air of the country is an example that might well be followed. Mr Taylor, of the Norton Arms Hotel, Wilderspool-road, was the caterer, and gave every satisfaction. Tan STRUGGLE WITH A PRISONER AT NEWTON POLICE STATION.—At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Joseph Walsh, who on the 9th inst committed a I violent assault upon Edward Spencer, a constable stationed I in Newton district, at the police station in that place, was brought up on remand to take his trial for the offence.—The ' particulars of the assault have been previously narrated IMr Jenkins, solicitor, Warrington. now prosecuted on behalf of the police, and the prisoner, who was also charged with I being drunk and disorderly at Newton on tbe 9th hut, was I undefended.—Mr Jenkins described how the prisoner was I apprehended on the minor charge of drunkenness by P.O !Spencer, and taken to Newton Police Station in custody. Whilst be was searching him at the station the prisoner' struck him in the face with his clenched flat, whereupon the I constable closed with him, and the two struggled for a con- siderable time. The constable was thrown and then drew' his Ye for protection, and struck the prisoner with it. Spencer was then so violently assaulted that he was ren- dered insensible, and remembered nothing mere Whilst lying on the floor insensible he received a violent kick on the head —Evidence was then called, aad it was shown that the constable's life was in jeopardy wten assistance arrived from outside, and he was rescued.—Prisoner was fined 5s and costs for beiag drunk and disorderly, and 40s and costs for the assault, or a month. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A Woafew.—& determined at- tempt at suicide took place near Warrington on Tuesday, when a woman named Mary Wilson, of Water-street, Har- Durhey, near Manchester, a widow, 63 years of age, at- tempted to drown herself in the river Mersey near Arpley. The woman was seen by John Coyne, Bostock-street, and Thomas Calmer, Wilderspool-road, as she was walking on the Lancashire side of the river, to look round one or two times, and then deliberately jump into the water. Mr Cap. nor at once got a boat ready, and Coyne and a man named Ward went to her assistance and succeeded in getting her into the bast. She was conveyed to the Workhouse in a critical state.--Yesterday morning the woman was brought before the borough magistrates and charged with attempt- ing to commit suicide.—Mr Calmer stated that he saw the prisoner walking upon the Lancashire side of the river on the morning in question. It was raining heavily at the time, and witness thought it strange to see her walking there. 'Prisoner turned round three or four times, apparently to see if any one was watching her, and then', having un- fastened her shawl, she sat down on the river bank. and "worked " herself into the water with her hands. When her legs were immersed she raised herself into the water, Witness sent two men named Ward and Coyne to her assist- ance with a boat and sent for a constable. The woman was rescued and taken to the police station. There was net great depth of water in the river —Mr Hunt (Chief Cow stable) said that the prisoner called herself a factory hand. She had met with some trouble of late, and came to War- rington. Having no means of subsistence and being tired of life, she walked into the river. She had been in the Workhouse since the occurrence.—Prisoner now said that she was very sorry for what she had done. At the time she committed the act she had had nothing to eat for two days. She was trying to get to Liverpool, where, she thought, she maid earn her living by washing ani doily, other work, in eating houses.—rhe Bench ordered the poor woman ,to be handed over to the Workhouse authorities.

He afterwards saw him ask assistance from some gentleman, to whom he said that he had been a wild ma. for some years, and bad now reformed.—Mr Pairclough You say he appeared drunk; was he drunk or only shamming drunkenness 7—Witness : He seemed to be very excited, he was either drunk or mad.—Prisoner : Is the man mad , this morning 7—Mr Fairclough : He acted like a drunken man? Yes.—Prisoner said that the police had ruined his character, bat he was not afraid of them. He could look the magistrates in the face with a clear conscience. They must telegraph to Walton and Kirkdale for his character— (laughter)—and, with the help of God, he would stand there till the character came.—The Mayor : You are talk- ing nonsense.—Prisoner : lam not talking nonsense, sir, I have been before many a dozen more than you. Ido not fear the magistrates of Warrington.—The Mayor : You are either mad or ahammin.g.—Prisoner : I am neither. I have worked for the devil 40 years, and I have been three Gr four days a Christian—l am not a maniac—He was final 5i and costs, or seven days, and refacing to pay, was re- moved in custody.

Iwas summoned for riding on the shafts of his lorry with- out reins at Knowsley on the 4th August and was tined 7s 61 and costs.—Samuel Smith was fined 74 6d and costs for , obstructing the highway st Roby by leaving his horse and cart thereon on the 11th inst. LODGING-lIOUSE KEEPERS IN TROUBLE.—Thomas Clarke, a lodging-house keeper. in High-street, Prescot, was sum- moned for a contravention of the by-laws by not having the floors of his lodging-house washed sod the walls lime- washed during the month of July.—Superintendent Barker remarked that according to the by-laws every lodging-house keeper was required to have his rooms washed and cleaned every year in the month of July, but the defendant had not complied in that respect.—The defendant was fined 53 and costs.--A like penalty was imposed on Matthew Carney, another lodging-house keeper, fora similar offence. _ -- ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. FRlDLY.—Before Alderman Mcßryde and Mr. A Sinclair.
